lessons.plain: Google Cloud gives you three main ways to run application code. Compute Engine rents you virtual machines, which are computers in a Google data centre that you set up and maintain yourself, including the operating system. Google Kubernetes Engine, called GKE, runs your packaged containers on a managed Kubernetes cluster, a system that schedules containers across many machines and restarts them when they fail. Cloud Run takes a container and runs it only when web requests or events arrive, while Google handles the servers underneath. Choosing between them is mostly about how much of the machine you want to manage and how your application is packaged and triggered.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has a small web API packaged as a container. Traffic arrives only during business hours, and nobody on the team wants to patch servers. Before reading further, which of the three options would you guess fits best, and what single fact about the app would change your answer?
lessons.teach: Start by asking who runs what. Compute Engine is infrastructure as a service: you pick the machine size and operating system, and you patch and secure it. A managed instance group can add or remove identical virtual machines, but you still own each machine's operating system. GKE is a managed Kubernetes cluster. Kubernetes is an orchestrator: you describe the desired state in configuration files, and it keeps containers running, restarts failed ones, and places them on nodes, which are the machines in the cluster. Google runs the control plane, the part that makes scheduling decisions, but you still design and manage the workloads. Cloud Run is a serverless container platform: you deploy a container image, and it starts instances in response to incoming HTTP requests or events, scaling down to zero when idle. You do not manage nodes or Kubernetes objects. Why this matters: the more the platform manages for you, the less control you have over the machine. Pick the least-managed option that still meets the requirement. Worked example: a small team runs a stateless JSON API with bursty traffic, needs no custom kernel modules, and has no Kubernetes experience. Step 1: the app is already a container. Step 2: it serves HTTP requests. Step 3: traffic drops to nothing overnight. Step 4: Cloud Run fits, because it scales to zero and charges for use. GKE would also run it, but would add a cluster to operate. Compute Engine would leave the team patching an operating system. Common mistake: choosing GKE because it sounds most powerful, even when the team only needs a web service. That adds operational work with no requirement behind it. Consequence: if a workload must run continuously outside any request, or needs full control of the operating system, Cloud Run's request-driven model works against it, and GKE or Compute Engine becomes the correct choice.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm packages a sensor-reading service as a container. The service opens a connection to 40 temperature sensors and reads each one every second in an endless loop. It never waits for an incoming web request. Work through the choice. Step 1: the service is already a container image. Step 2: it runs a continuous loop with no incoming requests to answer. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: so the platform must be GKE or Compute Engine, not Cloud Run.
choices: Confirm that the workload must keep running outside any request, which Cloud Run's request-driven model cannot provide.
Note that Cloud Run scales to zero, so an endless loop will cost less on it and no further check is needed.
Check whether the loop needs full control of the operating system, which settles the choice without looking at request timing.
Count how many nodes a cluster would need for 40 sensors before deciding, since that decides the platform.
questions.why: Cloud Run starts instances in response to requests or events, so a workload that must run continuously outside any request is the case where it is the wrong fit.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines GKE in the terms used by the teaching text?
choices: A managed Kubernetes cluster in which Google runs the control plane while you still design and manage the workloads on the nodes.
A managed instance group that adds and removes identical virtual machines while you own each machine's operating system.
A virtual machine service in which you choose the machine size and operating system and patch the operating system yourself.
A serverless platform that starts a container only when an HTTP request arrives and charges per request.
questions.why: The teaching text defines GKE as a managed Kubernetes cluster where Google runs the control plane but you still design and manage the workloads.

questions.prompt: A four-person team runs a service that generates thumbnails when a user uploads an image through a web form. The service is packaged as a container, needs no custom kernel modules, and the team has no Kubernetes experience. Which platform is the least-managed option that still meets the requirement?
choices: Compute Engine, with the team patching the operating system on each virtual machine.
Cloud Run, because it runs containers in response to HTTP requests and does not require the team to manage nodes or Kubernetes objects.
Compute Engine with a managed instance group, so the machines scale while the team keeps owning each operating system.
GKE, with a new cluster the team must operate for a service that handles one request type.
questions.why: Cloud Run is the least-managed option that fits because the container is triggered by HTTP requests and the team needs no node or Kubernetes management.

questions.prompt: A team picks GKE for a single stateless web service with occasional traffic, reasoning that it is the most powerful option. What is the main problem with this choice?
choices: GKE forces the team to write its own operating system kernel before any container can be deployed.
It adds cluster operation work that the web service's requirements do not call for, so the choice adds work with no requirement behind it.
GKE cannot run stateless containers, so the service will fail to start on the cluster.
GKE charges for every idle minute, which makes it impossible for a service with occasional traffic to stay within budget.
questions.why: Choosing GKE for a simple web service adds Kubernetes operation work with no requirement behind it, which the teaching text names as the common mistake.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Compute Engine, GKE, and Cloud Run for a new service. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking how much of the machine the team wants to manage and how the service is triggered. If it is a containerized web or event-driven service with variable traffic, Cloud Run is my first choice, because it scales to zero and removes node management. The tradeoff is that Cloud Run is built around requests and short-lived instances, so a workload that must run continuously in the background, or that needs control over the operating system, does not fit well. GKE is the option I would not pick first for a simple service. It gives full Kubernetes control and suits many interacting services, but the team then owns cluster configuration, upgrades and scheduling decisions. Compute Engine is for cases needing a specific operating system, kernel tuning or legacy software that cannot be containerized. The cost is that you patch and secure every machine yourself.
rubricPoints: Cloud Run is serverless and scales to zero, suiting request-driven containers.
GKE is managed Kubernetes, adding cluster operations in exchange for orchestration power.
Compute Engine gives full operating system control but leaves patching and scaling to the team.
Each option has a limit: request-driven model for Cloud Run, operational overhead for GKE, management burden for Compute Engine.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a platform is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario with several plausible near-miss options, and no listed mission covers this decision directly.

lessons.plain: A container is a way of packing an application together with everything it needs to run, so it behaves the same wherever it is started. Think of a sealed lunchbox that holds the whole meal, not just the recipe. Developers build this package from a set of written instructions, store it in a shared library of packages, and then ask a cloud platform to run it. Cloud Run is a service that runs these packages for you without you managing servers. GKE, short for Google Kubernetes Engine, is a managed cluster of machines that keeps many copies of your packaged application running and replaces any that fail. Choosing between them depends on how much control you need over the machines.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your application works on your laptop but fails on a cloud server with a different operating system version, what single change would most reliably make the two environments behave the same?
lessons.teach:
A container image is a read-only package that holds an application and its dependencies, such as its language runtime and libraries. You describe how to build an image in a text file called a Dockerfile, which names a starting base image, copies in your code, installs dependencies, and states the start command. Building the Dockerfile produces an image, which you tag with a version label and push to a registry, a managed store of images. Google's registry service is Artifact Registry.

Cloud Run accepts an image and runs it as a stateless HTTP service. Each deployment creates a revision, and the platform scales instances up and down with traffic, including to zero. GKE runs containers inside pods, the smallest unit a cluster schedules, and a Deployment object declares how many pod copies should exist. The cluster continuously works to match that declared state.

Worked example: a Python API. First, the Dockerfile starts from a slim Python base, installs requirements, copies the code, and starts the server on the port given by the PORT environment variable. Second, you build the image and tag it version 1.4.2. Third, you push it to Artifact Registry. Fourth, you deploy that exact tag to Cloud Run, which creates a revision and sends it traffic. For GKE, a Deployment referencing the same tag asks the cluster for three pods.

Common mistake: hard-coding a port, or deploying the tag latest. A service that listens on a fixed port other than PORT fails the platform's health check, so the revision never receives traffic. A latest tag makes it impossible to tell which build is running during an incident.

The consequence is that a versioned, immutable image is what makes rollback possible: you redeploy the previous tag rather than rebuilding from source under pressure.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's ticketing team has a Go service that reads the PORT environment variable and listens on it. Their Dockerfile builds a static binary, and the image is tagged 2.3.0. Their steps are: (1) build the image locally and tag it ticket-api:2.3.0; (2) push it to the Artifact Registry repository named tickets in europe-west1; (3) this step is missing and must be filled in: deploy the pushed image to Cloud Run using the exact tag 2.3.0, which creates a new revision; (4) confirm the new revision is receiving traffic. Which choice correctly fills in the missing step 3?
choices: Set the service's port to 8080 in the Dockerfile before pushing
Rename the image to latest and redeploy it to Cloud Run so the newest build is used
Rebuild the Go binary on the Cloud Run host from the source repository
Deploy the exact 2.3.0 tag to Cloud Run, creating a revision
questions.why: Deploying the pinned, immutable tag to Cloud Run creates a revision from that exact image, which is the step that makes the build traceable and rollback-ready.

questions.prompt: In Cloud Run, what does a single deployment create, and what is that object's role?
choices: A new pod inside a Deployment that holds three copies of the container
A revision, a fixed version of the service that the platform can send traffic to
A registry entry that replaces the image tag with a digest
A cluster node that hosts the container image permanently
questions.why: Each Cloud Run deployment creates a revision, and the platform routes traffic to revisions rather than to a loose collection of containers.

questions.prompt: A payments startup's container hard-codes port 9000, but the platform starts it with the PORT environment variable set to 8080. What is the likely result after deployment?
choices: The health check fails, so the new revision never receives traffic
Traffic is split evenly between port 9000 and port 8080 with no errors
The image is rejected by Artifact Registry before it can be deployed
The platform rewrites the Dockerfile and the service listens on 9000 automatically
questions.why: A service listening on a fixed port other than PORT fails the platform's health check, and a revision that fails that check does not receive traffic.

questions.prompt: A GKE Deployment declares six pod replicas of image tag 5.0.1. One pod crashes overnight. What does the cluster do next?
choices: It keeps running five pods permanently and updates the declared count to five
It rebuilds the image from source and tags it 5.0.2 automatically
It waits for an engineer to approve a new deployment before doing anything
It works to bring the running pods back to the declared six by creating a replacement
questions.why: A Deployment declares the desired number of pods, and the cluster continuously works to match that declared state, so it replaces the missing pod.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a container image is, how it gets from your code to Cloud Run or GKE, and name one limit or tradeoff of choosing Cloud Run over GKE for a service.
lessons.modelAnswer: A container image is a packaged, read-only copy of the application plus its runtime and libraries, built from a Dockerfile. We build it, tag it with a specific version, and push it to Artifact Registry. Cloud Run then runs that exact image as a revision that scales with requests, including to zero. GKE runs the same image inside pods that a Deployment keeps at a declared count. The tradeoff: Cloud Run gives less control over the machines and the networking and cluster-level behaviour, so a service needing custom node configuration, many long-running background processes, or fine-grained cluster policies is better on GKE, which brings more operational work in exchange.
rubricPoints: A container image is a immutable package built from a Dockerfile and pushed to a registry.
Cloud Run runs an image as a managed, request-driven service with revisions and scaling to zero.
GKE runs images inside pods that a Deployment keeps at a declared count, adding cluster operations work.
A stated tradeoff: Cloud Run gives less control over infrastructure, while GKE gives more control and more to operate.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine makes the learner build and deploy a container to Cloud Run or GKE, so the product steps are best read and reasoned about.

lessons.plain: Cloud providers run their equipment in buildings spread across the world. Each location belongs to a region, a broad area such as a country or part of a continent, and each region contains several zones, which are separate failure units inside that area. Some services live in a single zone, some span a whole region, and a few are spread across several regions. Where a service lives affects how quickly it answers your users, how well it survives a power cut or a building fault, and whether your data may sit in a particular country. Knowing these three shapes lets you choose a design that is fast and resilient enough without paying for more than you need.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose your web app runs on one virtual machine in one zone, and that zone loses power for two hours. Before reading further, what do you think happens to the app, and what would you change so users barely notice?
lessons.teach:
A region is a geographic area that holds several zones. A zone is an isolated place within a region with its own power and cooling, so a fault in one zone is meant to stay there. Latency is the time a request takes to travel to a server and for the reply to come back. Light in fibre takes time to cross distance, so a round trip grows with how far apart the two ends are. Within one continent a round trip is typically tens of milliseconds; across an ocean it can approach a hundred milliseconds or more.

A zonal resource, such as a single virtual machine or a disk attached to one zone, exists in only one zone. A regional resource is spread across several zones in one region, so losing one zone does not stop it. Some services are multi-regional or global, replicated across regions, which helps availability but may add latency for writes and may restrict where data is stored.

Worked example. Your API runs in region A and its database runs in region B, and each user request makes 20 sequential database queries. If one round trip takes 80 ms, the queries alone cost 1.6 seconds. Step one: note the cross-region hop. Step two: multiply by the query count. Step three: move the database into region A, where a round trip might take 1 ms, and the same work costs 20 ms.

Common mistake: assuming a service is resilient because it is in the cloud, when a single-zone resource still fails with its zone. Consequence: in a running system, a zonal outage can take down every instance placed only in that zone, while a regional design keeps serving traffic from the surviving zones.

questions.prompt: A mobile backend runs in the europe-west region and serves users there. For each app screen, it makes 12 sequential calls to a feature-flag service (a service that tells the app which features are switched on) hosted in asia-east. Each round trip, meaning the time for a request to reach the server and the reply to return, takes 150 ms. Step one: the calls cross from europe-west to asia-east, so the hop is cross-region. Step two: 12 calls multiplied by 150 ms gives 1800 ms per screen. Step three, which is missing: the team moves the feature-flag service into europe-west, where a round trip takes about 3 ms, and the calls are still made one after another. What is the total time per screen after step three?
choices: 36 ms
3 ms
150 ms
questions.why: Twelve sequential calls at 3 ms each is 36 ms, because the regional move changes the per-call round trip while the number of calls stays the same.

questions.prompt: A payments team runs its message queue on one virtual machine placed in a single zone. A zone outage occurs in that zone. What is the most accurate description of what happens to the queue?
choices: It keeps running only if the team's latency to the zone is under 10 ms.
It fails over automatically to another region without any configuration.
It keeps running because cloud virtual machines are isolated from zone faults by default.
It becomes unavailable, because a zonal resource exists in only one zone and fails with it.
questions.why: A zonal resource exists in only one zone, so when that zone fails the resource fails with it, unless the design spreads capacity across zones.

questions.prompt: A reporting service in region north-1 needs to read from a database in region south-1. It currently makes 40 sequential reads, each with a 30 ms round trip. Which change would cut the total waiting time the most, while keeping the database where it is?
choices: Add a larger disk to the reporting service's virtual machine.
Combine the 40 reads into a single request so only one round trip is paid.
Increase the size of the reporting service's virtual machine.
Rename the database so the request routing changes.
questions.why: Latency is the round-trip time multiplied by the number of sequential requests, so reducing the number of trips to one removes most of the waiting time.

questions.prompt: A healthcare startup must keep patient records stored inside one country and needs fast write times from its clinics there. A teammate proposes a global multi-regional storage service because it is highly available. What is the main risk of that proposal?
choices: Replication across regions improves availability but can add write latency and may not respect where data must be stored.
Global services remove the need for any backups.
Multi-regional services always have lower latency than single-region services.
Global services cannot store any data at all.
questions.why: Multi-regional or global services replicate across regions, which helps availability but can slow writes and may conflict with data-location rules, so the trade-off must be checked against the requirement.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is placing a new API and its database: what is the difference between a zonal resource and a regional resource, and what limit or tradeoff should they weigh when putting the API and the database in different regions?
lessons.modelAnswer: A zonal resource lives in one zone, so if that zone has an outage the resource is unavailable. A regional resource is spread across several zones in one region, so a single zone failure usually leaves it running. Placing the API and database in different regions adds a network round trip to every database call, so latency grows with each query the API makes, and a request that makes many sequential calls can become slow for users. The tradeoff is that a second region can help with disaster recovery or with serving users in another area, but it costs speed and often adds data-transfer charges. For most designs I would keep the API and its database in the same region, use regional resources for availability inside that region, and only split regions when a clear requirement, such as data residency or disaster recovery, justifies the extra latency.
rubricPoints: Defines a zonal resource as living in one zone and failing with that zone
Defines a regional resource as spread across zones in one region and surviving a single zone failure
Explains that cross-region calls add round-trip latency that multiplies with the number of calls
Names a tradeoff such as disaster recovery or data residency against speed and cost

suggested.rationale: Where services live and which are zonal, regional or multi-regional is factual catalogue knowledge best learned by reading the product documentation alongside this lesson.

lessons.plain: A load balancer is a front door that receives requests from users and passes each one to one of several copies of your application, so no single copy gets overwhelmed and one failed copy does not take the service down. Think of a host at a busy restaurant who seats each arriving group at a table with room and skips tables that are closed. Google Cloud offers several kinds of load balancer, and the right one depends on three questions: does the traffic come from the internet or only from inside your private network, does the balancer need to read the web request itself (its address, path, or headers) or only the raw connection, and do the copies live in one region or several.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web app runs on three identical servers. If you want users anywhere in the world to reach it through one address and to keep working when one server crashes, what would you put in front of the servers, and what would you need to know about each request to send it to the right place?
lessons.teach: A load balancer is a managed component that owns a single entry address and forwards each incoming connection or request to one healthy backend, which is a copy of your service. A health check is a periodic probe the balancer sends to each backend; a backend that fails its probes stops receiving traffic. Two layers matter. A layer 4 balancer works on the network connection: it sees IP addresses and ports and forwards packets without reading the web request. A layer 7 balancer terminates the HTTP or HTTPS request, so it can read the host name, URL path and headers, and route different paths to different backend groups. Google Cloud's main choices follow from the requirement. For a public website or API serving users worldwide through one anycast IP address, with routing by URL path and TLS handled at the edge, the global external Application Load Balancer fits; it is layer 7 and can send traffic to Cloud Run, GKE or Compute Engine groups in several regions. If users are in one region only, a regional external Application Load Balancer is the cheaper near-miss that keeps traffic in that region. For private traffic between services inside your VPC, an internal Application Load Balancer is layer 7 and reachable only from inside. A network (layer 4) load balancer passes raw TCP or UDP traffic without reading it, which suits non-HTTP protocols or cases where the client source address must reach the backend unchanged. Worked example: a request for https://shop.example/cart arrives at the global anycast address. The nearest Google edge terminates TLS, the URL map sees the path /cart and forwards to the backend service for the cart group, and health checks confirm which instances are up. If the cart group in one region fails its checks, traffic moves to another region. Common mistake: choosing a layer 4 balancer when you need path-based routing, which it cannot do because it never reads the HTTP request. Consequence: a balancer that routes only to healthy backends is what lets a crash or a deploy stay invisible to users; if health checks are wrong, traffic keeps flowing to dead copies. The choice is decided by where clients are, whether routing needs the HTTP request, and whether the service is internal or public.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has all of its customers in Germany and runs one public tracking API under one hostname. It must send /parcels requests to one service group and /labels requests to another. Its reasoning so far: Step 1. Path-based routing needs the HTTP request to be read, so a layer 4 balancer is ruled out and a layer 7 balancer is needed. Step 2. All customers are in one region, so a regional external Application Load Balancer is the right layer 7 choice rather than the global one. Step 3. A warehouse service inside the company's VPC calls the labels group and must not be reachable from the internet. Which balancer should the warehouse service use, and why?
choices: A regional external Application Load Balancer, because it is the cheaper choice for a single region
A network load balancer, because internal calls need no HTTP routing
An internal Application Load Balancer, because it is layer 7 and reachable only from inside the VPC
A global external Application Load Balancer, because it gives internal callers one anycast address
questions.why: An internal Application Load Balancer is layer 7, so it can route by path, and it is reachable only from inside the VPC, which matches the private requirement.

questions.prompt: A small team runs three copies of its API in one region behind a balancer. One copy starts failing its health checks while the other two pass. What does the balancer do?
choices: It deletes the failing copy from the project automatically.
It stops all traffic to all three copies until the failing one is repaired.
It keeps sending one third of requests to the failing copy so that it can recover on its own.
It stops sending new traffic to the failing copy and keeps the two passing copies serving.
questions.why: A backend that fails its health probes stops receiving traffic, while healthy backends keep serving, which is why a single failing copy stays invisible to users.

questions.prompt: A team puts a network (layer 4) balancer in front of a web app and wants requests for /api to go to a different group than requests for /static. Why will this design fail?
choices: It routes by path but cannot read the request headers, so the path is never visible to it.
Network balancers can route by path only when TLS is switched off, because encryption hides the path from them.
It forwards packets without reading the HTTP request, so it cannot see the URL path to route on.
It can route by path, but only to Compute Engine instance groups and not to other backend types.
questions.why: A layer 4 balancer sees only IP addresses and ports and never reads the HTTP request, so it cannot tell /api from /static; path routing needs a layer 7 balancer.

questions.prompt: A team runs a game server that uses raw UDP and needs each player's original source address to reach the server unchanged. Which balancer fits this requirement?
choices: A network (layer 4) balancer, since it forwards raw TCP or UDP traffic without reading it.
A global external Application Load Balancer, since anycast accepts any protocol.
An internal Application Load Balancer, since UDP traffic is always private.
A regional external Application Load Balancer, since it preserves UDP traffic end to end.
questions.why: A network (layer 4) balancer passes raw TCP or UDP without reading it, which suits non-HTTP protocols and cases where the client source address must reach the backend unchanged.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would pick between a global external Application Load Balancer and a regional passthrough network load balancer for a new service, and name one limit or tradeoff of the option you pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with where the clients are and what the traffic looks like. If the service is a public HTTP API used worldwide, I would choose the global external Application Load Balancer, because it gives one anycast address, reads the request so I can route by path or host, and can send traffic to backends in several regions. The tradeoff is that it is layer 7, so it terminates the HTTP request, adds some processing per request, and requires me to configure the URL map, backend services and health checks. If instead the traffic is raw TCP from a client that needs the original source IP, or the service is only needed in one region, a regional passthrough network load balancer is simpler and usually cheaper. Its limit is that it cannot route on paths or headers, and the backends receive the traffic directly, so TLS termination and routing decisions must be handled inside the application.
rubricPoints: Layer 4 balancers forward connections without reading HTTP; layer 7 balancers read host, path and headers.
Global versus regional scope is decided by where the users are and whether one address must serve several regions.
Internal balancers serve only traffic from inside the private network, while external ones face the internet.
Each choice has a tradeoff, such as extra per-request processing for layer 7 or lack of path routing for layer 4.

suggested.rationale: Choosing among load balancer types against a stated requirement is an exam-style reasoning task that benefits from scenarios more than memorised facts.

lessons.plain: Session affinity is a setting that tells a traffic router to send repeated requests from the same visitor to the same server, whenever it can. Think of a coffee shop where the same barista keeps serving you, so they already know your order. For content delivery, this can keep useful data warm on one machine and make responses faster. It is a convenience, not a guarantee, and it has costs when that one server is busy or goes away.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web app runs on three identical servers behind one traffic router. Each server keeps a small cache of recently fetched pages in its own memory. If the router sends every request from one visitor to the same server, what do you expect to happen to that visitor's page load times over several visits, and what might go wrong for the other servers?
lessons.teach: Session affinity (also called sticky sessions) is a load balancer setting that makes repeated requests from the same client land on the same backend. A backend is one of the identical server instances behind a load balancer, which is a component that spreads incoming traffic across them. Without affinity, the balancer picks a backend for each request on its own, often in rotation, so consecutive requests from one visitor may hit different machines. Affinity works by deriving a key from the request, such as the client IP address, a cookie the balancer sets, or a header value, and always mapping that key to the same backend. That mapping holds only while the backend passes its health checks, which are periodic probes that decide whether a backend should receive traffic. Why it helps performance: a backend that has already served a visitor holds warm in-memory caches, open connections and loaded state for that visitor, so later requests skip work. Worked example: three backends B1, B2 and B3 with client IP affinity. Visitor 203.0.113.7 maps to B2. Step 1: the first request goes to B2, which builds the page and caches it. Step 2: the second request from the same IP maps to B2 again and is served from cache. Step 3: B2 fails its health check and is removed from rotation. Step 4: the third request maps to B1, which has no cached copy, so it rebuilds the page. Common mistake: treating affinity as a reliability feature. It does not keep a visitor's session alive when its backend dies, and it can overload one backend when many users share one IP address behind a corporate or mobile network address translator, because all of them map to the same machine. Consequence: a hot backend slows every visitor mapped to it while other backends sit idle. Session affinity trades even load and simple failover for locality, so it is worth enabling only when the speed gained from warm, per-visitor data outweighs the imbalance it creates.

questions.prompt: A ticketing site runs four identical backends, E1 through E4, behind a load balancer set to cookie-based session affinity. The balancer sets a cookie that names the backend a visitor is mapped to. A visitor's browser sends the cookie value 'ck-72', which maps to E3. Step 1: The request carrying 'ck-72' goes to E3, which already holds the visitor's seat map in memory, so it answers from that warm copy. Step 2: E3 fails its health check and is removed from rotation. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: The visitor's next request is answered by E2, which has no seat map loaded, so E2 rebuilds it from the database before responding.
choices: The balancer keeps sending the visitor's requests to E3 because the cookie still names it, and E3 serves them from its warm copy once it recovers.
The balancer maps the visitor's cookie to a healthy backend, E2, which has no warm data for this visitor, so the visitor's next request goes there.
The seat map is copied from E3's memory into a shared store, and the balancer then holds the visitor's requests until E3 passes its health check again.
The balancer rejects the visitor's request with an error until E3 is back in rotation, so no backend has to rebuild anything.
questions.why: When the mapped backend fails its health check, affinity can no longer hold, so the balancer sends the visitor to a healthy backend, which lacks the warm per-visitor data, and that is why step 4 has to rebuild it.

questions.prompt: A regional news website uses five identical backends with client IP affinity turned on. Which statement best describes what affinity guarantees?
choices: Repeated requests from the same derived key, such as a client IP, are sent to the same backend as long as that backend is healthy.
Requests from any visitor are always answered from a cache shared by all five backends.
Every backend receives an equal share of traffic, because affinity spreads requests evenly across all five machines.
A visitor's session survives even if the backend it was mapped to crashes, because the balancer copies the session to another machine.
questions.why: Affinity maps a key derived from the request to one backend and holds that mapping only while the backend passes health checks, which is exactly the third option; the others describe failover, even load, or shared caching that affinity does not provide.

questions.prompt: A company's internal tool sits behind two backends with client IP affinity. About 300 employees reach it through one corporate network address translator, so every request appears to come from the same IP address. What is the most likely result?
choices: Each employee's session is protected from failure, because the translator keeps sessions alive.
Nearly all requests map to one backend, which becomes overloaded while the other sits mostly idle.
Both backends share the load evenly because the translator rotates the source address.
The balancer ignores affinity for internal traffic, so the load is spread across both backends.
questions.why: Because the shared IP is the affinity key, all those users map to the same backend, creating a hot spot; the other options wrongly assume balancing, protection, or ignored affinity.

questions.prompt: A team runs a stateless JSON API where every request carries all the data it needs and no visitor-specific state is kept on the server. Should they enable session affinity to improve performance, and why?
choices: No, because affinity only helps when warm per-visitor data is reused, and here it adds load imbalance without a real speed gain.
No, because affinity removes the health checks, which makes stateless APIs slower to recover.
Yes, because affinity keeps each visitor's requests on one backend, which always makes stateless requests faster.
Yes, because affinity is the setting that makes a load balancer health-check its backends.
questions.why: Affinity's performance benefit comes from reusing warm, per-visitor data, which a stateless API does not have, so the imbalance it creates is not justified; the other options misstate what affinity does.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what session affinity is, when turning it on helps content delivery, and one limit or tradeoff they should weigh before enabling it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Session affinity makes a load balancer send repeated requests from the same client to the same backend, usually keyed on client IP, a cookie, or a header. It helps content delivery when each backend keeps useful per-visitor data in memory, such as a warm cache or open connections, so later requests are faster. The limits are that it is not a guarantee: if that backend fails its health checks, the client moves to another backend and loses its warm state. It can also cause uneven load, since many users behind one shared IP all land on one machine. Before enabling it, I would check that the speed gain is real and that the app does not need that state to survive failover. If it does, that state belongs in shared storage instead.
rubricPoints: Defines session affinity as routing repeated requests from one client to the same backend.
Names a key used for affinity, such as client IP, cookie, or header.
Explains the performance gain through warm per-visitor state such as caches or connections.
States the limit: affinity breaks when the backend is unhealthy or removed, so it is not failover.
Notes the tradeoff of uneven load when many clients share one source address.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning about when affinity helps and what it costs, which is best checked by explaining it back.

lessons.plain: A cache is a small, fast copy of an answer you would otherwise have to work out or fetch again. Think of a sticky note on your desk with a phone number you call every day, instead of looking it up in the big directory each time. Applications use caches to take repeated load off a slower database or a remote service. Memorystore is Google Cloud's managed service that runs an in-memory cache for you, so you do not install, patch, or replace the cache server yourself. It keeps data in memory, which is very fast, and it trades a bit of freshness for speed.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a product page is read ten thousand times a minute but its details change only once an hour, what would you keep in a fast copy, and how old a copy would you accept?
lessons.teach:
A cache is a fast, temporary copy of data that is slower to fetch from its source of truth, such as a database. Memorystore is Google Cloud's managed in-memory cache: Google runs the cache servers, and your application connects to them over a private network address inside your virtual network. It offers two engines, Redis and Memcached. Both keep data in RAM, so reads are very quick, but RAM is limited and the contents are not a permanent record.

The mechanism is simple. The application first asks the cache for a key, which is the name of a stored item. A cache hit means the item is present and returns at once. A cache miss means it is absent, so the application reads the database, returns the answer, and writes a copy to the cache with a time to live, or TTL, which is how long the entry may live before it expires. When memory fills, the cache evicts entries, meaning it removes some to make room, usually the least recently used ones.

Worked example: the positions API serves a vehicle's location, which the database updates every few seconds. The app stores the key vehicle:42 with a TTL of 5 seconds. A request at 09:00:00 misses, reads the database, and stores the result. Requests at 09:00:01 and 09:00:03 hit. At 09:00:06 the entry has expired, so the next request misses and refreshes it. Database reads drop by roughly the number of requests that hit.

Common mistake: treating the cache as the source of truth, so a write goes only to the cache and is lost on restart or eviction. Another is giving every key the same TTL, so thousands expire together and a flood of misses hits the database at once.

Consequence: a cache that is empty after a restart or deploy sends all traffic to the database. Design so the cache can always be rebuilt from the database.

questions.prompt: A product-details service keeps prices in Memorystore for Redis under the key product:907. The price lives in a database, and the service uses a 30-second TTL. Trace the lookup at 10:00:00. The app asks the cache for product:907 and gets a miss. The app then reads the current price from the database and returns it to the shopper. Missing step: the app ___. At 10:00:12 another shopper asks for product:907 and gets a hit, so the database is not read.
choices: writes the price to the cache with no TTL so the entry never expires
writes the price back to the cache under product:907 with a 30-second TTL
skips the cache write because a miss means the cache has failed
sends the price to the database so the database can refresh the cache
questions.why: After a miss, the app stores a copy in the cache with a TTL, which is what makes the 10:00:12 request a hit.

questions.prompt: A reporting team keeps the only copy of its daily sales totals in Memorystore for Redis to avoid paying for a database. Which statement best describes the main risk?
choices: Memorystore requires a separate backup job before any key can be written.
The totals will be automatically copied to the database every hour by the cache.
Redis cannot store numbers, so the totals will be rounded on every read.
Memorystore keeps data in limited RAM and is not a permanent record, so the totals can be lost on restart or eviction.
questions.why: A cache is a temporary copy held in RAM, so a restart or eviction can erase data that exists nowhere else.

questions.prompt: A ticketing service loads 2,000 seat-map keys into its cache at 08:00 during a deploy. Every key is given a TTL of 600 seconds. What is the most likely problem at about 08:10?
choices: Most keys expire together, so many requests miss at once and flood the database.
The keys become permanent because they were written in the same second.
Each key expires at a different time, so the database sees a smooth, even load.
The cache will refuse new keys until the deploy is rolled back.
questions.why: Identical TTLs on keys written together make them expire together, causing a burst of simultaneous misses that all reach the database.

questions.prompt: A Memorystore cache is full and the application needs to write a new key. By default, which existing entry is usually evicted to make room?
choices: The most recently written entry, because it is the newest.
The least recently used entry.
The entry with the longest key name.
The entry whose TTL is closest to expiring.
questions.why: The teaching text says eviction usually removes the least recently used entries to make room for new ones.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only used a database what Memorystore does, why its contents can disappear, and the main tradeoff you accept when you add a cache with a TTL.
lessons.modelAnswer: Memorystore is a managed in-memory cache, so Google runs the servers and we reach them over a private address in our network. The app checks the cache first. On a hit it returns the stored value immediately. On a miss it reads the database and stores the result with a TTL, which is how long the copy may live. The contents live in RAM, so a restart, a failover, or eviction under memory pressure can remove them, which means the database must stay the source of truth. The tradeoff is freshness against load: a longer TTL cuts database reads but lets users see older data, and a short TTL keeps data fresh but sends more traffic to the database. We also have to stagger TTLs, or the cache can empty at once and flood the database.
rubricPoints: Describes a cache hit and a cache miss and what the app does on each
Explains that the cache is in memory and can lose data, so the database remains the source of truth
Names TTL and the tradeoff between data freshness and database load
Notes the risk of many keys expiring together or an empty cache after restart

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner diagnose a slow API caused by a cold cache after a deploy, which is the core caching idea behind Memorystore.

lessons.plain: An API is a set of agreed doors that one program uses to ask another program for something. When you build and deploy one, you decide how callers knock and what they get back. REST is the most common style: it treats things in your system as resources with web addresses, and callers use standard web verbs such as GET to read and POST to create. gRPC is a newer style built for speed between services: callers invoke named functions as if they were local, and messages travel in a compact binary format. Both let programs talk. They differ in how easy they are for outside callers to read, how fast they are, and how much shared tooling they need. Choosing well starts with knowing who the callers are.
lessons.guessPrompt: A mobile app needs to fetch one vehicle's latest position on demand, and a dispatch screen needs a live feed of position updates every second. Which style would you lean toward for each need, and what would you check before deciding?
lessons.teach:
A REST API models things in your system as resources, each with its own address (a URL path such as /vehicles/7/position). Callers use standard HTTP methods on those addresses: GET reads, POST creates, PUT or PATCH changes, and DELETE removes. Every response carries a status code, a three-digit number where 200 means success, 404 means not found, and 500 means the server failed. Data usually travels as JSON, a plain text format for key-value data. REST runs over ordinary HTTP, so browsers, scripts and command-line tools can all call it and inspect it by hand.

gRPC is a remote procedure call framework: the caller invokes a named method on a remote service as if it were local. The contract lives in a Protocol Buffers file, a schema that names each message, its fields and their types. Both sides generate client code from that file. Messages are sent as compact binary over HTTP/2, a newer transport that allows many concurrent calls on one connection and streaming in either direction.

Why it works: the schema or the resource map is the contract. A REST client needs only the URL and the verb. A gRPC client needs generated code that matches the schema.

Worked example: GET /vehicles/7/position. Step 1: the client sends the request with the path. Step 2: the service looks up vehicle 7. Step 3: it returns 200 and a JSON body with latitude, longitude and timestamp. Step 4: if vehicle 7 does not exist, it returns 404, so the caller can tell 'not found' apart from a server fault. The gRPC version is a GetPosition method whose request message holds the vehicle id.

Common mistake: returning 200 with an error inside the body. Monitoring, retries and caches then treat failures as successes. Another mistake is changing a field number or type in a .proto file, which silently breaks existing clients.

Consequence: REST responses can be cached and scaled with standard web tools. Long-lived gRPC connections can pile traffic onto a few instances unless the load balancer spreads individual requests rather than whole connections.

questions.prompt: A bike-share app lets a maintenance tool update one dock. The dock is a resource at /docks/9/status, and the tool sends PUT with a JSON body saying the dock is now out of service. Step 1: the tool sends the PUT request with the path and the new status in the body. Step 2: the service checks the body is valid and saves the new status for dock 9. Step 3: the service sends its response to the tool. What should step 3 contain?
choices: A 404 status, because the tool asked to change a dock that already existed, so the request must be treated as not found
A 500 status, because the server stores data and any write is a sign that the server has failed
A 200 status with a body reading error: dock locked, so the app can show the message to the mechanic
A 200 status with the updated dock as JSON, so the tool can confirm the change succeeded
questions.why: A successful update returns 200 with the new state, which tells the caller the change was made, while the other choices either misuse status codes or hide a failure inside a success response.

questions.prompt: In a REST API, what does it mean for something to be modelled as a resource?
choices: It is a streaming connection kept open over HTTP/2 so many calls can share it
It is a compiled binary message that both sides generate code for from a schema file
It is a named remote method that the caller invokes as if it were a local function
It is a thing in the system with its own address, such as a URL path, that callers act on with standard HTTP methods
questions.why: In REST, each thing is a resource with its own URL path, and callers use verbs like GET, POST, PUT and DELETE on that path, which is what distinguishes it from the procedure-call model of gRPC.

questions.prompt: A file-storage service returns 200 OK for a failed upload, with a JSON body containing an error field. A team's dashboard counts 200 responses as healthy. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The status code is changed to 404 by the load balancer, so clients get a clear not-found message
Retries and caches treat the failed upload as a success, so the failure stays hidden and is not retried
The dashboard shows a true failure rate because the error field is read automatically
The client stops working because HTTP/2 rejects any body that includes an error field
questions.why: Tools that act on status codes, such as monitoring, retries and caches, see a 200 and assume success, so the real failure is missed and never retried.

questions.prompt: A team has a gRPC service whose .proto file has a message field named total with field number 3. A developer edits the file so total uses field number 5 and keeps the same type. What happens to clients already deployed with the old generated code?
choices: They are automatically regenerated by the framework on the next call
They silently break, because fields are matched by number and the old client now reads or writes the wrong field
They receive a 404 status, because the framework cannot find field number 3
They keep working because the field name total is unchanged
questions.why: Because gRPC matches fields by number, changing a number silently breaks existing clients, and the correct answer must be the one that names this mismatch rather than the unchanged name.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose REST over gRPC for a new internal API, and name one limit or tradeoff of the choice you would make.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would pick REST when the callers are varied or outside our control, such as a web front end, partner scripts or a browser, because any HTTP client can call it and anyone can inspect a request with a simple tool. Its resources map naturally to URLs, and standard caching and status codes work without extra effort. The tradeoff is efficiency: JSON is larger and slower to parse than binary messages, and streaming is not part of the basic model, so a live feed would need a separate mechanism. If the callers were all our own backend services and we needed high-throughput calls or streaming, I would consider gRPC, accepting that both sides must share the schema, messages are unreadable without tools, and browsers need an extra proxy to call it directly. Either way, I would version the contract and never change the meaning of an existing field.
rubricPoints: Explains that REST uses resources, URLs and standard HTTP verbs with JSON bodies.
Explains that gRPC uses a shared schema, generated client code and compact binary messages over HTTP/2.
Names a concrete tradeoff such as readability and tooling for REST versus efficiency and shared-schema coupling for gRPC.
Mentions that changing an existing contract, such as a field or meaning, can break callers.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between REST and gRPC for a given caller and need is best checked by explaining the tradeoff back, and no listed mission or planned engine covers API design directly.

lessons.plain: An API is the door other programs use to ask your service for things, such as a list of orders. An API gateway is a managed front door that sits between those callers and your backend code, so shared rules are applied before any request reaches your application. Three rules matter most here. Rate limiting caps how many requests one caller may make in a time window, so one noisy client cannot starve everyone else. Authentication checks who is calling by requiring a credential the gateway can verify. Observability records what happened to each call, so you can see errors, slowness and traffic patterns. Doing these in one place is more consistent than rebuilding them in every service.
lessons.guessPrompt: A client key is allowed 100 requests per minute, and in one minute it sends 150. What should happen to the extra 50, and at which point in the request path would you prefer to stop them: the database, the application code, or the front door?
lessons.teach:
An API gateway is a managed front door that receives every API call before it reaches your backend and applies shared policies to it. Rate limiting is a cap on how many requests a caller may make within a set time window, such as 100 per minute. Authentication is the check that a caller is who it claims to be, usually by validating a token or key the caller presents. Observability means collecting logs, metrics and traces so you can see what each call did, how long it took and whether it failed. Apigee and Cloud API Gateway are Google Cloud products that provide these as configurable policies rather than code you write yourself.

Why it works: the gateway sits on the path of every request, so it can make one decision per call before any backend work starts. Rejecting an over-limit request at the edge costs far less than letting it run through your application and database. Keeping authentication there means each backend does not need its own copy of the logic, and gateway logs give one consistent record across services.

Worked example. A mobile client holds a key allowing 100 requests per minute. At 10:00:20 it sends its 101st request in that minute. Step one: the gateway checks the token and finds it valid. Step two: it looks up this client's counter for the current minute and sees 100 already used. Step three: it refuses the call with status 429, meaning too many requests, and does not forward it. Step four: it writes a log line and increments a rejection counter that an alert can watch.

Common mistake: teams often forget that the backend still has a public address. A caller that goes straight to the backend skips every rule above. The fix is to make the backend accept traffic only from the gateway.

Consequence: without a limit, one buggy client retrying in a loop can exhaust backend capacity and slow every other user, and without observability the team sees only the slowdown, not its cause. The gateway is only as protective as the path that forces all traffic through it.

questions.prompt: A small team runs a weather-data API behind a gateway. Each request must carry a token, and the token has an expiry date. A partner sends a request with a token that expired yesterday. Step one: the gateway reads the token and finds its expiry date has already passed. Step two: this is the missing step. Step three: the gateway writes a log entry recording the rejected call and the reason. Which step belongs in the blank?
choices: It refuses the call as unauthenticated and does not forward it to the backend.
It forwards the call to the backend, which then checks the token again.
It resets the partner's rate counter to zero so the partner can retry at once.
It increments the partner's request counter, so the rejected call still uses up part of their quota.
questions.why: Authentication is checked at the gateway before any backend work, so an invalid or expired token is refused at the edge and never forwarded.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes rate limiting in an API gateway?
choices: A check that the caller's token has not expired.
A cap on how many requests one caller may make within a set time window.
A log of every backend error grouped by the service that produced it.
A copy of each request stored so it can be replayed later.
questions.why: Rate limiting is defined as a cap on requests per caller within a time window; the other options describe authentication, logging and replay, which are different things.

questions.prompt: A payments sandbox allows each key 40 requests per 10 seconds. A client sends 41 requests in one 10-second window. What should the gateway do with the 41st request?
choices: Hold it until the next window and then forward it automatically.
Forward it, since the backend can handle the extra load.
Refuse it at the gateway and do not forward it to the backend.
Accept it but skip writing a log entry to save space.
questions.why: Once a caller reaches its limit within the window, the gateway rejects further calls at the edge rather than passing them to the backend.

questions.prompt: A team places a gateway in front of its order service, but the service still has a public address that anyone can call directly. A caller goes straight to that address and skips the gateway. What is the most effective fix?
choices: Add a longer time window to the rate limit so direct calls are counted less often.
Configure the backend to accept traffic only from the gateway, so every call passes the policies.
Ask callers to add a valid token to direct requests so the backend can check them.
Turn on more logging inside the gateway so direct calls show up in its records.
questions.why: Rate limits and authentication only apply to traffic that passes through the gateway, so the backend must refuse anything that does not come from it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we enforce rate limits and authentication at an API gateway instead of inside each service, and name one limit or tradeoff of doing it that way.
lessons.modelAnswer: We put these checks at the gateway because every request passes through it, so one policy covers all services and we reject bad or excessive traffic before it uses backend capacity. Authentication is checked once, and the logs from the gateway give us a single record of who called what. The tradeoff is that the gateway becomes a shared dependency and a bottleneck: if it is misconfigured or down, every API is affected. It also only protects us if the backends refuse traffic from anywhere else. A service reachable directly skips all these rules, so we have to lock the backend down too. Per-service logic still matters for fine-grained authorization, because the gateway usually knows the caller but not the business rules inside each operation.
rubricPoints: A gateway applies rate limits, authentication and logging once for every request before the backend runs.
Over-limit requests are rejected early, typically with a 429 response, protecting backend capacity.
The backend must not be reachable directly, or the gateway's rules can be bypassed.
The gateway is a shared dependency, and fine-grained authorization still belongs in the service.

suggested.rationale: A scenario where a team must choose which gateway controls to apply and reject a near-miss option reasons through the tradeoffs better than facts alone, and no listed mission covers gateway policies directly.

lessons.plain: Some work should not happen the moment something else asks for it. When a shop sells an item, checkout does not need to wait while the warehouse, the receipt mailer, and the accounting system each finish their jobs. Instead, the event is written down and other parts of the system pick it up on their own time. This lesson covers two Google Cloud services that do this. One is a message queue that holds events until a consumer confirms it handled them. The other is a router that notices things happening in the platform, such as a file being uploaded, and forwards them to a service that should react. Together they let parts of an application work independently, and they introduce failure modes you must plan for.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a checkout service sends a confirmation email by calling the email service directly, and the email service is down for ten minutes, what happens to checkout? What would you change so checkout does not depend on the email service being up?
lessons.teach:
A publisher is the part of a system that announces that something happened by sending a message. A topic is a named holding place for those messages. A subscription is a named reader attached to a topic. Each subscription keeps its own backlog, so several independent consumers can each receive every message. A consumer is the service that reads from a subscription and does the work. Pub/Sub is Google Cloud's managed messaging service. It stores messages and delivers them. The consumer must send back an acknowledgement, called an ack, once the work is actually finished. If no ack arrives before the deadline, the message is redelivered. Delivery is at-least-once by default, which means a message can arrive more than once, so consumers must tolerate repeats.

Eventarc is an event router. It watches for events from platform sources, such as an object being created in a storage bucket, an audit log entry, or a message on a Pub/Sub topic. A trigger states which events to match and which service should receive them. Eventarc then sends each matching event to that target, such as a Cloud Run service.

Worked example: an order service publishes an order-placed message to a topic. Billing and email each have their own subscription. Billing receives message 42, charges the card, and acks. Email receives message 43, crashes before finishing, and never acks. Pub/Sub waits past the deadline and redelivers 43 to email. If failures keep happening, a configured dead-letter topic can take the message after a set number of attempts, so the failure is visible and the rest of the backlog keeps moving.

Common mistake: treating the publish as the finish line, or acking before the work is done. Either way, a crash silently loses the job. Consequence in a running system: when consumers stall, the backlog grows and the oldest unacked messages age, so queue depth and oldest-message age are the signals to watch. Publishers stay fast while consumers lag, but the delayed work must be designed for, not ignored.

questions.prompt: A recipe-sharing app's upload service publishes a photo-added message to a topic called photo-events. Two subscriptions read that topic: resize and tagging. Here is the trace. Step 1: the resize consumer receives message 7, makes a thumbnail, and sends an ack. Step 2: the tagging consumer receives message 8, but its process hangs and no ack arrives before the deadline passes. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: the tagging consumer, now healthy, receives message 8 again and tags the photo. Which action fills in missing step 3?
choices: The publisher is notified and must resend message 8 by hand before any retry happens.
Pub/Sub redelivers message 8 to the tagging subscription, because that subscription never acked it before the deadline.
Pub/Sub deletes message 8 from the topic because the resize subscription already acked it.
The tagging subscription's missing ack is treated as complete, so message 8 is marked done without any tagging.
questions.why: Each subscription tracks its own acks, so an unacked message is redelivered to the subscription that did not acknowledge it once the deadline passes.

questions.prompt: In a messaging system, what is the main purpose of an acknowledgement (ack) sent by a consumer?
choices: To record the message's timestamp so that subscriptions can process messages in order.
To move the message into a dead-letter topic after a failure.
To confirm the message reached the topic, so the publisher can delete its own copy.
To signal that the consumer has finished the work, so the message can leave that subscription's backlog.
questions.why: An ack tells the messaging service that the work is actually complete, so it can stop redelivering that message to that subscription.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm wants its Cloud Run service to start automatically whenever a new shipping manifest file is created in a Cloud Storage bucket. Which mechanism fits, and why?
choices: An Eventarc trigger that matches the bucket's object-created events and names the Cloud Run service as its target, because Eventarc routes platform events to a target.
A longer ack deadline on a new subscription, because it gives the service more time to start.
A Pub/Sub subscription that the warehouse app polls every minute, because polling catches all new files.
A dead-letter topic, because it collects files that failed to upload.
questions.why: Eventarc is the event router that matches platform events such as object creation and sends them to a target, while a dead-letter topic and ack deadlines do not route events at all.

questions.prompt: A ticketing platform publishes one seat-reserved message to a topic that has three subscriptions: payments, seating-map, and analytics. The analytics consumer acks successfully, and the payments consumer crashes before acking. What happens to the seating-map subscription's copy?
choices: It is removed from the topic as soon as analytics acks, so seating-map never sees it.
It is delivered to nobody, because one failed subscription holds the message back from all of them.
It still gets its own copy and is unaffected, while only payments is redelivered.
It is redelivered to payments and seating-map together, because the topic must retry for every subscriber.
questions.why: Each subscription keeps its own backlog and ack state, so one consumer's failure causes redelivery only to that subscription.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a publisher should not wait for every consumer to finish before reporting success, and name one limit or tradeoff of this asynchronous design that the team must plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: If the publisher waits for every consumer, the user-facing request becomes only as fast and reliable as the slowest or most fragile downstream service, and one failing email or analytics consumer can block a purchase. With a topic and subscriptions, the publisher only needs the message to be durably stored, then returns. Each subscription processes at its own pace, and unacked messages are redelivered automatically if a consumer crashes. The tradeoff is that the work happens later, so the system is eventually consistent: a customer may briefly see an order without a confirmation email. Delivery is at-least-once, so the same message can arrive twice, which means every consumer must be idempotent, handling a repeat without doing the work twice. The team also needs dead-letter handling and monitoring of backlog age, so that messages that never succeed are noticed rather than silently piling up.
rubricPoints: Publisher returns once the message is durably stored, decoupling the request from slow or failing consumers
Work is completed later, so the system is eventually consistent and users may see delayed effects
Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent to handle duplicates safely
Failed messages need redelivery limits, dead-letter handling, and backlog monitoring

suggested.rationale: The messaging engine would let learners publish, deliver, ack, and redeliver events, which is the core skill this objective tests.

lessons.plain: A workload's resource requirements answer two simple questions: how much computing room does each running copy of your application need, and how many copies must run at once? You state the processor share (CPU), the memory, and often how many requests one copy can handle at the same time. Set these too small and the app slows down or gets stopped by the platform. Set them too large and you pay for room that sits empty. Getting them roughly right comes before any tuning for scale or cost.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your service runs fine with 10 users but fails when 200 users arrive, and each running copy of it has a fixed memory size. Before reading on, which would you check first: the memory size of each copy, the number of copies allowed to run, or the application code? Give your first guess and one reason for it.
lessons.teach:
Resource requirements are the amounts of processor time (CPU) and memory (RAM, the short-term working space a program uses) that a workload needs, plus the rules that decide how many copies of it run. A workload is the running application. On Cloud Run, the unit you size is an instance, which is one running copy of your container. You set CPU and memory per instance, a concurrency value (how many requests a single instance may handle at the same time), and minimum and maximum instance counts that bound scaling. On GKE, which is Google's managed Kubernetes cluster service, each container gets a request (the amount the scheduler reserves for it when choosing a machine) and a limit (the hard ceiling it may not exceed).

Why this works: the platform only places and bills work based on what you declare. Memory is a hard boundary. A process that goes past its memory limit is stopped by the platform. CPU is more forgiving. Going over the CPU share usually means slower responses, not a crash.

Worked example. A service uses about 100 MB of memory just to start, and each in-flight request adds about 20 MB. Step 1: with concurrency set to 10, the peak is 100 + (10 x 20) = 300 MB. Step 2: add about 30 percent headroom, giving roughly 390 MB. Step 3: round up to a standard size, 512 MB. Step 4: keep concurrency at 10 on that instance, then check the peak under real load rather than the average.

Common mistake: sizing memory from the idle figure, or raising concurrency to cut cost without rechecking memory. Under a traffic surge, instances get stopped mid-request, the platform retries, and users see errors even though average memory looked fine.

In a running system, a lower concurrency value starts more instances during a surge. That costs more, but it keeps each instance within its memory budget. Resource requirements are a set of numbers that must agree with each other, not three separate settings.

questions.prompt: A Cloud Run service for a parcel-tracking app is sized from two measurements. Its idle memory (the RAM it uses before any request arrives) is 180 MB, and each request in flight adds about 35 MB. The team sets concurrency (how many requests one instance handles at once) to 4. Step 1: the peak memory per instance is 180 + (4 x 35) = 320 MB. Step 2: adding about 30 percent headroom (a safety margin above the peak) gives roughly 416 MB. Step 3 is missing. What should the team do next to choose the memory setting?
choices: Set memory to the idle figure of 180 MB, since that is what the service uses when nothing is happening.
Raise concurrency to 8 so that fewer instances are needed at peak.
Round up to the next standard memory size, which is 512 MB.
Subtract the headroom again to return to the 320 MB peak figure.
questions.why: The sizing rule is to take the headroomed peak and round up to a standard memory size, which gives 512 MB here, because the platform sizes instances in standard steps.

questions.prompt: In the context of Cloud Run, what does the concurrency setting control?
choices: The amount of CPU time reserved for each instance in a second.
The maximum number of requests a single instance may handle at the same time.
The hard memory ceiling that stops an instance when it is exceeded.
The number of copies of the container the platform keeps running at the minimum.
questions.why: The teaching text defines concurrency as how many requests a single instance may handle at the same time, which is distinct from instance counts, CPU, and memory limits.

questions.prompt: A GKE container has a memory limit of 1 GiB. During a traffic spike its memory use climbs to 1.2 GiB. According to the rules for requests and limits, what most likely happens?
choices: The container's CPU share is cut in half until memory drops back under the limit.
The platform stops the container because memory is a hard boundary and it went past the limit.
The scheduler moves the container to a larger machine automatically, and no request fails.
The container keeps running but each response is slower, because memory is a soft target.
questions.why: Memory is a hard boundary, so a process above its memory limit is stopped by the platform, whereas going over a CPU share usually only slows responses.

questions.prompt: A team sized their Cloud Run memory from a reading taken while the service was idle. Later they doubled concurrency from 5 to 10 to lower cost. During a surge, instances were stopped mid-request and users saw errors, even though average memory looked fine. What is the most accurate explanation?
choices: Average memory is the right measure, so the errors must come from the network rather than from sizing.
Doubling concurrency doubled the CPU share, which caused the instances to crash under memory pressure.
The minimum instance count was too high, so the platform could not start enough copies to handle the surge.
Memory per instance grows with the number of requests in flight, so the idle reading understated the peak and concurrency was raised without rechecking memory.
questions.why: Each in-flight request adds memory to an instance, so sizing from idle memory and raising concurrency without checking the peak under load pushes instances past their memory budget.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would size a new container service before its first load test. Name the numbers you would set, how they depend on each other, and one limit or tradeoff of your estimate.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by measuring one copy at idle and under a single request, to get a base memory figure and the extra memory each request adds. Then I would pick a concurrency value, say 10, and calculate peak memory as base plus concurrency times per-request memory. I would add about 30 percent headroom and round up to a standard memory size. CPU would be chosen by checking how long requests take to finish under limited CPU. Minimum instances keep a few copies warm so the first users are not slowed by startup, and maximum instances cap cost and protect downstream systems. The limit is that my numbers come from a small test, and real traffic can include heavier requests. So I would confirm with a load test and watch memory use and restarts in production before trusting the figures.
rubricPoints: Memory must cover base usage plus per-request usage at the chosen concurrency, with headroom.
CPU, memory and concurrency depend on each other and must be sized together.
Minimum and maximum instance counts control warm capacity, cost and downstream load.
Estimates from small tests have limits, so verify with load testing and production monitoring.

suggested.rationale: Choosing CPU, memory and concurrency for a surge scenario is best learned by reasoning through a realistic situation where several numbers must agree.

lessons.plain: Optimizing for cost and resource usage means making an application pay only for the computing power, memory, storage and network traffic it actually needs. Think of renting a van: one that is too big wastes money, and one that is too small breaks down under load. Cloud bills are metered, so every idle server, oversized machine, unused copy of data, or repeated expensive lookup is money spent for nothing. The work is to match capacity to real demand, let capacity shrink when traffic drops, pick the cheapest option that still meets speed and safety needs, and avoid doing the same costly work twice.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app runs on a server sized for the busiest hour of the year, but it sits at about 5 percent CPU for the other 23 hours a day. Without any cloud knowledge, what are two different ways you could cut the bill while still coping with that peak?
lessons.teach:
Cost optimization in the cloud means spending less for the same useful work without breaking speed, reliability or security. Several levers matter. Right-sizing means setting the CPU and memory an instance or container is allowed, based on measured use rather than guesses. Scale to zero means a service with no incoming requests runs no instances and bills almost nothing; Cloud Run can do this for stateless HTTP services. Autoscaling means adding and removing copies of a service as load changes, within a minimum and maximum count you set. Commitment discounts trade a one-year or three-year promise of steady usage for a lower rate, and spot capacity, which Google may reclaim at short notice, offers large discounts for work that can be interrupted. Lifecycle rules move old storage objects to cheaper tiers or delete them. Caching answers repeated reads from memory instead of from an expensive database.

Why it works: most of a bill is paid for capacity that is reserved or running, not for useful work, so the gap between what you reserve and what you use is the waste to close.

Worked example: a photo-resize service averages 2 requests per second, with a peak of 50 per second for ten minutes at lunchtime. Step 1: measure the memory each request really uses, say 300 MB. Step 2: set the container memory to 512 MB rather than 4 GB. Step 3: set the minimum instance count to 0 so nothing runs overnight. Step 4: set the maximum instance count to a cap that protects the database behind it. Result: you pay roughly for the requests served, not for a machine idling all day.
