Common mistake: setting a minimum above zero, or sizing for peak around the clock, or cutting memory below what the real peak needs. Under-sizing causes out-of-memory restarts and slow responses, and retries then cost more than the saving.

Consequence in a running system: a maximum that is too low turns a cost saving into a queue of failed requests during a surge, so every cost setting must be checked against a realistic load test.

questions.prompt: A team runs a stateless internal API for expense reports on Cloud Run, a managed service that runs containers and adds or removes copies of them as traffic changes. The API's database accepts at most 20 open connections, and each running copy of the service opens 2 of them. Load testing shows the realistic weekday peak needs about 6 copies. Here are the first two steps the team applied. Step 1, measure: each request peaks at 180 MB, so the team sets the container memory to 256 MB instead of 2 GB. Step 2: the team sets the minimum instance count to 0, so nothing runs overnight or at weekends. Step 3 is missing: the team must set the maximum instance count, which caps how many copies can exist during a surge. Which completion of step 3 is correct?
choices: 10 instances, because 10 copies times 2 connections each equals the database limit of 20, so a surge cannot exhaust the connections.
100 instances, because Cloud Run can scale quickly and the database can be upgraded later if needed.
1 instance, because the lowest possible cap is always the cheapest setting.
No maximum, because the minimum of 0 already keeps the bill low and a surge should never be refused.
questions.why: Dividing the database's connection budget by the connections each copy opens gives a cap that protects the database during a surge while still leaving room above the 6-copy peak.

questions.prompt: A data team runs a nightly batch job that takes about three hours. The job saves its progress and can be restarted if the cloud provider reclaims the machine. Which cost lever fits this job best?
choices: A three-year commitment discount, because nightly work is predictable enough to promise.
Spot capacity, because it is heavily discounted and the job can be interrupted and restarted.
A minimum instance count of five, so the job starts instantly every night.
A lifecycle rule that deletes the job's output after one day to save storage.
questions.why: Spot capacity is cheap but can be reclaimed at short notice, which suits interruptible work; a commitment needs steady usage, and a minimum count or lifecycle rule does not address the job's compute price.

questions.prompt: An HR portal's stateless HTTP service on Cloud Run receives about 3 requests per day. The team sets its minimum instance count to 3 so that no visitor waits for a cold start. What is the main cost consequence, and what is the right adjustment?
choices: Nothing changes in cost, because Cloud Run bills only per request, so a minimum has no price.
Raising the memory to 4 GB reduces cold starts and so lowers the total bill.
Three copies run all day and bill for idle capacity; set the minimum to 0 and confirm the occasional cold-start delay is acceptable.
A minimum of 3 is required for any service with more than one user, so the setting should stay.
questions.why: A minimum above zero keeps copies running and billing even when there are no requests, so for very low traffic the right move is a minimum of zero while checking that the wait for a cold start is tolerable.

questions.prompt: A small image-tagging service has been measured at a peak of 90 MB per request, but its container is set to 4 GB of memory. What is the correct cost action?
choices: Lower the memory toward the measured peak plus a safety margin, then retest under realistic load.
Raise the minimum instance count to match the memory, so the copies share the cost.
Leave the memory at 4 GB so the service never runs out of memory under any load.
Cut the memory to 64 MB, which is the average use, so it is as cheap as possible.
questions.why: Right-sizing means setting the allowance from measured use, so the memory should move down toward the measured peak with a margin, then be confirmed with a load test, since cutting below the real peak causes restarts and slow responses.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would reduce the cost of a service without making it fail under peak load. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by measuring, not guessing: look at real CPU and memory use over a week, including the peak. Then I would right-size the service so each instance has memory above the observed peak with a safety margin, because cutting too far causes out-of-memory restarts that cost more in retries. For a service with long idle periods I would allow scale to zero or set a low minimum, so nights and weekends cost little. I would set a maximum instance count to protect the database behind it. The tradeoff is cold starts: when an instance is created from zero, the first request waits longer, so latency-sensitive endpoints may need a small minimum, which costs something all day. Commitment discounts or spot capacity can help further, but only for steady work or for work that can safely be interrupted.
rubricPoints: Measure real usage, including the peak, before changing sizes
Right-size memory and CPU to observed need with a safety margin
Scale to zero or set minimums to match idle and steady periods
Name a tradeoff such as cold-start latency or a thin safety margin
Cap maximum instances so cost controls do not overload dependencies

suggested.rationale: A planned fictional-credit cost model would let the learner test sizing and scaling choices against a load pattern without a real bill.

lessons.plain: When a data centre has a bad day, your data should still be there. Google Cloud spreads its buildings into zones, and groups of zones into regions. Data replication means keeping copies of the same data in more than one place, so if one place fails, another copy can take over. A zonal model keeps copies inside one region across separate zones, which guards against a single building failing. A regional model keeps a copy in a second region, which guards against losing a whole geographic area. The trade-off is how fast copies can be made and how much recent work could be lost if you switch to one.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your application stores orders in a database. You keep a second copy in a different building in the same city. Would that copy keep the business running if the entire city lost power? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A zone is an isolated location inside a region, and a region is a geographic area containing several zones. Replication is copying data from a primary copy to one or more replicas. Failover is switching work from a failed copy to a healthy one. Two models matter here. In a zonal model, the primary and its replica sit in different zones of the same region. This survives the loss of one zone, and because the copies are close together, copying is fast. In a regional model, the replica sits in another region. This survives the loss of a whole region, but the distance adds delay, so copying is often asynchronous: the primary confirms a write before the replica has received it. That gap determines two numbers. Recovery point objective (RPO) is how much recent data you can afford to lose, measured in time. Recovery time objective (RTO) is how long you can be down before service returns.

Worked example: an orders database has a primary in zone a and a replica in zone b of the same region, plus an asynchronous replica in another region. Step 1: zone a fails at 10:00. Step 2: the zone-b replica is promoted and clients are pointed at it. Downtime is minutes and little or no data is lost, because the copy was fast and current. Step 3: suppose the whole region fails instead. The remote replica is promoted, but writes made in the final 30 seconds before the failure never reached it. Your RPO is therefore about 30 seconds, and those orders must be recovered or reconciled by hand.

Common mistake: treating a zonal replica as disaster protection. It shares a region with the primary, so a region-wide event takes both down together.

The consequence is that a promise of zero data loss across regions usually cannot be kept with asynchronous copying. The business must accept a stated RPO, or pay for slower synchronous copying that waits for the remote copy before confirming each write.

questions.prompt: A ticketing service keeps its primary in zone c of region north-2, a same-region replica in zone d, and an asynchronous replica in region south-5. Step 1: region north-2 fails at 16:00. Step 2: the south-5 replica is promoted and clients are pointed at it. Step 3: that replica's last received write is timestamped 15:56, so writes from 15:56 to 16:00 never reached it. Step 4 is missing. Which choice correctly completes step 4 by stating the RPO for this failure?
choices: About 4 minutes of recent writes, the gap between the last replicated write and the failure.
Zero minutes, because asynchronous copying waits for the remote region before confirming.
About 16 minutes, the length of the outage, since the region was down.
Zero minutes, since the same-region replica already had every write.
questions.why: RPO is the amount of recent data that can be lost, measured in time, and here the replica was missing writes from the final 4 minutes before the failure.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's replica sits in a different region from its primary. Which capability does that cross-region replica add that a replica in another zone of the same region does not provide?
choices: Faster copying of each write to the replica.
Survival of the loss of an entire region.
Protection against the loss of only its own zone.
A recovery point objective of zero.
questions.why: A cross-region replica survives the loss of a whole region, while a same-region replica does not, and the teaching notes that cross-region copying is usually slower rather than faster.

questions.prompt: A retail app's primary database runs in zone f of region east-1, with a replica in zone g of the same region. Zone f loses power at noon. Which outcome does the zonal failover model give?
choices: Work moves to the zone-g replica after a short outage, with little or no data lost.
The app keeps running with no interruption because both zones share the same copy.
Data is lost entirely because a zone failure stops all replicas in the region.
Work moves to a replica in another region, which adds the delay of distance.
questions.why: In the zonal model the replica in another zone of the same region is promoted after a zone failure, and the teaching says this gives minutes of downtime and little or no data loss because the copies are close and current.

questions.prompt: A health records startup needs zero data loss even if a whole region fails. It is considering asynchronous copying to a replica in another region. Which conclusion follows from the teaching?
choices: Asynchronous copying usually cannot keep zero data loss across regions, so the startup must accept a stated RPO or pay for synchronous copying.
A same-region zonal replica can provide the same protection against a region-wide failure.
Zero data loss across regions is guaranteed once the replica is promoted within minutes.
Asynchronous cross-region copying meets the requirement as long as the zones are different.
questions.why: The teaching says a zero-loss promise across regions usually cannot be kept with asynchronous copying, so the business must accept a stated RPO or use slower synchronous copying that waits for the remote copy.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a replica in another zone of the same region does not protect you from a regional outage. Then name the main trade-off between a nearby replica and a distant one, and say how RPO fits in.
lessons.modelAnswer: A zonal replica sits in a different zone of the same region, so it survives one building or zone failing. But both copies still sit inside one geographic area. If the whole region has an outage, primary and replica go down together, so that replica offers no protection there. A replica in another region covers that case. The trade-off is distance. Copying across regions is slower, so the replica is usually updated asynchronously, which means the newest writes can be missing when you fail over. That missing window is the RPO, and I would tell the business it is a number of seconds or minutes rather than promise zero loss. Nearby replicas give faster failover and less data loss for a zone failure, while distant replicas cost more latency but protect against losing a whole region.
rubricPoints: A zonal replica only protects against a single zone failing, not a whole region failing
A regional replica covers region-wide outages but is farther away and slower to copy
Asynchronous cross-region copying means recent writes can be lost, which is the RPO
Recovery targets such as RPO and RTO should be stated as numbers, not promised as zero loss

suggested.rationale: The dr-planner engine would let the learner set RPO and RTO targets and check which replica placement meets them, which is the core decision in this objective.

lessons.plain: When you release a new version of an app, you rarely want every user to hit it at once. Traffic splitting means a platform sends a chosen share of incoming requests to the new version and the rest to the old one, and you change that share as you gain confidence. Think of a shop opening a new checkout lane with only a few customers at first, watching for jams, and opening more lanes only when it runs smoothly. The same mechanism supports three things: a gradual rollout, a fast rollback when something breaks, and a way to compare two versions in an experiment. The platform does the routing; you choose the percentages and decide what counts as healthy.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your service runs version 1 and handles all traffic. You deploy version 2. If you send 5 percent of requests to version 2 and those requests start failing, what would you do first, and why is that safer than sending 100 percent of requests to version 2 at once?
lessons.teach:
A revision is one fixed snapshot of a Cloud Run service: a container image plus its settings. Deploying usually creates a new revision rather than changing the old one in place. Traffic splitting is the rule that says what percentage of requests each revision receives; the percentages must add up to 100. On Cloud Run you set these weights on the service. On GKE you get the same effect by sending traffic to two versions of an app behind one name, using weighted routing in a gateway or service mesh. The idea is identical on both platforms: the router, not the app code, picks a version for each request.

It works because the old version keeps serving most requests while the new one gets a small, measurable slice. You judge health by comparing metrics for each revision, such as error rate and latency, over the same time window.

Worked example. Your service handles 1,000 requests per minute on revision v1. You deploy v2 and set the split to 95 percent v1 and 5 percent v2, so about 50 requests per minute reach v2. Step 1: you watch v2 for 15 minutes. Step 2: v2 shows 4 percent errors while v1 shows 0.3 percent. Step 3: you set v1 to 100 percent and v2 to 0. Only about 50 requests per minute were exposed to the bad version, not all 1,000. Rolling back here is a traffic change; nothing is rebuilt.

Common mistake: using a per-request split for an A/B test of user experience. Each request is assigned independently, so one user can bounce between variants and the comparison becomes unreliable. Keeping each user on one variant needs a stable assignment rule, which is a separate design choice.

Consequence: if a bad revision is moved to 100 percent before anyone checks it, the only way back is a redeploy under pressure, which is slower and creates yet another revision. A split that starts small keeps the blast radius small and the rollback a single change.

questions.prompt: A ticketing service runs on Cloud Run. Revision r7 serves 100 percent of its 2,000 requests per minute. The team deploys r8, a new fixed snapshot with a changed container image, and sets the split to 90 percent r7 and 10 percent r8, so about 200 requests per minute reach r8. Step 1: the team leaves the split at 90/10 for 20 minutes. Step 2: r8 shows a p95 latency of 900 ms while r7 shows 280 ms over the same window, and r8's error rate is also higher. Step 3 is missing. Which action completes the response to this bad revision?
choices: Set r7 to 100 percent and r8 to 0 percent, which is a traffic change that rebuilds nothing
Rebuild r7 from its source code and redeploy it as r9 at 100 percent
Edit the container image inside r8 in place so its latency drops, then keep the split
Set r7 to 0 percent and r8 to 100 percent, then wait for the next deploy to fix r8
questions.why: Because each revision is a fixed snapshot and the router chooses versions, moving all traffic back to r7 is a single weight change that sends no requests to the bad revision and needs no rebuild.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines traffic splitting on Cloud Run?
choices: A rule that copies each request to every revision so results can be compared side by side
A rule that limits how many requests one client can send per second
A rule inside the application code that decides which version of a function to call
A rule that sets the percentage of requests each revision receives, with the percentages adding to 100
questions.why: Traffic splitting is the router's weight rule that assigns percentages of requests to revisions, and those percentages must total 100.

questions.prompt: A team runs an A/B test of two checkout page layouts. They set a 50/50 split on the service, and the router assigns each incoming request independently. A shopper who reloads the page sometimes sees layout A and sometimes layout B. What is the best fix?
choices: Add a stable assignment rule that keeps each shopper on one variant, as a separate design choice from the percentage split
Deploy a third revision so the router has more options to rotate through
Turn off metrics collection so the shopper's experience is not compared
Lower the split to 10/90 so fewer shoppers see the test
questions.why: Per-request weights assign each request independently, so one user can bounce between variants, and only a stable assignment rule keeps each user on one variant.

questions.prompt: A team sends 100 percent of traffic to a new revision on its first deploy, skipping any small initial slice, because they are confident the change is safe. The new revision has a bug that raises errors for every user. What is the main consequence?
choices: Traffic automatically returns to the previous revision after the first minute
Every request is exposed to the bug, and undoing it usually means a redeploy under pressure that creates another revision
Only a fraction of users is affected, so the team can compare error rates safely
The bug is contained because the old revision still gets a small share of requests
questions.why: Sending everything to the new revision at once removes the small exposed slice and the easy weight-change rollback, so recovery becomes a slower redeploy that adds yet another revision.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would roll out a new version of a Cloud Run service using traffic splitting, and name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would deploy the new version as its own revision and send it no production traffic at first, then give it a tagged address so testers can reach it directly. Next I would move a small share, say 5 percent, to the new revision and compare its error rate and latency with the old revision over a fixed window. If it stays healthy, I would step up to 25, then 50, then 100 percent, checking at each step. If it degrades, I would set the old revision back to 100 percent, which is the rollback, and investigate afterward. The tradeoff is that a small slice only exposes a fraction of users, so rare bugs or bugs that appear only under full load may not show up until the percentage rises. During the split, both versions also have to work with the same data and database format, which limits what changes can ship safely.
rubricPoints: Describes a gradual increase of traffic share with health checks at each step
Explains that rollback means moving traffic back to the previous revision, not redeploying
Names a limit such as rare bugs or full-load issues being invisible at small percentages
Notes that both versions must remain compatible with shared data during the split

suggested.rationale: The deploy-shift engine would let the learner set traffic weights, step them up, and roll back, which is the core skill of this objective.

lessons.plain: Real applications often need several steps to happen in the right order, at the right time, or in response to something that happened elsewhere. Orchestration means deciding what starts each step, what happens next, and what happens when one fails. Google Cloud offers four tools for this. A scheduler fires work at set times. An event router reacts when something changes in another service. A task queue holds many small pieces of work and feeds them out at a controlled pace. A workflow engine runs an ordered sequence of steps and remembers where it is. Picking the right one depends on what triggers the work, whether it must be paced, and whether the steps depend on each other.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly report must run at 02:00, and a second job must run only if the first one succeeded. Which service would you reach for first to fire the job at 02:00, and what would you still need to handle the only-if-succeeded part?
lessons.teach:
Each of the four tools answers a different question. Cloud Scheduler is a managed timer. You give it a schedule, written in cron syntax (a pattern of minute, hour, day, month and weekday), and at each time it sends one request to a target such as an HTTP endpoint. Eventarc is an event router. When something happens in another service, such as a file landing in a storage bucket, it delivers an event describing that change to a target service you name. Cloud Tasks is a managed queue. You add work items to it, and it delivers each one to an HTTP endpoint at a rate you cap, retrying failures. Workflows runs a defined sequence of steps, calls services in order, branches on results, and keeps its place between steps.

Why it works: each tool holds only the part of the job it is built for. The timer does not know what happens after it fires. The queue smooths bursts so the receiving service is not overwhelmed. The workflow keeps the ordering and the decision logic in one visible place.

Worked example: a nightly report. Cloud Scheduler fires at 02:00 and sends a request to the workflow's start endpoint. Step 1 calls the extract service. If it succeeds, step 2 calls the render service. If step 1 fails, the workflow retries a set number of times, then takes an error path that notifies the on-call channel. Each result decides the next step.

Common mistake: treating a retry as harmless. Cloud Tasks and Scheduler can both deliver the same request more than once, so the receiving handler must be idempotent, meaning running it twice gives the same result as running it once. Otherwise a retried 'charge customer' task charges the customer twice.

Consequence: a queue with no rate cap can flood a database during a burst, and a timer whose job runs longer than its interval can start overlapping runs. Choose by trigger and shape. Time-based work points to Scheduler, something-happened-elsewhere points to Eventarc, many independent items that need pacing point to Cloud Tasks, and ordered steps with branching point to Workflows.

questions.prompt: A pharmacy chain has a list of 9,000 patients who are due a refill reminder text. The reminders should go out each weekday at 07:30, and the SMS provider accepts at most 20 requests per second. Step 1: Cloud Scheduler, a managed timer, fires at 07:30 on weekdays and sends one request to the start endpoint of a small reminder service. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: each item is delivered to the SMS provider no faster than 20 per second, and any failed send is retried by the managed service. Which choice correctly fills in step 2?
choices: The service adds one work item per patient to a Cloud Tasks queue whose dispatch rate is capped at 20 per second.
Eventarc delivers one event per patient record to the SMS provider, and the provider paces itself.
The service sends all 9,000 texts in one loop inside the request, with no queue, so the provider receives a burst.
Cloud Scheduler creates 9,000 separate timers, one per patient, all set to fire at 07:30.
questions.why: Cloud Tasks is the managed queue that holds the individual items, paces delivery to the cap, and retries failures, which is the job step 2 needs; the other choices either create a burst or use the timer and event router for work they are not built for.

questions.prompt: A property-management firm needs its meter-reading summary recalculated every 15 minutes. The recalculation does not need to react to any other system. Which Google Cloud tool fits best?
choices: Cloud Tasks, because each recalculation is a work item that needs pacing
Cloud Scheduler, because the trigger is purely time-based on a fixed interval
Workflows, because the recalculation has ordered steps with branching
Eventarc, because the recalculation should fire whenever a new meter reading arrives
questions.why: A fixed-interval trigger that depends only on the clock is the time-based case, which points to Cloud Scheduler, while the other three options answer different trigger shapes.

questions.prompt: A refund handler is invoked by Cloud Tasks. A retry sends the same refund request a second time. A handler is idempotent if running it twice with the same request gives the same final result as running it once. What property must the handler have so that the customer is not refunded twice?
choices: Idempotent, so repeating the same request ends in the same state as running it once
Ordered by Workflows, so each step begins only after the previous one finishes
Scheduled, so it runs only at fixed times and never by retry
Rate-capped, so fewer requests reach the handler at the same moment
questions.why: Idempotency is the property that makes a duplicate delivery harmless, whereas a rate cap, a fixed schedule, or step ordering does not stop the same request from being processed twice.

questions.prompt: A Cloud Scheduler job is set to fire every 5 minutes. Each run of the job takes 7 minutes to finish. What risk does this create, and what is its effect?
choices: Eventarc drops any events that arrive while the job is running
The queue floods the database during a burst of work items
Runs can overlap, with a new run starting before the previous one has finished
The job is billed twice for each request it sends
questions.why: When a timer's job runs longer than its interval, the next fire arrives before the previous run ends, so runs can overlap, which is the timer-specific consequence named for this situation.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Cloud Tasks and Workflows for sending one notification per customer after a nightly batch finishes, and name one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use Cloud Tasks for the per-customer notifications, because each notification is an independent item, there may be thousands of them, and I want them paced so the notification service is not flooded. A workflow would be the wrong tool here because it is built for a fixed sequence of steps with branching, not for fanning out thousands of similar items. The batch completion itself could be the trigger for the enqueueing, and a workflow could coordinate the batch and then hand off to the queue. The tradeoff is that the queue delivers at least once, so retries can send a duplicate notification. I would make the notification handler idempotent, for example by recording the customer and batch ID and skipping any already sent. I would also accept that per-item ordering is not guaranteed unless I design for it.
rubricPoints: Identifies Cloud Tasks as the fit for many independent items that need rate control and retries
Explains that Workflows suits ordered steps with branching rather than large fan-out
Names at-least-once delivery and the need for an idempotent handler
States a concrete tradeoff such as no guaranteed ordering or duplicate delivery

suggested.rationale: Choosing among four similar services is best practised by reasoning through a realistic trigger-and-shape situation, which is where the exam-style judgement is built.

lessons.plain: Data retention means keeping stored files for as long as you must, and data organization means removing them when you no longer need them. In Google Cloud Storage, a bucket is a container for files called objects. A lifecycle rule is an automatic instruction, such as moving old files to a cheaper storage tier or deleting them after a set age. A retention lock is a stronger promise: it stops anyone, even an administrator, from deleting or overwriting files before a set period ends, and once that promise is locked in, it cannot be undone. Together these tools help you cut storage costs and meet legal or audit rules.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bucket must keep audit files for seven years, and a cleanup rule is set to delete files after thirty days. Do you expect the files to be deleted at thirty days, and why?
lessons.teach:
Key terms first. An object is one stored file plus its metadata. A bucket is the container that holds objects. A storage class is a price and access tier, such as Standard for frequent use or Archive for data rarely read. A lifecycle rule is a bucket setting with a condition (for example, the object is 90 days old) and an action (change its storage class or delete it). A retention policy is a bucket setting that says objects cannot be deleted or overwritten until they reach a minimum age. Bucket Lock is the step of locking that retention policy so it can never be shortened or removed.

Why it works: lifecycle rules run in the background across the whole bucket, so you do not write a cleanup job yourself. The service checks conditions periodically, so an action may happen some time after its condition is met, sometimes up to a day later. Retention is enforced by the storage service itself, not by your code or by people's good behavior.

Worked example: a bucket holds audit logs that must be kept seven years and then removed. Step 1: set a retention policy of seven years on the bucket. Step 2: add a lifecycle rule that deletes objects older than seven years. Step 3: lock the retention policy to satisfy an auditor. A delete request on a two-year-old log fails because its retention period has not passed. The lifecycle rule waits and removes each log only once it is seven years old.

Common mistake: treating a lifecycle rule as a retention guarantee, or expecting it to delete a file that retention protects. The rule cannot override retention, so a delete-after-30-days rule on a bucket with a one-year retention period does nothing until the year passes.

Consequence: because a locked policy cannot be shortened, a wrong retention period is permanent for data already stored, and the bucket cannot be deleted while protected objects remain. Choose retention periods carefully before locking them.

questions.prompt: A clinic keeps scanned consent forms in a Cloud Storage bucket. Each form must be kept for 6 years and must never be deleted or overwritten before then, even by an administrator. The clinic also wants forms moved to the Archive storage class once they are 1 year old, since they are rarely read. The plan has three steps. Step 1: set a retention policy of 6 years on the bucket. Step 2: add a lifecycle rule whose condition is object age of 1 year and whose action is to change the storage class to Archive. Step 3: [missing step]. The missing step is the one that stops anyone from ever shortening or removing the 6-year retention policy.
choices: Add a second lifecycle rule that deletes objects at 6 years of age
Lock the retention policy, which is Bucket Lock, so it can never be shortened or removed
Have the application code check each form's age before it allows a delete
Set the lifecycle rule to run every hour so the Archive move happens sooner
questions.why: Bucket Lock is the step that makes the retention policy permanent, while the other choices either change timing, add a delete action the plan does not need, or rely on application code, which the storage service does not use to enforce retention.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does a lifecycle rule consist of in a Cloud Storage bucket?
choices: A permanent lock that prevents the retention period from ever being shortened
A minimum age that stops any object in the bucket from being deleted or overwritten
A condition, such as object age, paired with an action, such as changing the storage class or deleting the object
A list of user accounts that are allowed to change the bucket's storage class
questions.why: The teaching text defines a lifecycle rule as a bucket setting with a condition and an action, which the first choice states while the others describe retention, locking, or access control instead.

questions.prompt: A bucket has a retention policy of 400 days. A lifecycle rule in the same bucket deletes objects once they are 200 days old. An object in the bucket is now 250 days old. What happens to it?
choices: It is moved to the Archive class and kept, because a delete rule always falls back to a storage class change
It is deleted immediately because its age has passed the 200-day condition of the lifecycle rule
It is deleted on the day the lifecycle rule runs, because the rule always overrides retention
It is not deleted yet, because retention protects it until it reaches 400 days, and the lifecycle rule cannot override that
questions.why: A lifecycle rule cannot override a retention policy, so the object stays protected until its retention period ends at 400 days regardless of the rule's 200-day condition.

questions.prompt: A team sets a retention policy of 3 years on a bucket and then locks it by mistake, realizing afterward that 2 years would have been enough. Which statement describes the situation correctly?
choices: The team can shorten the policy to 2 years at any time from the console, since locking only affects new objects
The retention period cannot be shortened or removed, and the bucket cannot be deleted while protected objects remain, so the wrong period is effectively permanent for data already stored
The team can delete the bucket immediately, since a locked policy only blocks deletion of individual objects
The team can shorten the policy only if all objects in the bucket are first moved to a different bucket
questions.why: Once a retention policy is locked it can never be shortened or removed, and the bucket cannot be deleted while protected objects remain, so the wrong period cannot be corrected for data already stored.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a lifecycle rule and a locked retention policy, and name one limit or tradeoff of locking a retention policy.
lessons.modelAnswer: A lifecycle rule is an automatic action on a bucket: when an object matches a condition such as age, the service changes its storage class or deletes it. It is a cost and tidiness tool, and it can be edited or removed at any time. A retention policy is different: it sets how long objects must be kept, and the service refuses to delete or overwrite them before that age. Locking the policy with Bucket Lock makes it permanent, so nobody can shorten or remove it. The main tradeoff is that a wrong period cannot be corrected for data already stored, and the bucket cannot be deleted while protected objects remain. Also, lifecycle actions may run some time after the condition is met, not at the exact moment it becomes true.
rubricPoints: A lifecycle rule automatically changes storage class or deletes objects when a condition such as age is met.
A retention policy blocks deletion or overwriting until objects reach a minimum age, and a lifecycle rule cannot override it.
Bucket Lock makes the retention policy permanent and cannot be shortened or removed.
A tradeoff of locking is that a wrong retention period is permanent for existing data and blocks bucket deletion.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers retention, so a scenario where the learner picks lifecycle, retention, or lock for a stated requirement is the best practice available.

lessons.plain: Some web applications need two kinds of security help: keeping the wrong people out, and finding weaknesses before attackers do. Identity-Aware Proxy is a gatekeeper placed in front of an app. It checks who is asking and whether that person is allowed in before any request reaches the app, so the app does not need its own login system and users do not need a VPN. Web Security Scanner is a tool that visits a web app much as a curious visitor would, follows its links and forms, sends test inputs, and reports known kinds of weakness it finds. One controls access; the other looks for flaws. Neither replaces careful building of the app.
lessons.guessPrompt: An internal admin dashboard is reachable from the public internet. Before reading anything, what would you put in front of it so only company staff can reach it, and how would you check whether the dashboard itself has holes an attacker could use?
lessons.teach: Identity-Aware Proxy, usually shortened to IAP, is a service that sits between users and an application. Every request first passes through it. It confirms the user has signed in with an identity provider (the system that knows who your company's people are), then checks an authorization policy (a rule saying which identities may reach which app). Only allowed requests are forwarded. It works because the app never sees unauthenticated traffic, and the app can trust the identity details IAP attaches to each forwarded request, as long as nothing reaches the app without going through IAP. Web Security Scanner is a dynamic scanner: it crawls a running web app starting from URLs you give it, fills in forms, and sends inputs designed to trigger known weaknesses such as cross-site scripting (where an app echoes attacker-supplied script back to other users), mixed content (secure pages loading insecure resources), and outdated libraries with known flaws. Worked example: a staff member opens the dashboard. Step 1: the request hits IAP. Step 2: IAP sees no session and redirects to company sign-in. Step 3: after sign-in, IAP checks the user is in the allowed group. Step 4: IAP forwards the request with a signed identity header. Step 5: a scanner run, pointed at a test copy and given a sign-in it can use, crawls pages behind that login and reports any cross-site scripting it triggers. Common mistake: treating a clean scan, or IAP, as proof the app is secure. IAP does nothing about flaws a signed-in user can exploit, and a scanner only finds what its tests reach. Consequence: if the app's address is reachable directly, a caller can skip IAP and forge the identity header, so the app must accept traffic only from the gate. Run scans against environments you are allowed to test, because scans generate real load and requests.

questions.prompt: A regional bus-booking company wants to find weaknesses in its new booking site before launch. Its team follows these steps: (1) they point Web Security Scanner, a tool that crawls a running web app from starting URLs and sends test inputs to trigger known flaws, at a staging copy of the site and list the starting URLs; (2) they give the scanner a test account so it can reach pages behind sign-in; (3) the scanner crawls the pages and submits forms; (4) the missing step: the team ____; (5) they fix each reported flaw and run the scan again. Which step fills the gap?
choices: Turns on IAP so the scanner is blocked from reaching the booking pages
Disables the test account so that the findings stay accurate
Deploys the scanner into the live production site to replace the staging copy
Reviews the findings report to see which flaws the scanner actually triggered
questions.why: After a scan runs, the report lists the flaws the scanner triggered, and that review is what the team acts on before fixing and rescanning.

questions.prompt: IAP (Identity-Aware Proxy, a gate that sits in front of an app and decides which signed-in users may reach it) guards a retail company's internal inventory tool. Which description best states what IAP does with each incoming request?
choices: It stores each user's password so the tool never has to show a sign-in page.
It scans the tool's source code for known weaknesses before each deployment.
It crawls the tool's pages and submits forms to find cross-site scripting.
It confirms the user has signed in and checks an authorization policy before forwarding the request.
questions.why: IAP's job is to confirm sign-in and check the authorization policy, and only then forward the request; the other options describe a code scanner, a password store, or a dynamic scanner.

questions.prompt: A team's Cloud Run service (a managed service that runs containers and gives each one its own web address) has IAP turned on for its public hostname, but the service's default address also accepts traffic. An attacker sends a request straight to that default address with a forged identity header. What is the main risk, and what fixes it?
choices: No risk, because forged headers are discarded automatically by Web Security Scanner.
The attacker can read the scanner's test accounts, so the fix is to delete those accounts.
The attacker can skip the gate and the app may trust the forged identity, so the app must accept traffic only from the gate.
IAP will cache the forged request and serve it to other users, so the fix is a longer cache lifetime.
questions.why: If the app is reachable without passing through IAP, the identity header can be forged, so the app must only accept traffic that comes through the gate.

questions.prompt: A team must find cross-site scripting (an app echoing attacker-supplied script back to other users) in a running web app they are allowed to test, and the check must reach pages behind sign-in. Which mechanism fits best, and why is each near-miss not enough?
choices: Web Security Scanner given a test sign-in, since it crawls running pages and sends inputs designed to trigger the flaw.
Only a code review, because a scanner cannot send requests to a running app.
A clean IAP log, because it proves the app has no injected script.
IAP, because it stops cross-site scripting by checking every request's content against a list of known attack patterns.
questions.why: Web Security Scanner is the dynamic scanner that reaches pages behind a supplied sign-in and sends triggering inputs, while IAP only gates access and a log or code review does not test a running app.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate suggests skipping the VPN and running Web Security Scanner against production every night so the app is secure. In your own words, explain what Identity-Aware Proxy and Web Security Scanner each do, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on the scanner.
lessons.modelAnswer: Identity-Aware Proxy controls access. It sits in front of the app, checks that the user is signed in and allowed by policy, and only then forwards the request, so we avoid a VPN for staff access. Web Security Scanner finds weaknesses by crawling the running app and sending test inputs for known problems like cross-site scripting or outdated libraries. The main limit is coverage: it only finds what its crawl reaches and what its tests check, so a clean report does not mean the app is safe. Another tradeoff is that scans create load and real requests, so running them nightly against production could disturb users or fill logs. I would run it against a staging copy with a test sign-in, treat the results as a list to triage, and keep IAP as the access control that the app is built to trust.
rubricPoints: Identity-Aware Proxy checks identity and authorization before forwarding requests to the app
Web Security Scanner crawls a running app and sends test inputs to find known weaknesses
A clean scan is not proof of security because coverage is limited to what the scanner reaches
Scans generate real traffic, so they belong in a test environment rather than unplanned production runs

suggested.rationale: Choosing between access control and vulnerability scanning in a realistic situation is what separates the two tools, so reasoning through a scenario adds the most.

lessons.plain: When a scanner finds a known weakness in software your team ships, someone has to decide what to do: fix it now, fix it later, or accept it with a reason. On Google Cloud, two services report these weaknesses. Artifact Analysis checks container images, which are packaged bundles of your application, against lists of known problems. Security Command Center gathers findings from many sources into one place for an organization. This objective is about turning those reports into a sensible sequence of actions: sort them, fix the ones that matter, redeploy, and confirm the problem is gone.
lessons.guessPrompt: A scanner reports a serious known vulnerability in the base layer of your container image, and the vendor has already released a patched base. What would you do first, and what would you check before you redeploy?
lessons.teach:
A vulnerability is a known flaw in software that someone could use to cause harm. A container image is the packaged bundle of your application plus the operating system layers it sits on, often called the base image. Artifact Analysis is the Google Cloud service that scans images stored in Artifact Registry, the image store, and records each known problem it finds as an occurrence, meaning a finding attached to one specific image digest. A digest is a fingerprint of the exact image contents, so a finding applies to that build and no other. Security Command Center is the central dashboard for security findings across projects and an organization. It can show Artifact Analysis results alongside findings from other scanners and misconfiguration checks.

Why a structured response works: most findings already have a fix available, usually a newer package version or a patched base image. The reliable loop is to sort findings by severity and whether a fix exists, rebuild the image on the patched base, push it, deploy the new digest, and then confirm the rescan no longer reports the flaw. A finding you cannot fix yet should be accepted or muted only with a written reason and a named owner.

Worked example: a scanner reports a high-severity flaw in a library inside image api with digest sha256 abc. Step 1: check that a fixed version of the library is listed, and it is. Step 2: update the base image and rebuild, producing digest def. Step 3: deploy def to Cloud Run as a new revision. Step 4: wait for the scan of def and confirm the flaw is absent. Only after that do you retire the old revision.

Common mistake: updating the tag name, such as api:latest, but deploying the old digest, or assuming a rebuild happened because the tag name stayed the same. Tags can be moved, so the digest is what proves what is actually running.

Consequence: until the new revision receives traffic, the vulnerable image keeps serving requests, so the finding stays open in Security Command Center even after the code has been fixed.

questions.prompt: Pebble Dental runs its online booking site as a container on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE, a managed Kubernetes cluster that runs containers). A scan of image digest 77c1 reports a high-severity flaw in the openssl package, and a patched openssl version is listed. The team rebuilt the image with the patched package, which produced digest 9e02. They then changed the GKE Deployment to use digest 9e02, and the rollout finished. The one step not yet done is checking the scan result for the new digest. Which action completes the loop?
choices: Retire the old Deployment now, because the rollout already finished.
Mute the openssl finding in Security Command Center with a note saying it is handled.
Mark the old digest 77c1 as the latest tag so the tag points at the fixed build.
Confirm that the scan of digest 9e02 no longer lists the openssl flaw, and only then retire the old version.
questions.why: A rollout finishing only proves the new digest is running; the flaw is cleared only when a rescan of that exact digest no longer reports it, and only then is the old version retired.

questions.prompt: In Artifact Analysis, what is an occurrence?
choices: A copy of an image stored in a second region for disaster recovery.
A log entry showing when a Cloud Run revision last received traffic.
A project-wide severity score that rolls up every image in a registry.
A finding attached to one specific image digest, recording a known problem in that exact build.
questions.why: The teaching text defines an occurrence as a finding tied to one image digest, so it applies to that exact build and no other.

questions.prompt: A team finds a high-severity flaw in an image, but no patched package version exists yet. Which response best fits the recommended approach?
choices: Delete the image from Artifact Registry so the flaw cannot be deployed.
Accept the finding with a written reason and a named owner, and revisit it when a fix becomes available.
Rebuild the image under the api:latest tag and assume the flaw is gone.
Mute the finding silently so the dashboard stays clean until a fix appears.
questions.why: The teaching text says a finding that cannot be fixed yet should be accepted or muted only with a written reason and a named owner.

questions.prompt: A payments team rebuilt its image after patching a library and pushed it under the same tag, payments:stable. The Cloud Run service still shows the old flaw. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The service is still running the old digest; the tag name alone does not change what is deployed, so the new digest must be deployed and rescanned.
Artifact Analysis cannot scan rebuilt images, so the finding will remain open permanently.
Security Command Center only reads findings from a different project, so the fix must be copied there.
Security Command Center refreshes findings once a week, so the flaw will clear on its own.
questions.why: Tags can be moved and do not prove what is running, so the old digest still serving traffic keeps the finding open until the new digest is deployed and rescanned.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would respond to a critical vulnerability reported for a container image we run in production, and name one limit or tradeoff of your plan.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by checking the finding in Artifact Analysis and Security Command Center: which image digest is affected, how severe it is, and whether a fixed version exists. If a fix exists, I would rebuild the image on a patched base, push it, and deploy the new digest as a new Cloud Run revision, sending it traffic only after it passes health checks. Then I would confirm that the rescan of the new digest no longer reports the flaw and only then close the finding. The tradeoff is time. A critical flaw may need an emergency rebuild outside the normal release cycle, which adds the risk of breaking the app. If no fix exists yet, I would not simply mute the finding. I would record a justification, an owner, and a review date, and look at compensating controls such as tighter network access until a patch is available.
rubricPoints: Identify the affected image digest and severity from Artifact Analysis or Security Command Center.
Check whether a fixed version exists before acting.
Rebuild and redeploy the new digest, then confirm the rescan is clean.
Accept or mute a finding only with a written reason, an owner, and a review date.
Name a tradeoff such as emergency release risk or residual exposure while the old image runs.

suggested.rationale: Triage across findings is best practiced by reasoning through an exam-style situation, since no listed mission or planned engine covers vulnerability response.

lessons.plain: A secret is any value that proves who you are or unlocks something, such as a database password, an API token, or an encryption key. Keeping these inside source code or config files is risky, because anyone who can read the code can copy them. Google Cloud offers a managed secret store that holds such values, a managed key service that creates and guards encryption keys, and a way for code running outside Google to borrow short-lived Google credentials without keeping a permanent key file. Together they let you store, read, and change sensitive values safely. The core idea is to keep the value in one locked place, give each program only the permission it needs, and replace the value on a schedule.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a service needs a database password, where would you store it so that a teammate who can read the code cannot see it, and how would you change it later without redeploying the service?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A secret is a stored value whose disclosure would cause harm. Secret Manager is Google Cloud's managed store for secrets: you create a named secret, add versions (each new value becomes a numbered version), and a program reads a chosen version through an API. Cloud KMS, the Key Management Service, holds encryption keys organised into key rings and keys; the key material stays inside the service, so callers ask it to encrypt or decrypt data for them. Workload Identity Federation lets an identity from outside Google, such as a token issued by another cloud or a CI system, be exchanged for a short-lived Google access token, so no long-lived service account key file is needed. A service account is an identity used by a program rather than a person. IAM, Google's permission system, decides which identities can perform which actions on which resources.

Why it works. Separating the value from the code means you can rotate it without rebuilding, and every read is governed by a permission that can be granted or revoked per identity. A common pattern is envelope encryption: a data encryption key encrypts your bulk data, and KMS encrypts that small key with a key-encryption key, so the master key never touches the bulk data.

Worked example. A service needs a database password. Step 1: store the password as the first version of a secret named db-password. Step 2: grant the service's service account a role that allows reading that one secret. Step 3: at startup the service fetches the latest version and keeps it only in memory. Step 4: to rotate, add version 2 with the new password, let the service pick it up, then disable version 1.

Common mistake. Downloading a service account JSON key file and committing it to a repository, or pasting the secret into a plain environment variable visible to everyone with console access. Prefer an attached service account or federation.

Consequence. A leaked long-lived key works until someone notices and deletes it. Federation and short-lived tokens shrink that window, and managed rotation limits how long any one value stays valid.

questions.prompt: A small logistics firm exports invoice files and encrypts each one with envelope encryption. Envelope encryption means a short-lived data encryption key (DEK) encrypts the bulk file, and a key-encryption key held in Cloud KMS (Google's Key Management Service) wraps that small DEK. The firm's key ring is named orders-ring and its key is named invoice-key. Worked steps for writing an export: (1) generate a new DEK in the export job's memory. (2) Encrypt the invoice file with that DEK. (3) Send the DEK to Cloud KMS, which encrypts it with invoice-key and returns a wrapped DEK. (4) Store the encrypted file and the wrapped DEK together. To read a file back, the job must recover the plaintext DEK first. Which single step completes the read path?
choices: Send the encrypted invoice file itself to Cloud KMS, which decrypts it and returns plaintext to the job.
Ask Cloud KMS to decrypt the wrapped DEK using invoice-key, then use that recovered DEK in memory to decrypt the file.
Download the raw key material for invoice-key so the job can decrypt both the DEK and the file locally.
Decrypt the file directly with invoice-key, since KMS keys are meant for bulk data, and skip the wrapped DEK.
questions.why: The wrapped DEK is the small key that KMS protects, so KMS decrypts it, and the recovered DEK then decrypts the bulk file, matching the envelope pattern in which the master key never touches the bulk data.

questions.prompt: In Workload Identity Federation, a CI system outside Google presents a token that is exchanged for a Google credential. What kind of credential does the exchange produce, and why does that matter?
choices: A new Secret Manager version that holds the CI system's password
A Cloud KMS key ring that encrypts the CI system's token before it is sent
A short-lived Google access token, so no long-lived key file has to be created or stored
A permanent service account JSON key that the CI system stores for future runs
questions.why: Federation exchanges an outside identity for a short-lived Google access token, which removes the need for any long-lived service account key file.

questions.prompt: A developer commits a service account JSON key file to a shared code repository and the repository is later copied by an outside party. What is the main security consequence?
choices: Cloud KMS rotates the key each time a commit happens, so the copied key becomes invalid within minutes.
IAM disables any key found in a repository after twenty-four hours, which limits the exposure to one day.
The key remains usable until someone notices the leak and deletes or disables it, so the copier can act as that service account in the meantime.
Git automatically blocks the file from being copied, so the outside party cannot use the key at all.
questions.why: A long-lived key file stays valid until it is revoked, so a leaked copy works until someone detects and removes it, which is the window federation and managed rotation are designed to shrink.

questions.prompt: A team has two needs: (a) an API token that its application reads at startup and sends to a vendor, and (b) a key that encrypts files the application uploads, where the application should never see the raw key. Which pairing of services fits best?
choices: Workload Identity Federation for both, because federation stores values and also encrypts uploads.
Secret Manager for both, because a secret version can hold an encryption key that the application encrypts with locally.
Cloud KMS for the API token, because KMS stores token values, and Secret Manager for the upload encryption key.

Secret Manager for the API token, because it stores a secret value the program reads, and Cloud KMS for the upload key, because KMS performs encrypt and decrypt while keeping key material inside the service.
questions.why: Secret Manager stores a value that a program reads, while Cloud KMS keeps key material inside the service and performs encryption on request, so the raw key is never handed to the application.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we keep the database password in a managed secret store instead of the config file, and name one limit or tradeoff of that approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: A config file gets copied into repositories, backups, and logs, so anyone with read access to it effectively has the password, and changing it means redeploying. A managed secret store keeps one protected copy, records who reads it, and lets us add a new version and disable the old one without touching the code. Each service gets its own identity with permission to read only the secrets it needs. The tradeoff is that the service now depends on the secret store being reachable at startup, and a misconfigured permission can stop the app from booting. We also have to manage the lifecycle ourselves: rotation is not automatic unless we set it up, and a stale version left enabled is still a risk.
rubricPoints: Secrets should not live in code or config files because copies spread and are hard to revoke.
A managed store centralises the value and lets you rotate by adding a new version without redeploying.
Access is granted per identity with least privilege, and reads are auditable.
A real tradeoff exists: a runtime dependency on the store and possible startup failure from wrong permissions, plus rotation and cleanup remain the team's job.

suggested.rationale: That mission makes the learner fix how a deploy receives a credential without exposing the secret, which is the core skill of this objective.

lessons.plain: Every time your application talks to a Google Cloud service, the service needs to know who is asking, much as a building guard checks a badge before opening a door. Authentication is that proof of identity. Some applications prove themselves with a robot account that Google Cloud gives them, some with a signed token that carries claims, some with a permission a user grants when they click allow, and some with a sign-in flow for their own customers. This lesson sorts those methods so you can pick the right one for a situation and avoid putting secret keys into code.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your application runs on a Google Cloud virtual machine and needs to read files from a Cloud Storage bucket. No person is typing a password at runtime. How do you think the application should prove who it is, and why might pasting a key file into the code be a poor choice?
lessons.teach:
Authentication means proving an identity. On Google Cloud, a program usually proves its identity as a service account, which is an identity for a workload rather than for a person. Application Default Credentials, often shortened to ADC, is the lookup order that Google client libraries follow to find a credential automatically: an environment variable pointing to a key file, a credential set up for local development, or the identity attached to the machine or container where the code runs. The good habit is that the code never contains the secret; the platform supplies the identity.

A JSON Web Token, or JWT, is a signed, compact string that carries claims such as who issued it, who it is for, and when it expires. The receiver checks the signature before trusting those claims. OAuth 2.0 is a delegation standard: a user grants an app a limited, expiring access token to act on their behalf, without sharing their password. Identity Platform handles sign-in for your application's own end users. Workload Identity Federation lets an external system, such as a CI job running outside Google Cloud, exchange its own trusted token for a short-lived Google credential, so no downloaded service account key ever exists. The Cloud SQL and AlloyDB Auth Proxy wraps a database connection so the client authenticates to Google Cloud with IAM identity over an encrypted channel, instead of managing IP allowlists by hand.

Worked example: a Cloud Run service reads from Cloud Storage. Step 1: Cloud Run starts the container with a service account attached. Step 2: the Storage client library asks ADC for a credential. Step 3: ADC finds the identity provided by the runtime and receives a short-lived token. Step 4: Cloud Storage checks that identity against the IAM roles on the bucket and allows or denies the read.

Common mistake: committing a downloaded service account key file into a code repository. Anyone who can read that file can act as the service account until the key is revoked. A long-lived leaked key can be used from anywhere, which is why short-lived credentials are preferred whenever the platform allows them.

questions.prompt: A retail analytics team runs a nightly batch job on a Compute Engine virtual machine (a rented server in Google's data centre) that writes summary rows to a BigQuery table. Application Default Credentials (ADC, the lookup order Google client libraries use to find a credential automatically) is used by the job. The flow is: (1) the VM starts with the service account batch-writer attached, meaning the identity the workload runs as; (2) the BigQuery client library asks ADC for a credential; (3) this step is missing; (4) BigQuery checks batch-writer's IAM (Identity and Access Management, Google's permission system) roles on the table and allows or denies the insert. Which sentence correctly fills in step 3?
choices: ADC finds the identity provided by the VM's runtime and receives a short-lived token for batch-writer.
The client library sends a developer's personal password to BigQuery so that BigQuery can confirm who is calling.
ADC pauses the nightly job and asks a human to approve an OAuth consent screen before each insert.
The team copies a downloaded JSON key for batch-writer onto the VM and points ADC at that file, so the job never needs the attached identity.
questions.why: ADC locates the identity supplied by the runtime and obtains a short-lived token, which is the credential that step 4 then checks against IAM roles.

questions.prompt: A mobile app's own end users sign in with email and password. Which Google Cloud product is designed to handle sign-in for those end users, rather than for the backend workloads that call Google APIs?
choices: Workload Identity Federation, which exchanges an external system's token for a Google credential
Identity Platform, which handles sign-in for the application's own end users
Application Default Credentials, which finds a credential for the code's runtime identity
The Cloud SQL Auth Proxy, which wraps a database connection in an encrypted channel
questions.why: Identity Platform is the product that handles sign-in for an application's own end users, while the other three address workload or database authentication.

questions.prompt: A continuous integration (CI) pipeline runs on a third-party build server outside Google Cloud and must deploy to a Google Cloud project. The team wants to avoid creating any long-lived service account key file. Which mechanism fits best, and why?
choices: Set the build server's environment variable to a public URL that returns a permanent access token.
Commit a service account key into the repository so every build can read it, then rotate it yearly.
Use Workload Identity Federation, so the build server's own trusted token is exchanged for a short-lived Google credential.
Share a human engineer's password with the build server so it can sign in as that person.
questions.why: Workload Identity Federation lets an external system exchange its trusted token for a short-lived Google credential, so no downloaded key ever exists.

questions.prompt: A service receives a compact, signed string that states which system issued it, which service it is meant for, and when it expires. Before the service trusts those statements, what must it verify?
choices: That the string is shorter than 500 characters, since longer tokens are always forged.
That the signature is valid, because the receiver checks the signature before trusting the claims in a JWT.
That the claims match the username stored in the service's own database table.
That the requesting user has accepted an OAuth consent screen for this service.
questions.why: A JWT is only trustworthy once the receiver has checked its signature, which confirms the claims were issued by a party it trusts and have not been altered.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a Cloud Run service should authenticate to Cloud Storage, and name one limit or tradeoff of using a downloaded service account key instead.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would attach a service account to the Cloud Run service and grant that account only the storage role it needs on that one bucket. The client library then uses Application Default Credentials, which finds the identity from the runtime and gets a short-lived token, so the code holds no secret. The tradeoff of a downloaded key file is that it is long-lived and portable. If it leaks, anyone can act as that account from anywhere until someone notices and revokes it, and it needs rotation and careful storage. Keys are sometimes unavoidable for systems outside Google Cloud, but for workloads that run inside it, or that can federate, I would avoid them. Workload Identity Federation covers the external case by exchanging a trusted token for a short-lived credential.
rubricPoints: Names a service account as the identity a workload uses, not a person.
Explains that ADC finds credentials automatically from the environment without hardcoded secrets.
States that downloaded long-lived keys can leak and are harder to control than short-lived tokens.
Mentions Workload Identity Federation for external workloads, or OAuth or Identity Platform for end users.

suggested.rationale: That mission has you wire a deploy's credentials so it authenticates without exposing the secret, which is the core habit of this objective.

lessons.plain: When a program runs in the cloud, it needs its own identity so the cloud can decide what it is allowed to touch. Google Cloud calls that identity a service account, which works like a badge for an application rather than a person. IAM, short for identity and access management, is the system that checks that badge against a list of allowed actions. Securing a resource with IAM roles for service accounts means giving each application's badge only the specific roles it needs, such as reading one storage bucket, and nothing more. Think of a contractor who gets a key to the one room they are repairing, not a master key to the building. The skill is choosing the smallest set of permissions that still lets the app work.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app needs to read files from one storage bucket. Would you give its identity the Editor role on the whole project so it never hits an error, or read-only access on that one bucket? Which would you pick, and what could go wrong with the other choice?
lessons.teach:
A principal is anything that can be granted access: a person, a group, or a service account. A permission is one specific action on a resource, such as reading an object from a bucket (a container for stored files in Cloud Storage). A role is a named bundle of permissions. IAM attaches a policy to a resource, and the policy holds bindings. Each binding says these principals hold this role on this resource. A grant applies at the level where it is attached and flows down to everything beneath it, so a grant on a project (the container that groups a set of cloud resources) reaches every resource inside that project.

Why this works: when an application calls a Google Cloud API, the request carries the identity the application runs as. The service checks whether that identity holds a role containing the needed permission on the resource being touched. If it does, the call proceeds. If not, the call fails with a permission-denied error. Because the check runs on every call, the narrowest grant is the safest default.

Worked example. A Cloud Run service must read thumbnail images from one bucket called thumbs. Step one: create a dedicated service account called thumb-reader. Step two: bind that account to a predefined read-only role for objects, attached to the thumbs bucket only. Step three: deploy the service so it runs as thumb-reader. At runtime, reading a thumbnail is allowed because the role includes the read permission on that bucket. A write attempt is refused, because the role contains no write permissions.

Common mistake: granting the project-level Editor role to the service account so the errors stop. That role reaches almost every resource in the project, so a compromised service could change or delete data it never needed.

Consequence: if a role is removed or the account is deleted, the running service begins returning permission-denied errors on live traffic, even though the deploy itself succeeded. Access is checked at request time, not at deploy time, so the narrow grant must be tested against real calls.

questions.prompt: A Cloud Run service named invoice-export in the ledger-prod project must upload CSV files to one bucket, exports-hl, and nothing else. The team has completed these steps: (1) create a service account called export-writer in ledger-prod. (2) STEP MISSING. (3) Deploy invoice-export so that it runs as export-writer. Which completion fills the missing step 2?
choices: Create a second service account and route the uploads through it instead.
Enable versioning on exports-hl so that any denied upload is retried automatically.
Bind export-writer to a role that allows creating objects, attached to the exports-hl bucket only.
Grant export-writer the Editor role on the ledger-prod project so that uploads cannot be refused.
questions.why: Attaching an object-creating role to the exports-hl bucket alone gives export-writer exactly the write access it needs and nothing wider, whereas the other choices either broaden access across the project or do not grant any permission at all.

questions.prompt: A payments team runs a batch job as the service account pay-batch. Which statement correctly describes a role in this setting?
choices: A single action such as reading one object from a bucket.
A named bundle of permissions that can be granted to a principal.
The account the job runs as, which can be granted access to resources.
The policy document attached to a resource that lists its bindings.
questions.why: A role is a named bundle of permissions, while a single action is a permission, the account is a principal, and the policy is the document holding the bindings.

questions.prompt: A service account has the viewer role granted on the project analytics-dev. That project contains three buckets: raw-logs, tmp-cache and model-store. Which buckets can the service account read?
choices: None, because project-level grants never reach buckets.
All three, by inheritance from the project.
Only raw-logs, the first bucket listed.
Only buckets created after the grant was made, since grants are time-bound.
questions.why: A grant applied at the project level flows down to every resource inside that project, so all three buckets are readable by that role's permissions.

questions.prompt: A Cloud Run service was deployed successfully to run as the service account ticket-bot. An administrator later deletes ticket-bot while the service is still receiving traffic. What happens to live requests?
choices: Requests keep succeeding until the service is restarted about a week later.
Requests are quietly sent to the default compute account, so nothing fails.
Requests fail with permission-denied errors, because the identity is checked on every call.
The service is blocked at deploy time and cannot be redeployed until a new account is made.
questions.why: Access is checked at request time against the identity the service runs as, so once that account is deleted, each live call is refused even though the earlier deploy succeeded.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to cloud why each service should run as its own service account with a narrow role, and name one real limit or tradeoff of doing this.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each service should run as its own service account because the account is the identity Google Cloud checks on every API call. If services share one broad account, a flaw in one service gives an attacker everything that account can reach, and the audit logs no longer show clearly which service did what. A narrow role, such as read-only access on one bucket, limits the damage to exactly what the service needs. The tradeoff is effort and friction. Someone must work out which permissions each service truly needs, and a service missing one fails at request time with a permission-denied error, not at deploy time. Teams usually start from a predefined role close to the need, test the real calls, and then tighten further. For anything handling customer data or money, the upkeep is worth it.
rubricPoints: Each service has its own identity, so a compromise stays contained to that service.
Roles should match the exact actions needed, attached to the narrowest resource.
Permissions are checked at request time, so a missing role breaks live traffic rather than the deploy.
The tradeoff is upkeep: finding the minimum permissions takes time and testing.

suggested.rationale: Deciding whether a service account's roles allow a given action on a resource is exactly what an authorization policy evaluator would let the learner practise.

lessons.plain: When one piece of software calls another over a network, that conversation should be private, and the receiving side should be able to confirm who is calling and refuse callers it does not trust. This objective is about choosing the Google Cloud tool that secures those calls between services. Some tools encrypt traffic and check identity on every call, some limit which containers may talk to which, some give a serverless app a route into your private network, and some give your network private addresses for managed databases and Google services. Each one solves a different part of the problem, so choosing well means knowing which part your requirement describes.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your checkout service calls your payments service inside the same cluster. Without any special setup, what would stop an unrelated workload in that cluster from calling payments too, and what would tell payments who is really on the other end of the call?
lessons.teach:
Service-to-service communication means one running service sending requests to another. Securing it raises three questions: is the traffic encrypted, can each side prove who it is, and is this caller allowed to make this call. Each option answers different ones.

Cloud Service Mesh is a managed service mesh based on the open-source Istio project. A mesh places a small proxy beside each workload, called a sidecar, and routes its traffic through that proxy. The proxies can use mutual TLS, written mTLS, where both client and server present certificates, so each side verifies the other and the bytes are encrypted. Authorization policies then state which identities may call which services.

Kubernetes network policies work at a lower level. A network policy is a rule object that selects pods by their labels and states which incoming or outgoing connections they accept. A pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes runs, usually one container. Pods that no policy selects accept traffic from anywhere, so the first policy you add changes the default. Network policies match on IP address and port, not cryptographic identity, and they need a network plugin that enforces them.

Direct VPC egress lets a Cloud Run service send outbound traffic straight into a subnet of your virtual private cloud, which is a private network you control, so it can reach internal resources by private address and be governed by firewall rules. Private service connectivity gives your network a private path to managed services that live elsewhere, such as a managed database, without sending traffic over the public internet.
