The IDE blocks the call by checking tool names before anything is sent to the server.
The deletion succeeds only if the assistant repeats the request a second time.
The deletion fails, because the server's own identity lacks permission, even though the tool is exposed.
questions.why: An MCP server's tools are only as powerful as the access its own identity holds, so a read-only identity cannot delete buckets even if the tool is offered.

questions.prompt: A developer's coding assistant suggests a database query while she is working in her IDE. Which handling matches how AI suggestions should be treated?
choices: Accept the query as final, because the assistant could see the open file.
Commit the query immediately and let code review catch any problems later.
Treat the query as a draft and read, run and test it before trusting it.
Run the query against production first to see whether it works.
questions.why: Assistant output is a draft suggestion, so the developer must review and test it before relying on it.

questions.prompt: A developer wants her coding assistant's MCP configuration to authenticate to Google Cloud for local development. Which approach fits the guidance for local work?
choices: Paste a service account key file into the assistant's settings.
Give the MCP server owner access so that authentication is never needed.
Sign in with her own user login so local code finds the identity it should use.
Commit the key file to the repository so teammates can reuse it.
questions.why: Signing in with a personal user login lets local code find the right identity without creating a long-lived key file that can leak.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an MCP server is and how you would connect one to an AI assistant in your IDE without giving it more access than it needs. Name one limit or tradeoff of doing this.
lessons.modelAnswer: An MCP server is a small connector program that lets an AI coding assistant use outside tools or data through a standard protocol. Each tool it exposes is something the assistant can ask to do, such as reading logs or listing storage buckets. To set one up, I would first decide the task, for example reading error logs from a test project. Then I would give the server its own identity with only the read role on that project, not my personal owner account, and keep any key out of the repository, using a secret store or a short-lived sign-in instead. I would check the tool list to confirm no delete or write actions are exposed before enabling it. The tradeoff is that more connected tools make the assistant more useful but widen what goes wrong if a prompt is misleading, so I would add connectors one at a time and review what each one can do.
rubricPoints: Defines an MCP server as a connector that exposes specific tools or data to an AI assistant.
Gives the connection its own least-privilege identity limited to the task.
Keeps credentials out of prompts, settings files and version control.
Reviews the exposed tool list for write or delete actions before enabling it.
Names a tradeoff: more connected access makes the assistant more useful but raises risk.

suggested.rationale: Judging which identity and connection an assistant should get is an exam-style decision best practised through a scenario, and no listed mission covers IDE or MCP setup.

lessons.plain: Turning an app into a container means packaging it with everything it needs to run, so it behaves the same on any machine. A build service takes your source code and its packaging recipe, runs the steps that produce that package, and then stores the result somewhere your running services can fetch it from. In Google Cloud, Cloud Build does the building and Artifact Registry does the storing. Think of Cloud Build as a kitchen that follows a recipe the same way every time, and Artifact Registry as the labelled cold store where finished meals wait until a service asks for one. This matters because the exact same tested package can then move from a test environment to production unchanged.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your team builds an app package on your own laptop and copies it to a server, what could make the server's version behave differently from the one you tested, and how might an automated build service prevent that?
lessons.teach:
A container image is a sealed package holding an application together with the libraries and settings it needs to run. It is usually built in layers from a recipe file called a Dockerfile, which lists the steps for assembling the package. Building an image from source means turning the code and that recipe into the finished package. Cloud Build is Google Cloud's managed build service: you describe the work as an ordered list of steps in a build configuration file, and each step runs inside its own container on Google's infrastructure, so you need no build server of your own. Artifact Registry is the managed store where finished images are kept, organised into repositories and controlled by access permissions. The usual pattern is that one build step produces the image and a push step sends it to the registry, where runtimes such as Cloud Run or GKE later pull it by reference.

Why it works: the build is repeatable, because the same source and recipe produce the same image, and the registry gives every stored image a digest, a fingerprint of its exact contents that does not change when the image is copied.

Worked example: a team commits an app with a Dockerfile, and a build is triggered. Step one runs a docker build command and tags the result with a name that includes the registry location, the repository, the image name and the commit ID. Step two pushes that image to Artifact Registry. The registry stores it and reports a digest, a sha256 value. The deploy stage then names the image by that digest, so it always runs exactly the bytes that were tested.

Common mistake: deploying the tag latest. A tag is only a label that can be moved to point at a different image later, so the running system may not match the code anyone reviewed, and rolling back becomes guesswork. Pin deployments to a specific commit tag or to the digest.

Consequence: if the build's identity lacks permission to write to the repository, the build fails at the push step; if the runtime lacks permission to read from it, the deployment fails when the service tries to start.

questions.prompt: Harbor Lane Software builds its invoice service, called billing-api, in the europe-west1 region, with the repository ledger-images and commit ID 7c3e9a1. Step 1: the build runs docker build and tags the result europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/harbor-lane/ledger-images/billing-api:7c3e9a1. Step 2: the build pushes that image to Artifact Registry, which reports the digest sha256:4b1f...e02a for it. Step 3 is missing from the team's notes. Their deploy stage is then run to start the Cloud Run service. What belongs in the missing step 3?
choices: Rebuild the image inside the deploy stage so the deployed bytes are produced fresh from the source.
Grant the Cloud Run runtime permission to write to the ledger-images repository before deploying.
Deploy the tag latest so the service picks up whichever image was pushed most recently.
Record the sha256 digest the registry reported in step 2 and name the image by that digest in the deploy.
questions.why: The digest is a fingerprint of the exact image contents that does not change when copied, so naming it in the deploy ensures the service runs the bytes that were pushed and reviewed.

questions.prompt: A team pushes an image to Artifact Registry and the registry reports a digest for it. Which statement describes that digest?
choices: The repository's access permissions listing which service accounts may pull images.
The number of layers the Dockerfile produced during the build.
A human-friendly name the team can reassign to a newer image at any time.
A fingerprint of the image's exact contents that stays the same when the image is copied.
questions.why: A digest is a fingerprint of an image's exact contents and does not change when the image is copied, unlike a tag, which is only a movable label.

questions.prompt: Quarry Peak Logistics runs a Cloud Build job. The docker build step succeeds, but the push step to Artifact Registry fails with a permission error. Which fix addresses the actual failure?
choices: Shrink the Dockerfile so the image is smaller before it is pushed.
Give the Cloud Run service that runs the app read access to the repository.
Switch the deploy configuration to use the tag latest so the push step is skipped.
Grant the build's identity permission to write to the target repository.
questions.why: A push fails at that step when the build's identity lacks permission to write to the repository, so the build's identity needs write access; read access for the runtime addresses a different failure.

questions.prompt: A team's deploy config names its image as repo/app:v2. A later build pushes new code under the same tag v2, overwriting the label. What is the main risk?
choices: The digest changes on every push, so Cloud Run stops pulling the image entirely.
The build is no longer repeatable because Cloud Build deletes earlier steps from the configuration.
Deploys can run code nobody reviewed, and rolling back to the earlier version becomes unclear.
Artifact Registry will refuse the second push and keep the old image in place.
questions.why: A tag is only a movable label, so after it is reassigned the running system may not match the reviewed code and the earlier version is hard to recover.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we build the container image once in the pipeline and store it, instead of having each server build from source when it starts. Explain the idea to them in your own words, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Building once and storing the image means every environment runs the same bytes that were tested. If each server built from source at startup, two servers could end up with different library versions or different results, and a server would spend time building before it could serve traffic. Cloud Build makes the image from the code and Dockerfile, and Artifact Registry keeps it with a digest that identifies its exact contents. The tradeoff is that the stored images need management: they take storage, old ones pile up, and the build and runtime identities need correct read and write permissions. Also, a fix in a base image does not reach stored images until we rebuild, so we have to schedule rebuilds deliberately.
rubricPoints: Explains that one stored image gives identical, repeatable deployments across environments
Distinguishes the build step (Cloud Build) from the storage step (Artifact Registry)
Notes that pinning by digest or commit tag avoids drift that a moving tag like latest causes
Names a real tradeoff such as storage upkeep, permissions, or the need to rebuild for base-image fixes

suggested.rationale: Choosing which build and storage service fits a scenario is exam-style reasoning that a short situation to work through teaches better than reading alone.

lessons.plain: Imagine a factory that only ships a product if its label proves it passed inspection at the right station, checked by an inspector the company trusts. Build provenance is the written record of how a piece of software was made: where the source came from, which build steps ran, and who or what ran them. Binary Authorization is a checkpoint at the door of the running system. Before it lets a container image start, it checks that the image carries signed proof from trusted build steps. An image without that proof is stopped, even if someone copied it in by hand. This lesson explains how those two pieces fit together in Google Cloud.
lessons.guessPrompt: A teammate builds a container image on their laptop and pushes it straight to production, skipping the normal pipeline. What single control would you want in place so the production platform refuses that image, and why might checking only the image's name or tag not be enough?
lessons.teach:
Build provenance is a record describing how an artifact was produced: the source revision, the build steps, the builder, and the inputs. An attestation is that record plus a cryptographic signature made with a private key that belongs to a trusted party. An attestor is the named identity that holds the key and is allowed to vouch for a build. A Binary Authorization policy is a rule set attached to a deployment target, such as a GKE cluster or a Cloud Run service, that lists which attestors must have signed an image before it may run.

Why it works: the check does not trust the image name, the tag, or whoever pushed it. It trusts only a signature it can verify with a public key. A tag such as prod-ready can be moved to point at different contents, but an image digest, a fixed fingerprint of the exact bytes, cannot change without breaking any signature tied to it.

Worked example: a Cloud Build pipeline builds an image from commit 4f2a, records provenance, and an attestor signs the digest sha256:abc123. The policy for the production cluster requires that attestor. A deploy asks to run sha256:abc123. The admission check at the cluster finds a valid signature from the required attestor and allows the deploy. Later, someone pushes a new image under the same name with digest sha256:def456 by hand. It has no attestation, so the check denies it.

Common mistake: writing a policy that looks for a tag like prod-ready instead of a signature from an attestor. Anyone with push rights can apply that tag, so it proves nothing about how the image was built.

Consequence: when the policy blocks an image, the rollout stalls, and a live service may not get the fix it needs. Teams therefore plan an explicit, audited exception path rather than switching enforcement off. Enforcement only applies where a policy is attached, so a deployment target without one has no protection.

questions.prompt: Lumen Bikes runs a GKE cluster called tracker-prod. Its Cloud Build pipeline builds from commit 71bd and records build provenance, which is the record of how the image was produced (source revision, build steps, builder, inputs). The attestor ci-signer, the named identity that holds the signing key, signs the image digest sha256:5e0f. The tracker-prod Binary Authorization policy, the rule set attached to that cluster, requires ci-signer. A deploy asks to run sha256:5e0f, and the admission check at the cluster finds a valid signature from ci-signer, so the deploy is allowed. Later, an engineer pushes a hand-built image to the tag stable, which resolves to digest sha256:b19c, and tries to deploy it. The check finds no attestation for sha256:b19c and denies it. Lumen now wants sha256:b19c allowed through the same policy. The one step that has to happen first is missing from this account: ___.
choices: Lumen renames the image to tracker:v2, since the check reads image names
Lumen adds the tag stable to the policy's allowed list so the check stops looking at digests
Lumen switches off enforcement for the tracker-prod namespace until the image is redeployed
ci-signer signs the digest sha256:b19c, which requires a build whose provenance is recorded and then attested
questions.why: The check trusts only a valid signature from a required attestor over the exact digest, so sha256:b19c needs its own attestation from ci-signer before the policy will accept it.

questions.prompt: In Binary Authorization, what is an attestor?
choices: A tag such as approved that marks an image as safe to run
A fixed fingerprint of the exact bytes of an image
The rule set attached to a deployment target that lists required signers
The named identity that holds a signing key and is allowed to vouch for a build
questions.why: An attestor is defined in the teaching text as the named identity that holds the private key and is allowed to vouch for a build by signing its attestation.

questions.prompt: Quill Labs writes a Binary Authorization policy that requires an image to carry the tag reviewed. A developer with push rights moves that tag onto an image nobody reviewed. What is the flaw in the policy?
choices: The policy is sound because only trusted staff have push rights
Anyone with push rights can apply the tag, so it says nothing about how the image was built
Tags are limited in length, so the check cannot read the full name
Cloud Run only accepts digests, so the policy is ignored at deploy time
questions.why: The teaching text says a tag can be applied by anyone with push rights and proves nothing about how the image was built, so the policy should require an attestor's signature instead.

questions.prompt: Ferncliff Tools runs a Cloud Run service that has no Binary Authorization policy attached. An unsigned image is deployed to that service. What happens?
choices: The image runs but is recorded as unsigned, and the deploy is still allowed
The image is blocked by a default policy that Cloud Run applies to every service
The image runs, because enforcement only applies where a policy is attached
Cloud Build rejects the deploy before it reaches the Cloud Run service
questions.why: The teaching text states that enforcement only applies where a policy is attached, so a target with no policy has no protection and the unsigned image is not checked.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what build provenance and a Binary Authorization policy each do, and name one limit or tradeoff of requiring signed images before every deploy.
lessons.modelAnswer: Build provenance is a signed record of how an image was built: the source commit, the build steps, and the builder. The pipeline produces it, and an attestor, a trusted identity with a signing key, vouches for it. A Binary Authorization policy sits on the deployment target, such as a GKE cluster or Cloud Run service, and says which attestors must have signed an image before it can run. When a deploy arrives, the check verifies the signature against the image digest, not the tag, so a hand-pushed image or a rebuilt tag is refused. The main tradeoff is operational: if the signing step breaks or the policy is too strict, legitimate deploys stop, including urgent fixes. So the team needs a documented, audited exception process, and it must remember that a target without a policy gets no protection at all.
rubricPoints: Provenance is a record of how an artifact was built, and an attestation is that record signed by a trusted attestor
The policy is attached to a deployment target and checks signatures, not image names or tags
Verification works on the image digest, so a tag moved or a hand-pushed image is refused
A real limit: strict enforcement can block urgent deploys, so an audited exception path is needed

suggested.rationale: Choosing which control stops an unverified image is an exam-style situation that is best reasoned through, and no listed mission covers signing or attestation.

lessons.plain: A unit test is a small automated check that runs one piece of your code, such as a single function, with chosen inputs and confirms the output matches what you expected. An AI coding assistant is a tool built into your editor that suggests or writes code from your written instructions. Using one to write unit tests means it can draft test cases quickly, including edge cases you might forget, such as empty input or bad values. The catch is that its draft is only a suggestion. You still decide what the correct behavior is, run the tests, and check that they would actually catch a bug.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose an AI assistant writes a test for a function that converts a fuel reading from text into a number, and the test passes on the first run. What would you check before trusting that test, and why might a passing test still be worthless?
lessons.teach:
A unit test checks one small unit of code in isolation. An assertion is the line in a test that states an expected result, such as the output should equal 6.5. An AI coding assistant is a language model inside your editor that proposes code and tests from a prompt. It works well for drafting many test cases quickly and for suggesting edge cases such as empty strings, zero, or negative numbers, because it has seen many similar functions. It does not know what your function is supposed to do unless you state the rules, so its expected values are guesses based on patterns and on the code you show it.

Worked example. Suppose the function parse_fuel turns text like 6.5 into a float of litres per 100 km, and it must raise a ValueError for negative or empty input. You ask the assistant for pytest tests covering empty input and negative values. Step 1: it returns three tests, one asserting that the text 6.5 gives 6.5, one expecting a ValueError for a negative value, and one expecting a ValueError for an empty string. Step 2: you run them and all three pass. Step 3: you read each expected value against the written rules, not against the code. Step 4: you temporarily change the function to return the absolute value, so negatives no longer raise. The negative-value test should now fail. If it still passes, the test is too weak.

Common mistake: treating a green run as proof. A test whose expected value was copied from the function's current output locks in a bug, so it passes forever.

Consequence: in a team pipeline, a bad test passes the build and the bug ships with a green check mark that looks like evidence of correctness. Also check your organisation's policy before pasting confidential code or secrets into an assistant.

An AI assistant speeds up drafting unit tests, but you remain responsible for the expected behavior, the test's ability to fail, and what the code is allowed to send to the tool.

questions.prompt: A developer asks an AI coding assistant for pytest tests of apply_coupon(price, percent), a function that returns the price after taking off the given percent. The written rules say apply_coupon(100, 20) must return 80.0, and percent above 100 must raise a ValueError. The assistant returns four tests and all four pass on the first run. The developer then compares each expected value with the written rules, and the 80.0 expectation matches them. Step 4 is missing: the developer must confirm that the discount test can actually fail. Which action completes that step?
choices: Copy the function's current output for apply_coupon(100, 20) into the expected value, since the code is the source of truth
Edit apply_coupon so it ignores the percent argument, run the tests, and confirm the discount test now fails
Ask the assistant to regenerate the tests until every one of them passes, then accept the whole set
Merge the tests now, because a green run in the pipeline shows that the expected values are correct
questions.why: Deliberately breaking the function and seeing the test fail shows the test can detect a wrong result, which a green run alone cannot show.

questions.prompt: In a unit test, what is an assertion?
choices: The line in a test that states the expected result the code is compared against
A comment in the code that explains the author's intent for the function
The summary report the pipeline prints after all tests have finished
The function under test, which the assistant generates from your prompt
questions.why: An assertion is the statement of the expected result; the test passes or fails depending on whether the actual result matches it.

questions.prompt: A function median_latency(samples) returns 0.0 when given an empty list. The written rules say an empty list must raise a ValueError. An assistant wrote a test expecting 0.0 for empty input, and that test passes today. What is the correct action?
choices: Keep the expected 0.0, since the test passes and the function has behaved that way for months
Change the assertion to expect a ValueError, as the written rule requires, and let it fail until the function is fixed
Replace the expected value with whatever the function returns today so the suite stays green
Delete the test, because an empty list is not a realistic input for a latency measurement
questions.why: The expected value must come from the written rules, not the current output, so the test should fail until the function is corrected.

questions.prompt: A team member wants to paste a module that contains a live cloud API key into an AI coding assistant to get unit tests written faster. Which step is correct?
choices: Paste the module after the tests are generated, because only the generated tests are sent to the tool
Remove the key first and check your organisation's policy, because the code you send leaves your machine and may be stored by the tool
Paste the module as is, since the assistant only reads the function and discards the rest
Paste it only if the key belongs to a test project, because test projects carry no risk
questions.why: Anything you send to an assistant may leave your environment, so secrets must be removed and the organisation's policy followed before sharing code.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has just started using an AI assistant for tests what the assistant is good for in writing unit tests, where you must not trust it, and one limit or tradeoff of relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: The assistant is good at producing a first draft of many test cases fast, including edge cases I might not think of, like empty input or boundary values. It also saves time on setup boilerplate. I would not trust it for the expected values. It does not know what the function is supposed to do, so it often copies whatever the code currently returns, which locks in bugs. My check is to write the rules myself, compare each assertion against them, and then break the function on purpose to confirm a test fails. The tradeoff is that reviewing generated tests takes real effort, and a suite that looks thorough can give false confidence if nobody checks that the tests can actually fail. We also need to confirm the tool is approved before sending it any proprietary code.
rubricPoints: The assistant drafts test cases and edge cases quickly but does not know the intended behavior.
Expected values must be checked against written requirements, not copied from the code's output.
A useful test must be able to fail, so break the code on purpose to confirm it catches the bug.
Passing tests only prove something if they are reviewed, and the tool must be allowed to see the code.

suggested.rationale: That mission asks you to harden a config loader with error handling and tests, which is exactly where you can practise reviewing assistant-drafted tests against the rules.

lessons.plain: Cloud Build is Google Cloud's managed service that runs a list of steps for you, such as every time someone changes the code. An integration test checks that several real parts of an application work together, such as the code plus a real database, instead of checking one function in isolation. Putting integration tests inside the automated build means every change is checked with those parts running before it is allowed to move forward. Think of an assembly line with an inspector who can stop the line when a part is faulty.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a unit test passes on one function but the release still breaks in production, what kind of check might have caught the problem, and why would it need more than one part running at a time?
lessons.teach:
A build configuration file is a text file, usually written in YAML, that lists the steps a build runs in order. Each step runs one container image with a command you choose. The steps share a workspace, a folder that every step can read and write, so one step can produce files that a later step uses. An integration test runs several real components together, such as your application plus a real database, so it can find problems that unit tests of single functions miss. Each step succeeds or fails by its exit code: zero means success and any other number means failure. When a step fails, the build is marked failed and later steps are skipped. This is how a test step acts as a gate in front of a deployment step.

Why it works: the build machine starts a fresh, disposable environment for each run, so the result does not depend on what happened on someone's laptop, and the database a step starts is one that the test owns rather than a shared one.

Worked example. Step 1 starts a throwaway database container on a network the steps share. Step 2 loops up to thirty times, checking whether the database port answers, and exits with an error if it never does. Step 3 runs the test command with the database address passed in as an environment variable. Step 4 deploys. Suppose one assertion in step 3 fails, so the test command exits with code 1. The build is marked failed, step 4 is skipped, and nothing reaches users.

Common mistake: wrapping the test command so its exit code is hidden, for example adding a pipe to another command or a fallback that always succeeds. The step then reports success, the build turns green, and the deploy runs on broken code.

Consequence: in a running system, a gate that quietly passes lets a bad release out, and the team learns about it from customers. A passing gate is only as trustworthy as the exit code behind it.

questions.prompt: A team builds an order service with a four-step build file. Step 1 starts a Postgres database container on the shared network. Step 2 runs a schema migration script against that database, which writes schema-version.txt into the shared workspace. Step 3 is still missing. It must run the integration test suite, pass the database address in as an environment variable, and let the build fail when any test fails. Step 4 deploys to Cloud Run. Which setup for step 3 correctly completes the gate?
choices: Run pytest in the background with an ampersand so the step ends at once and the deploy starts in parallel with it.
Append a fallback that always succeeds, so the build stays green while the team reviews failing tests later.
Run pytest directly, with the database address as an environment variable and no pipe or fallback.
Pipe pytest's output to a logging tool so the step reports success whatever the tests do.
questions.why: A failing test must produce a nonzero exit code that reaches the build, which marks it failed and skips step 4, and any pipe or fallback hides that code.

questions.prompt: In a build configuration file, what determines whether a single step counts as passed?
choices: Whether the step's log output contains the word PASS somewhere.
Its exit code: zero means success and any other number means failure.
How long the step took compared with the previous successful run.
Whether the container image used by the step has the newest version tag.
questions.why: Each step succeeds or fails by its exit code, with zero meaning success and any other number meaning failure.

questions.prompt: A build step runs the tests as ./run_tests.sh | tee out.txt. The script exits with code 2 when a test fails. What does the build see for this step?
choices: An exit code of 2, so the build is marked failed and later steps are skipped.
The failure is ignored because tee writes the output to a file.
An exit code of 0 from tee, so the step passes and the build continues.
A pause in the build until someone opens out.txt and reads the failure.
questions.why: Piping hides the test command's exit code, so the step reports success and the gate passes even though a test failed.

questions.prompt: An integration test passes on a developer's laptop but fails in the build. Which explanation fits the idea that build steps run in a fresh environment?
choices: Build machines are slower than laptops, so timeouts fire before the tests finish.
The build workspace is shared with the laptop by default, so files from one appear in the other.
The build starts a fresh, disposable environment, so any reliance on the laptop's leftover state or local database shows up there.
Integration tests cannot run on a laptop at all, so the laptop result is meaningless.
questions.why: Each build run starts clean, so a result that depended on something present only on the laptop will fail in the build, which is the point of the fresh environment.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an integration test running inside an automated build decides whether a release goes ahead, and name one limit or tradeoff of running integration tests there.
lessons.modelAnswer: The build runs its steps in order, and the integration test step is a command whose exit code decides the outcome. If the test command exits with zero, the build continues to the deploy step. If it exits with anything else, the build is marked failed and the deploy step is skipped. The test step usually starts its own dependencies first, such as a throwaway database, and waits until they are ready, so the result does not depend on a shared environment. One tradeoff is speed: integration tests start real services, so they take much longer than unit tests and slow every change. Another is that they can be flaky if a dependency takes an unpredictable time to become ready, so the team has to add proper readiness checks instead of fixed sleeps.
rubricPoints: Explains that each step passes or fails by its exit code and a failed step stops later steps such as deployment.
Describes starting real dependencies inside the build and waiting until they are ready before running tests.
Names a concrete limit, such as slower runs than unit tests or flakiness from unreliable readiness.
Notes that a hidden or ignored exit code can let a broken build pass.

suggested.rationale: Repairing a broken CI pipeline makes the learner work with build steps, test gating and exit codes, which is the core of this objective.

lessons.plain: Deploying from source code means handing your project folder to a hosting service and letting it turn your code into a running web service, instead of building a packaged image yourself. On Cloud Run, Google's service for running containers that start on demand and scale with traffic, one command uploads your folder, builds it into a container, and starts it. The result is a new version of your service that receives requests. The platform handles the packaging and running, so your job is to make sure the app is set up to be run that way. Knowing which parts are your job and which are the platform's is what keeps a deploy from failing quietly.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you run one command to deploy a folder of Python code to a container platform, what do you think must be true about the network port your app listens on for the platform to start sending it requests?
lessons.teach:
Cloud Run is a managed service that runs containers and starts them when requests arrive. A source deploy is a command that takes a folder of your code, has Google's build service turn it into a container image, stores that image in a registry (a private store of versioned images, here Artifact Registry), and starts that image as a new revision. A revision is one fixed version of your service. Each deploy normally creates one.

The build step looks at files such as requirements.txt or package.json to detect the language, then uses a buildpack, a tool that produces a working container without you writing a Dockerfile. If you include your own Dockerfile, that is used instead. Cloud Run starts the container and passes the port number in an environment variable named PORT. Your app must listen on all network interfaces at that port. Cloud Run only sends traffic to a revision after the container answers on that port.

Worked example. You have app.py that starts a web server, and you run a deploy command for a service named orders from the project folder. Step 1: the folder is uploaded. Step 2: the build detects Python and creates an image. Step 3: the image is pushed to the registry. Step 4: revision orders-00001 starts with PORT set to 8080, and the app binds to 0.0.0.0 on that port. Step 5: the revision answers, so traffic moves to it.

Common mistake. Hardcoding port 5000 or binding only to 127.0.0.1. The build succeeds and the container starts, but nothing answers on the port Cloud Run expects, so the deploy fails and the previous revision keeps serving.

Consequence. Traffic moves only to a revision that starts successfully, so a bad deploy usually leaves the old version live. Scaling settings such as minimum and maximum instances, plus memory and CPU per instance, are set on the service and apply to the new revision as well.

questions.prompt: A logistics team called Brightwater deploys a service named route-planner from a folder that contains a go.mod file and no Dockerfile. Their app binds to 127.0.0.1 on port 9000 and ignores the PORT variable. Here is the trace. Step 1: the folder is uploaded. Step 2: the build sees go.mod, identifies Go, and uses a buildpack to produce a container image. Step 3: the image is pushed to Artifact Registry as a versioned image. Step 4: revision route-planner-00003 starts with PORT set to 8080, but the app listens only on 127.0.0.1:9000, so nothing answers on 8080. Step 5 is missing. Which statement correctly fills it?
choices: Traffic moves to route-planner-00003 because the container started successfully.
Cloud Run retries the build using a Dockerfile it generates itself.
Cloud Run raises the maximum instance count so the app gets more chances to answer.
Traffic stays on the previous revision because the new one never answers on the PORT value.
questions.why: Cloud Run only sends traffic to a revision after its container answers on the PORT it was given, so a revision that never answers leaves the previous revision serving.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a buildpack in a Cloud Run source deploy?
choices: A tool that turns your source code into a working container without you writing a Dockerfile.
A setting that decides how many instances a service may run at once.
A saved copy of a running container that Cloud Run restarts after a crash.
A private store where versioned images are kept until they are deleted.
questions.why: A buildpack detects the language from files like requirements.txt or package.json and produces a runnable container image without a hand-written Dockerfile.

questions.prompt: A team's service has a minimum of 2 and a maximum of 10 instances. Their new code binds only to 127.0.0.1 on port 3000, while Cloud Run sets PORT to 8080. What happens to user traffic after they deploy?
choices: Traffic moves to the new revision, and the minimum of 2 instances keeps it answering on port 3000.
Traffic splits evenly between the old and new revisions while the instance count rises to 10.
Traffic stays on the previous revision, because the new revision never answers on the port Cloud Run expects.
The service stops serving entirely until the team sets a new maximum instance count.
questions.why: The app must listen on all interfaces at the PORT value, and Cloud Run only shifts traffic once the container answers, so a bad binding leaves the old revision live.

questions.prompt: A source folder contains both a package.json file and a Dockerfile. Which build method does the source deploy use?
choices: A combination of both, where the buildpack runs first and the Dockerfile edits its output.
Neither, so the deploy stops and asks you to choose one before the image is built.
The Dockerfile, because a Dockerfile you include yourself is used instead of the buildpack.
A buildpack that detects Node.js from package.json, with the Dockerfile ignored.
questions.why: When you include your own Dockerfile, the source deploy uses it in place of the buildpack, which is the rule the teaching text states directly.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what happens between running a source deploy to Cloud Run and the new version receiving traffic. Then name one limit or tradeoff of deploying from source instead of from an image you build and test yourself.
lessons.modelAnswer: When we deploy from source, the folder is uploaded and Cloud Build turns it into a container image, using a buildpack unless the project has its own Dockerfile. The image is stored in Artifact Registry, and Cloud Run starts it as a new revision. The container gets a PORT variable, and Cloud Run only shifts traffic to the revision once it answers on that port. If the app ignores PORT, the revision never becomes healthy and the old one keeps serving. The tradeoff is that the build is less controlled. The buildpack chooses the base image and dependencies, so two deploys of the same folder can differ if the upstream tools change. If we need exact reproducibility, we build and test our own image with a Dockerfile and deploy that image instead.
rubricPoints: Source deploy uploads the folder and builds a container image, using a buildpack or the project's Dockerfile.
The image is stored in a registry and started as a new revision of the service.
The app must listen on the port given in the PORT variable, or the revision never receives traffic.
Traffic moves to the new revision only after it starts successfully, so a failed deploy usually leaves the old version live.
A tradeoff is less control over the build, since buildpack choices can change over time.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly product-specific deploy steps and console or command facts, which are best learned by reading the deploy flow rather than through a listed mission.

lessons.plain: Some apps should not wait to be asked. Instead, something happens elsewhere, such as a file being uploaded or a message being published, and that event should start the app. A trigger is the wiring that watches for such an event and delivers it to a service ready to handle it. A Cloud Run service is a small web app that runs when it receives a web request, so it needs a trigger to be called automatically. Pub/Sub is a message queue: producers publish messages to a topic, and subscriptions pass them on to a receiver. Eventarc is a router that connects many kinds of Google Cloud events to a destination. In both cases the service receives an HTTP request carrying the event and must answer correctly, because the sender uses that answer to decide what happens next.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a service receives a message, does its work, then crashes before sending back a success reply. What do you think the message system does next, and why might that be a problem for the work already done?
lessons.teach:
A trigger is a configuration that links an event source to a target, here a Cloud Run service. Cloud Run services are stateless web endpoints that scale to zero when idle, so they only run when a request arrives. Pub/Sub is a managed message queue. A publisher sends messages to a topic. A subscription attached to that topic holds the messages until a receiver takes them. A push subscription sends each message as an HTTP POST to a URL you choose, which can be your Cloud Run service's address. Eventarc is a managed event router. It listens for events such as Cloud Storage changes, audit logs, or Pub/Sub messages, wraps each one in a standard event envelope called CloudEvents, and delivers it to a Cloud Run service over HTTP.

The mechanism is delivery plus acknowledgement. The sender keeps a message until the receiver returns a success status code such as 200. Any error or timeout means the message is redelivered later. This is at-least-once delivery, so the same event can arrive more than once. Your handler must therefore be idempotent, meaning that handling the same event twice has the same effect as handling it once.

Worked example: an order-created message is published to a topic. A push subscription targets the Cloud Run service URL and presents a service account identity. Cloud Run checks that identity against the invoker permission. The service reads the order ID, records it, and returns 200. Pub/Sub marks the message done. If the service had crashed and returned 500, Pub/Sub would retry after a backoff period.

A common mistake is forgetting to grant the sending identity permission to invoke the service. The request is then rejected, the handler never runs, and messages keep retrying until they reach a dead-letter topic if one is configured.

In a running system, a slow or failing handler causes repeated deliveries and a growing backlog, so the trigger's retry settings and the service's capacity must be configured together.

questions.prompt: Harbor Bread Co. stores photos of its loaves in a Cloud Storage bucket named loaf-photos. An Eventarc trigger is set up so that each new upload sends an event to a Cloud Run service called thumbnailer. Trace one upload. Step 1: a photo named rye.jpg is uploaded to loaf-photos. Step 2: Eventarc wraps the upload notice in a CloudEvents envelope. Step 3: [missing step, described below]. Step 4: thumbnailer writes a small copy of the photo, returns 200, and Eventarc marks the delivery as done. The missing step 3 is the moment when Eventarc, before sending the request, checks the identity that sends the event against the invoker permission on thumbnailer. Which statement correctly completes step 3?
choices: Cloud Run starts two instances of thumbnailer so that a second delivery is always handled.
Harbor Bread Co. renames the file to a timestamp so that the event envelope stays unique across any retries that happen later.
The sending identity is checked against the invoker permission on thumbnailer, and without that grant the request is rejected and the handler never runs.
Thumbnailer deletes rye.jpg from the bucket so that the same photo cannot trigger a second event.
questions.why: The invoker permission check on the sending identity is the gate that decides whether the request reaches the service at all, and the other options describe unrelated actions.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does a push subscription do with a Pub/Sub message?
choices: It converts the message into a CloudEvents envelope and routes it by event type to the right service.
It sends each message as an HTTP POST to a URL you choose, such as a Cloud Run service address.
It holds the message in a queue until the receiving program comes back and pulls it out.
It deletes the message after one delivery attempt, whether or not the receiver returns a success code.
questions.why: A push subscription is defined by sending each message as an HTTP POST to a chosen URL, while the other options describe pull subscriptions, Eventarc routing, or a wrong deletion rule.

questions.prompt: A Cloud Run service named invoice-check at Lindqvist Staffing receives an event from a Pub/Sub subscription. The handler hits a database outage and returns HTTP 503 for one event. What happens next, according to how the trigger mechanism works?
choices: The sender keeps the message and redelivers it later, so invoice-check may see the same event again.
The message is marked done because the service did send a response, so the event is not retried.
The event is converted into a new event with a fresh ID, so the failed copy is removed from the queue.
The sender retries immediately in an unlimited loop with no waiting period between attempts.
questions.why: Any error or timeout means the sender holds the message and redelivers it after a backoff, which is why a duplicate arrival is possible and the handler must be idempotent.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company runs a Cloud Run service named seat-hold-writer that receives messages from a Pub/Sub topic. The same message describing hold H-88 has been redelivered after a timeout. The service already recorded H-88 on the first delivery. What should the handler do on the second delivery?
choices: Check whether hold H-88 is already recorded, and if so return 200 without creating a second hold.
Delete the topic so that no further copies of H-88 can be delivered to any subscriber.
Return 500 so the sender stops retrying this message and the duplicate is dropped from the topic.
Create a second hold for H-88 because the message arrived as a new request and should be processed again.
questions.why: An idempotent handler produces the same result whether an event arrives once or twice, so checking for the existing record and returning success is the correct behaviour.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a Pub/Sub message reaches a Cloud Run service through a push subscription or Eventarc, and name one limit or tradeoff the team must design around.
lessons.modelAnswer: A publisher sends a message to a Pub/Sub topic. A push subscription, or an Eventarc trigger that wraps the event, sends it as an HTTP request to the Cloud Run service URL, using a service account that has permission to invoke the service. The service does its work and returns a success code, and only then does Pub/Sub consider the message delivered. The main limit is that delivery is at-least-once, so a message can arrive twice after a timeout or a retry. The handler therefore has to be idempotent, for example by recording the event ID and skipping duplicates. The team should also watch retry behavior and the dead-letter setting, because a failing handler creates backlog rather than losing messages.
rubricPoints: Describes the path: topic or event source, then push subscription or Eventarc, then HTTP request to the Cloud Run service.
Explains that the service must return a success code for the message to be acknowledged.
Names at-least-once delivery and the need for an idempotent handler.
States that the sending identity needs permission to invoke the service.

suggested.rationale: That mission makes the learner reason about redelivery and failing messages, which is the acknowledgement behaviour this objective depends on.

lessons.plain: When something happens in a cloud system, such as a file being uploaded or a message being published, the event needs to reach the code that should react to it. An event receiver is the listening arrangement that decides which events matter and where they are delivered. Eventarc routes events from many sources to a destination such as a Cloud Run service. Pub/Sub is a message queue that holds messages until a consumer takes them. Getting these settings right decides whether your code runs at all, and whether a delivered event is retried or lost.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a photo is uploaded to a storage bucket and you want a small service to resize it automatically, but the service is not running at the moment the upload happens. What do you think should sit between the bucket and the service, and what happens to the upload notice if the service is busy or down?
lessons.teach: An event is a small record that something happened, such as a file being written or a message being published. An event receiver is the configuration that catches those records and delivers them to your code. Two Google Cloud pieces do most of this work. Eventarc is a routing layer: you create a trigger that names an event source, an event type to match, and a destination, often a Cloud Run service. Pub/Sub is a managed message bus: a topic receives messages from publishers, and a subscription holds them for consumers. A push subscription sends each message as an HTTP POST to an endpoint you provide; a pull subscription has the consumer ask for messages itself. Eventarc uses Pub/Sub underneath to carry events.  Why it works: the sender never needs to know your service exists, and the queue absorbs bursts while your service scales. The receiver acknowledges an event by returning a success status, and anything else tells the system to try again later. Delivery is at least once, so the same event can arrive more than once.  Worked example: a bucket receives an upload. First, storage emits a create event. Second, an Eventarc trigger matches that event type and forwards it to the Cloud Run service's URL as an HTTP POST in the CloudEvents format. Third, the service reads the event, does the work, and returns a 2xx status. Fourth, the trigger treats that status as delivered. If the service returns an error instead, the event is retried with increasing delays.  Common mistake: returning a success status before the work finishes, or after it has failed, which either loses work or hides errors. Another is assuming exactly-once delivery and writing a handler that charges a customer again on every retry.  Consequence: if the identity used by the trigger or subscription lacks permission to call the service, every event is rejected, the queue grows, and no code runs at all. Event receivers must be configured and tested as carefully as the handler itself.

questions.prompt: A parcel-tracking company sends warehouse scanner messages through a Pub/Sub topic named parcel-scans. A push subscription named scan-push delivers each message as an HTTP POST to https://tracker-svc-demo.example.run.app/scan. Step 1: a warehouse scanner publishes a message containing a parcel ID to parcel-scans. Step 2: the subscription sends that message to the /scan endpoint as an HTTP POST. Step 3: the handler finds the parcel, updates its location, and returns HTTP 200. Step 4 (missing from this walkthrough): the handler's database is briefly unavailable, so it returns HTTP 503 for a scan it could not record. Complete step 4: what does Pub/Sub do with that message?
choices: Pub/Sub marks the message as delivered and deletes it, then reports the failure to the warehouse scanner.
Pub/Sub skips the message and moves on to the next one, leaving the failed scan unrecorded with no retry.
Pub/Sub treats the non-success status as not delivered and tries the message again later, with increasing delays between attempts.
Pub/Sub immediately POSTs the same message again with no delay, repeating until the handler returns 200.
questions.why: Any status other than a success status means the receiver has not acknowledged the message, so Pub/Sub retries it later with increasing delays.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does a push subscription do with each message it holds?
choices: It sends the message as an HTTP POST to an endpoint you provide, so your service does not need to ask for messages.
It forwards the message to a topic that has no subscribers, so that other topics can read it.
It stores the message permanently in a database so that later queries can search it by content.
It holds the message until a consumer in your code asks for it, then deletes it once it has been read.
questions.why: A push subscription sends each message as an HTTP POST to an endpoint you supply, which is the defining behaviour of push delivery.

questions.prompt: An Eventarc trigger uses a service account that does not have permission to call the Cloud Run service it targets. Which outcome follows?
choices: The handler runs but its results are discarded, while the trigger reports every event as delivered.
Every event is rejected, the queue grows, and no handler code runs at all until the permission is fixed.
Events are queued for the handler and delivered once the handler is redeployed, without any permission check.
Eventarc detects the missing permission and grants it automatically on the first event, so nothing is lost.
questions.why: When the trigger's identity cannot call the service, every event is rejected, so the queue grows and no code runs.

questions.prompt: A payment handler charges a customer each time it receives an event, and a developer assumes each event arrives exactly once. A customer is charged twice after a retry. What change best addresses this?
choices: Return HTTP 500 on every request so that the system never retries the event at all.
Return HTTP 200 before the charge runs, so the system never sends the same event again.
Make the handler idempotent, so that handling the same event a second time does not repeat the charge.
Switch from a push subscription to a pull subscription so that each event is delivered only once.
questions.why: Delivery is at least once, so duplicates happen; making the handler safe to repeat is the fix, not changing the status or subscription type.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an uploaded file's event reaches a Cloud Run service through Eventarc and Pub/Sub, and name one limit or tradeoff of this design that they must handle in their code.
lessons.modelAnswer: The storage bucket emits an event when a file is written. An Eventarc trigger matches that event type and forwards it to our Cloud Run service over HTTP, wrapped in the CloudEvents format. Eventarc uses Pub/Sub underneath, which holds the message until delivery is acknowledged, so a burst of uploads queues rather than overwhelming the service. The service must return a success status only after the work is actually done; any error status causes the event to be sent again. The tradeoff is at-least-once delivery: the same event can arrive more than once and possibly out of order, so the handler must be idempotent, for example by recording the event ID and skipping duplicates. The trigger's identity also needs permission to call the service, or events are rejected and pile up.
rubricPoints: Eventarc matches events from a source by type and routes them to a destination such as Cloud Run
Pub/Sub buffers messages and delivers them by push or pull, absorbing bursts
A success status acknowledges delivery; an error status causes retries
Delivery is at least once, so the handler must be idempotent
The invoking identity needs permission to call the service or events are rejected

suggested.rationale: The messaging engine would let the learner trace events through a topic and subscription with retries and duplicates, which is the core of configuring receivers.

lessons.plain: An API is the doorway other programs use to ask your application for things. Once you publish one, you need ways to manage it: version numbers so older callers keep working, rules about who may call it, limits on how often they may call it, and a record of what happened. Apigee is Google Cloud's API management product. It sits in front of your backend services as a gateway, so these rules live in one managed place instead of being rebuilt inside every service. Think of it as a reception desk that checks credentials, sends each visitor to the right office, and keeps a count of visits.
lessons.guessPrompt: If ten different apps call your backend directly and you want each app limited to 100 calls an hour, where would you rather enforce that limit: inside every backend service, or once in front of all of them? Why?
lessons.teach: An API (application programming interface) is a set of addresses and rules that lets other programs call your application. An API gateway is a component that sits between those callers and your backend services and receives every request first. Apigee is Google Cloud's managed API gateway and management product. In Apigee you build an API proxy, a public-facing endpoint that runs a sequence of policies and then forwards allowed requests to a target endpoint, which is the real backend. A policy is one small rule step, such as verifying an API key, enforcing a quota, or rewriting a path. Versioning means publishing the API under labels such as /v1 and /v2 so that old clients keep using the old contract while new clients move to the new one. The gateway works because the same checks run on every request before any backend code executes, so the rules are consistent and changed in one place. Worked example: a driver app calls https://api.example.com/v2/positions with an API key header. Step 1: the proxy matches the /v2 base path and routes the call to the version 2 backend. Step 2: a verify-key policy looks the key up; if it is missing or revoked, the gateway returns 401 and stops. Step 3: a quota policy counts this key's calls in the current hour; over the limit, it returns 429. Step 4: the request is forwarded to the target backend. Step 5: the response goes back to the app, and the gateway logs the call. Common mistake: leaving the backend reachable on its own public address. Anyone who finds that address skips every policy, so keys and quotas protect nothing. Consequence: during a surge from one unauthenticated caller using that direct address, the backend absorbs the full load and its capacity runs out for everyone else. A gateway only protects the traffic that is forced through it.

questions.prompt: A company called Parkwise runs a parking-payment API. A call to https://pay.parkwise.example/v3/sessions arrives with an API key header and passes through the gateway, which is the managed component that receives every request before the backend does. Step 1: the proxy matches the /v3 base path and routes the call to the version 3 backend. Step 2: a verify-key policy checks the key; a valid, active key passes, and an unknown key gets a 401 and the call stops. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the request is sent to the target backend, which only understands paths beginning with /sessions and has no version prefix. Which step 3 makes the forwarded request work?
choices: The gateway stores the full response and returns it without checking the key on later calls.
A quota policy counts this key's calls per day and returns 429 when the daily limit is passed.
A path-rewrite policy removes the /v3 prefix so the backend receives /sessions.
The backend's own public address is handed back to the caller so later calls can skip the gateway.
questions.why: The backend expects paths without the version prefix, so a path-rewrite policy must strip /v3 before the request is forwarded, while the quota policy would only count calls and not change the path.

questions.prompt: In this course, what is the core job of an API gateway such as Apigee placed in front of a backend service?
choices: To store the backend's database records so the backend can restart faster.
To send copies of backend logs to a separate analytics project for long-term storage.
To compile the backend's source code into container images for deployment.
To receive every incoming request first and run its policy checks before any backend code executes.
questions.why: The teaching text defines the gateway as the component that receives every request first, and its checks run before the backend code, which is the reason its rules stay consistent.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company, Lumen Tickets, puts an API proxy with a quota policy in front of its seat-booking backend. A reseller discovers the backend's own public address and calls it directly at high volume, with no key. What is the most likely result?
choices: The reseller's calls are counted against the quota, but the response is slower because the proxy is bypassed.
The reseller skips every policy, so no key check or quota applies and the backend's capacity can be exhausted for other callers.
The gateway returns 401 for every call, which protects the backend from the surge.
The quota policy automatically blocks the reseller because the backend is still registered to the proxy.
questions.why: The gateway only protects traffic forced through it, so a caller who reaches the backend directly skips the key check and quota, and the backend absorbs the full load.

questions.prompt: A fitness app version 1.4 still calls /v1/workouts, and the team wants to change a field in the workout response. Which approach keeps the existing app working while new clients adopt the change?
choices: Ask every user to update the app before the change is made, then remove the old path the same day.
Publish the changed contract under a new /v2 path, keep /v1 routed to the old backend, and move new clients to /v2.
Replace the /v1 proxy so that old and new clients both receive the changed response from the same path.
Turn off the gateway for /v1 and let the app call the backend directly with its existing address.
questions.why: Versioning exists so that old clients keep the old contract while new clients use the new one, so keeping the old path intact is the approach that avoids breaking current users.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would version, expose, and secure a public API using Apigee, and name one limit or tradeoff of putting a gateway in front of your services.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would publish each major API version under its own path, such as /v1 and /v2, with a separate API proxy or route for each, so existing clients keep their contract while new clients adopt the new one. To expose it, the proxy's public endpoint is the only address callers see, and it forwards to the backend as the target endpoint. To secure it, I would attach a key verification or OAuth token check as the first policy, then a quota policy per key, and make sure the backend only accepts traffic from the gateway. The main tradeoff is that the gateway becomes an extra hop that adds latency and a new component to operate and monitor; if it fails or is misconfigured, every API goes down with it, so it needs its own availability planning.
rubricPoints: Versioning uses separate paths or routes per major version so old clients are not broken.
The gateway is the only public entry point, with the backend reachable only through it.
Security is applied through policies such as key or token verification and quotas.
Names a real limit or tradeoff such as added latency, a new point of failure, or operational cost.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers API gateway configuration, so reading the concepts and product catalogue is the best fit for this objective.

lessons.plain: Think of a shop that needs several identical cashiers working at once. You write the job down once: which uniform, which till software, how many cashiers. A manager keeps that many cashiers on shift, replaces anyone who leaves, and sends customers to whichever cashier is free. Google Kubernetes Engine, called GKE, does this for containers. A container is a packaged copy of your application. You give GKE the packaged image and a description of how many copies you want. GKE runs them on a cluster of machines, keeps the count right, and gives them one steady address. Deploying here means handing over that description, not copying files onto a server by hand.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you tell a platform to run three copies of your app and one of the copies crashes, what do you think should happen next, and who should be responsible for making it happen: you or the platform?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A container image is a packaged, read-only snapshot of an application together with the libraries it needs. A cluster is the set of machines GKE manages; each machine is a node. A Pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes runs: one or more containers that share a network address and start and stop together. A Deployment is an object that states a desired result, such as keep three Pods running this image, and a controller keeps reality matching that statement. A Service gives a set of Pods one stable address. It finds its Pods through label selectors, which are matching key-value tags attached to Pods.

Why it works: you rarely start Pods yourself. You declare the image, the replica count and the labels. The controller constantly compares desired state with actual state and creates or removes Pods to close the gap. When you change the image tag, the Deployment starts new Pods and retires old ones a few at a time. This is a rolling update, and it keeps traffic flowing. Kubernetes also keeps the revision history, so you can go back to an earlier version.

Worked example. You deploy an app called positions-api with replicas set to 3, image tag 1.4.2, and label app equals positions. Step 1: the Deployment asks for three Pods. Step 2: the scheduler places each Pod on a node with spare capacity. Step 3: the Service with selector app equals positions collects the three Pod addresses. Step 4: you change the tag to 1.4.3. The controller starts one new Pod, waits until it runs, removes one old Pod, and repeats until all three run 1.4.3.

Common mistake: using a floating tag such as latest, or editing a running Pod by hand. Then nothing records which build is live, and a restart may pull a different build from the one you tested.

Consequence: if the Service selector does not match the Pod labels, the Service has no endpoints. The Pods can be healthy and running while callers still get refused, because traffic has nowhere to go.

questions.prompt: A team deploys returns-api, a new internal service, to GKE. Their Deployment asks for 4 Pods running image returns-api:3.2.0, and each Pod carries the label team=returns. Their Service uses the selector app=returns-api. The trace so far: Step 1: the Deployment asks for four Pods. Step 2: the scheduler places each Pod on a node with spare capacity, and the Pods start and run. Step 3 is missing from this trace and must be filled in. Step 4: callers send requests to the Service address and get connection refused. Which choice correctly fills the missing Step 3?
choices: The Service copies the image tag from the Deployment and starts its own Pods.
The Deployment changes its selector to team=returns and restarts all four Pods.
The scheduler moves the Pods onto a single node so the Service can reach them.
The Service looks for Pods whose labels match app=returns-api, finds none, and so has no endpoints to send traffic to.
questions.why: A Service finds its Pods through label selectors, so with no Pod carrying app=returns-api it has no endpoints, which is why callers are refused even though the Pods are running.

questions.prompt: A checkout-web Deployment is set to 6 replicas of image tag 5.0.1. The controller counts 4 Pods running that image, and none are failing. What does the controller do next?
choices: It deletes all four Pods and starts six fresh ones.
It lowers the replica count to 4 to match what is running.
It creates two more Pods running 5.0.1 to close the gap.
It waits for an operator to enter a new replica count before acting.
questions.why: The controller continually compares desired state with actual state and creates or removes Pods to close any gap, so it adds two Pods here.

questions.prompt: A team sets the image tag on a billing worker's Deployment to latest. What is the main risk?
choices: The Deployment refuses to create any Pods until a numbered tag is added.
After a restart, the Pods may pull a different build from the one tested, and nothing records which build is live.
The Service selector stops matching the Pods' labels.
Kubernetes deletes the revision history for that Deployment at once.
questions.why: A floating tag like latest can point to a different build over time, so a restart may pull an untested build and the revision history no longer shows which version is live.

questions.prompt: A Deployment for order-events runs 3 healthy Pods labelled track=stable. Its Service uses the selector track=beta. A caller sends a request to the Service. What happens?
choices: The Pods restart, and the Service then matches them and answers.
The caller is refused, because the Service has no endpoints.
The request reaches one of the Pods at random and gets a normal reply.
The Service automatically relabels the Pods to track=beta and forwards the request.
questions.why: Because no Pod carries the label track=beta, the Service has no endpoints, so traffic has nowhere to go even though the Pods are healthy.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a Deployment, a Pod and a Service each do when you deploy a containerized app to GKE, and name one limit of a rolling update.
lessons.modelAnswer: A Pod is the smallest thing Kubernetes runs: one or more containers sharing an address. You almost never create Pods directly. A Deployment holds the desired state: which image, how many replicas, and which labels. Its controller keeps that many Pods running and replaces any that die. A Service sits in front of them and gives them one stable address. It chooses Pods by label, so callers never need to track individual Pod addresses, which change as Pods come and go. To ship a new version you change the image tag in the Deployment, and a rolling update replaces Pods a few at a time. The limit is that a rolling update only helps if the new version starts cleanly and works alongside the old version during the overlap. If the new version fails on startup or breaks a shared database schema, the rollout can stall or hurt users, so you still need a way to roll back.
rubricPoints: A Pod is the smallest running unit, made of one or more containers sharing an address.
A Deployment declares desired state, such as image and replica count, and a controller keeps it true.
A Service gives Pods a stable address and selects them by label.
A rolling update replaces Pods gradually, and its limit is that old and new versions must coexist safely or the rollout must be rolled back.

suggested.rationale: Deployment strategies such as rolling updates are the core skill here, and a planned engine would let the learner practise changing versions safely and reasoning about the overlap.

lessons.plain: A health check is a regular question the platform asks your running app: are you alive, and are you ready to take visitors? Kubernetes is a system that runs many copies of your app in units called pods and decides where traffic goes. If one copy stops responding properly, the system needs to know, so it can stop sending requests to that copy or restart it. Health checks let an app report its own condition. That makes the whole service more likely to stay up even when one copy breaks.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web app runs as three copies behind one address. One copy gets stuck in an endless loop, but its process is still running. Without any extra setup, what do you think happens to the users whose requests land on that copy, and what would you add to the app so the platform can tell running apart from working?
lessons.teach: A pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes runs, usually one container. A probe is a check that the kubelet, the agent on each machine that runs pods, performs on a container on a schedule. There are three probe types. A liveness probe asks whether the container is stuck in a way only a restart fixes. If it fails repeatedly, the kubelet restarts the container. A readiness probe asks whether this container should receive traffic right now. If it fails, the pod is removed from the list of endpoints (the pod addresses a Service sends requests to), but the container is not restarted. A startup probe holds off the other two while a slow-starting app finishes booting. Each probe can use an HTTP request, a TCP connection, or a command, and has settings such as periodSeconds, which is how often it runs, and failureThreshold, which is how many failures in a row count as a problem. The reason this works is that the platform cannot see inside your app. The app exposes a cheap endpoint, and the probe turns the answer into an action. Worked example: a pod has a readiness probe that calls an HTTP path every 10 seconds with failureThreshold set to 3. At second 0 the app is loading its cache, so the path returns an error. Failures are recorded at 10, 20 and 30 seconds. After the third failure the pod is marked not ready and drops out of the Service. At second 60 the cache is loaded, the path succeeds once, and the pod rejoins. No restart happened, because readiness never restarts anything. The common mistake is pointing the liveness probe at a path that also checks the database. When the database has a brief outage, every pod fails liveness at the same moment, the kubelet restarts all of them, and the restarts add load to a system that was already struggling. Keep dependency checks in readiness, and keep liveness limited to whether this process can make progress. In a running system, correct readiness probes keep traffic away from warming or stuck pods, while a badly chosen liveness probe turns a short dependency blip into a restart storm.

questions.prompt: A reporting service runs in a pod whose liveness probe calls the path /healthz every 15 seconds with failureThreshold set to 2. The /healthz handler also checks whether the reporting database is reachable. At second 0 the database becomes unreachable. The probe fails at second 15 and again at second 30. Step 1: after the second failure at 30 seconds, the kubelet ____. Step 2: the replacement container starts at 31 seconds, the database is still down, so the probe fails at 46 and 61 seconds and the kubelet acts again.
choices: keeps running the container and waits for failureThreshold to reach 3 before acting
sends an alert to the operator but leaves the container alone
restarts the container
removes the pod from the Service endpoints and waits for the readiness probe to pass
questions.why: A liveness probe that fails failureThreshold times in a row makes the kubelet restart the container, and removing a pod from endpoints is the job of a failed readiness probe, not a liveness probe.

questions.prompt: A team wants a check that decides whether a container should currently receive requests from a Service, without restarting the container when the check fails. Which probe type fits?
choices: liveness probe
startup probe
readiness probe
command probe run once at container creation
questions.why: A readiness probe controls whether a pod is listed as an endpoint for traffic, and a failure removes the pod from the endpoints without restarting it.

questions.prompt: A container's readiness probe fails four times in a row, which meets the failureThreshold. Which outcome is correct?
choices: The pod is deleted and rescheduled onto another node.
The kubelet restarts the container immediately.
The pod is marked not ready and removed from the endpoints, but the container keeps running.
The Service sends the pod extra traffic to compensate.
questions.why: Readiness failures take the pod out of the endpoint list and never restart the container, which is the key difference from a liveness failure.

questions.prompt: A Java service takes about 90 seconds to load its model before it can answer any request, and liveness checks begin failing during that load. Which probe should be added to stop the liveness and readiness probes from acting during startup?
choices: a readiness probe pointed at the database
a TCP probe that restarts the container after 10 seconds
a second liveness probe with a shorter periodSeconds
a startup probe, which holds off the other two probes until the app finishes booting
questions.why: A startup probe suspends the liveness and readiness probes while a slow-starting app is still booting, which prevents premature restarts.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we have both a liveness probe and a readiness probe, and why the liveness probe should not call the database. Explain it to them in your own words, and name one limit or tradeoff of using probes.
lessons.modelAnswer: Liveness and readiness answer different questions. Liveness asks whether the container is stuck in a state that only a restart fixes, so a failing liveness probe makes the kubelet restart the container. Readiness asks whether this copy should get traffic right now, so a failing readiness probe only removes the pod from the Service's endpoints and leaves it running. Pointing liveness at the database is a mistake because restarting our app does not fix a database outage. Every pod would fail together and restart, adding load exactly when the system is struggling. Dependency checks belong in readiness, so traffic pauses without any restarts. The tradeoff is that probes cost resources and can be misconfigured. A readiness probe that is too aggressive can pull healthy pods out during a brief blip, so we tune the period and failureThreshold. Probes also do not replace error handling and retries inside the application.
