A billing account that pays for the API calls made by a particular service.
A Google Cloud identity that belongs to an application or workload rather than to a human.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a service account as an identity owned by an application or workload instead of a person, and the other options describe unrelated things such as passwords, billing, or network allow-lists.

questions.prompt: A Cloud Run service at a different company, Quillmark Foods, has a service account that holds the Storage Object Viewer role on the bucket menu-archive-2023. The service then gets a permission denied error when reading from bucket recipe-drafts-2024. Which explanation fits the teaching text?
choices: The client library cached an old token that cannot be used for a second bucket.
The account's token expired, and it must wait for a longer-lived one to be issued.
Roles are granted on specific resources, so the viewer role on menu-archive-2023 does not grant any permission on recipe-drafts-2024.
Cloud Run blocks all reads from buckets whose names end in a year, regardless of roles.
questions.why: Authorization checks whether the identity holds a role that grants the needed permission on the resource being accessed, and a role granted on one bucket does not extend to another.

questions.prompt: A developer at Tallgrass Logistics commits a downloaded JSON key file for a service account into a shared code repository, and the repository is later made public. Based on the teaching text, what is the most important response?
choices: Rotate or delete that key so that anyone who copied it can no longer act as the account, then move the workload to use the attached identity instead.
Delete the code repository and assume the key has no further effect, since the key was only in the history.
Wait for the key to expire on its own, since keys become unusable after a few hours.
Grant the account a broader role so that its calls keep working while the team investigates.
questions.why: A downloaded key is a long-lived secret, so a leaked copy stays usable until it is rotated or deleted, and the safer design is to avoid such keys by attaching the identity to the workload.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to cloud how our application uses a service account to call a Google Cloud API. Name one limit or tradeoff of this approach, such as the risk of over-broad roles or of long-lived key files.
lessons.modelAnswer: Our service runs as its own service account, which is an identity for the program rather than a person. When it calls an API, the client library gets a short-lived token for that account, and the API checks whether the account has the role that allows the action. So the call works without anyone's password being stored in the code. The main tradeoff is that the account is only as safe as its permissions. If we grant a broad role to make an error disappear, any bug in the service can do much more than it should. A downloaded key file is a second risk, because it does not expire by itself and can leak. That is why we attach the identity to the workload, grant the narrowest role that works, and avoid key files.
rubricPoints: A service account is an identity for an application, not a human user.
Calls are authenticated with short-lived credentials obtained for the attached account, not stored passwords.
Roles should be granted narrowly, so the account holds only what the job needs.
Long-lived key files are a leak risk and are avoided when an attached identity is available.

suggested.rationale: That mission practises wiring a deployed workload's credentials correctly without exposing the secret, which is the same habit this objective needs.

lessons.plain: Observability means being able to ask a running program what it is doing, using evidence the program produces on purpose. Instrumenting code means adding that evidence to the code itself. There are three kinds. Metrics are numbers summed up over time, such as how many requests arrived per minute or how long the slowest tenth took. Logs are written records of individual events, such as an error with its details. Traces show the path one request took through several services, with timing for each step. When code is instrumented well, a problem that was invisible becomes a question you can answer from data instead of guessing. Google Cloud's observability tools collect all three in one place.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your checkout service sometimes takes 9 seconds to respond, but only for a few users, and the slowness appears only after a second service call. Which of metrics, logs, or traces would you add first to find which step is slow, and why?
lessons.teach:
Three signals. A metric is a number recorded repeatedly and aggregated, like a counter of requests or a histogram of latencies. It tells you how much and how often, cheaply. A log entry is a timestamped record of one event. It tells you what happened in detail. A trace is the record of one request as it travels across services. Each step of that journey is a span, a named segment with a start and end time. All spans from the same request share one trace ID, a unique identifier passed along with the request.

Why it works: metrics are small and cheap to keep, so they reveal that something changed. Logs and traces are richer and point to why and where. Correlation is the key idea. If each log line carries the trace ID of the request that produced it, you can move from a slow trace to the exact log lines for that request.

Worked example: a dispatch request enters service A and calls service B. Step 1: A starts a trace and receives trace ID abc. Step 2: A records a span named call-B with its start and end times. Step 3: A forwards abc in a request header to B. Step 4: B writes a log entry with severity ERROR and a trace field set to abc. Step 5: In the trace view, the B span lasts 8.7 seconds. Filtering logs by abc shows a timeout from a database call.

Common mistake: writing unstructured text such as 'request failed' with no request ID, or putting personal data and secrets into logs. Structured logs, meaning key-value fields such as severity, message and trace, can be searched and filtered. Free text cannot.

Consequence: if the trace ID is not passed across the service boundary, each service's data becomes a separate story, and the slow step cannot be linked to the request that failed.

questions.prompt: Harborline Tickets runs a checkout service and an inventory service, both on Cloud Run. A trace is the record of one request as it moves between services, and each step within it is a span, a named segment with start and end times. Here is how one checkout request is traced. Step 1: the checkout service receives the request and starts a trace with ID q7x. Step 2: checkout records a span named reserve-seats with its start and end times. Step 3: checkout forwards q7x in a request header to the inventory service. Step 4: [missing] Step 5: on the dashboard, the inventory service's error-rate metric shows a spike that lines up with the slow reserve-seats span. What should belong in Step 4 so that the failing inventory work can be linked back to this request?
choices: The inventory service starts a new, separate trace ID so its work is kept apart from checkout's trace.
The inventory service copies its error-rate metric into a log entry so the spike is easier to find.
The inventory service writes a structured log entry with severity ERROR and a trace field set to q7x.
The checkout service writes a free-text log line saying 'seat reservation failed' with no request ID.
questions.why: A structured log entry carrying the same trace ID is what lets the failing inventory work be tied to the one request, because the trace field matches the ID that was forwarded in Step 3.

questions.prompt: A team wants a signal that tells them how many payment requests failed per minute across all instances, and it must be cheap to store for months. Which signal fits best, and why?
choices: A span, because it has a start and end time for each step of a request.
A trace, because it records the full path of every request across services.
A metric, because it is a number recorded repeatedly and aggregated, which is cheap to keep and shows how often something happens.
A log entry, because it is a timestamped record of each event with full detail.
questions.why: Metrics are small aggregated numbers that show how much and how often, which suits a per-minute failure count kept long term.

questions.prompt: A booking service calls a pricing service, but the booking service does not forward its trace ID in the request header. An engineer later sees a slow pricing span and a pricing error log, but cannot find which booking request caused them. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The metric for pricing errors was aggregated too coarsely.
Each service's data became a separate story because the trace ID was not passed across the service boundary.
The pricing service was not given enough memory to write logs.
Spans cannot be stored when the request crosses two services.
questions.why: Without the shared trace ID in the header, the pricing service's spans and logs cannot be correlated to the booking request that triggered them.

questions.prompt: A developer writes log lines such as 'user login failed for jane.doe@example.com, password was wrong' as plain text. Which change best follows good logging practice for this application?
choices: Write the log as structured key-value fields such as severity and trace, and leave out the email address and password details.
Keep the email address but move it into a trace span name so it is easier to search.
Replace the log with a metric counter only, so no event detail is recorded at all.
Keep the text as it is, since more detail always makes a log more useful.
questions.why: Structured fields make logs searchable and filterable, and personal data and secrets should never be written into logs, so the password detail and email must be removed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what instrumenting code with metrics, logs and traces means, and name one limit or tradeoff of adding too much of it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Instrumenting means putting measurement points in our code so production tells us what it is doing. We record metrics, which are cheap aggregated numbers such as request counts and latency distributions, to notice that something changed and to alert on it. We write structured logs, with fields such as severity and a trace ID, to explain individual events. We pass a trace ID across service calls so each request's spans, which show how long each hop took, can be tied to that request's logs. The tradeoff is cost and noise. Metric labels with many unique values, such as user IDs, multiply the number of series and the bill. Verbose logs can bury the important lines or leak personal data. So we keep a small set of useful metrics, sample traces, and keep logs structured and free of secrets.
rubricPoints: Defines metrics, logs and traces by what each tells you
Explains that a shared trace ID links spans and logs for one request
Names a concrete tradeoff such as cost from high-cardinality labels or noisy or sensitive logs
Notes that logs should be structured and free of secrets or personal data

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a slow-request incident across metrics, logs and traces adds more than any single listed mission, since none of them has the learner instrument code.

lessons.plain: When a running app misbehaves, you need to see what it is doing rather than guess. Google Cloud Observability is the set of tools that collects that evidence. Metrics are numbers recorded over time, like requests per minute or error rate. Logs are written records of events the app noticed. Traces show the timing of one request as it moves through several services. Error reporting groups repeated crashes into one list. Think of a car dashboard plus a black box recorder: the numbers tell you something changed, the records tell you what happened, and a shared request ID lets you follow one failing request across services.
lessons.guessPrompt: A checkout page is suddenly slow, but only for some users, and the team does not know which part of the system causes the delay. Which kind of evidence would you check first, and why?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A metric is a number recorded at regular intervals, such as request count or error rate per minute. p95 latency means the time within which 95 percent of requests finish. A log entry is a timestamped record an app writes about something it did or failed to do. A trace is the timing record of one request as it passes through several services; each step inside it is called a span. A trace ID is a unique label stamped on that request so its spans and log lines can be matched together. Error Reporting groups repeated exceptions into one entry so a single bug is not counted a thousand times. Cloud Observability is the Google Cloud suite that stores and displays all of these.

Why it works. You rarely start with the detail. First a metric or alert tells you that something changed and roughly when. Then you narrow down: a trace shows which span got slower or failed, and the log lines carrying that same trace ID show the exact error and the inputs involved. Each signal answers a different question: is it happening, where is it, and why.

Worked example. An alert fires for the positions API. Step 1: the latency metric shows p95 rising from 200 ms to 2 s just after a 09:00 release. Step 2: you open a slow request's trace; one span, a database query, takes 1.8 s while the others are normal. Step 3: you copy that trace ID and filter the logs by it; the log line reports a cache miss followed by a full table scan. The release removed a cache key, and that is the cause to fix.

Common mistake. Engineers write log lines without a request or trace ID, so the logs cannot be tied to a trace and the search becomes guesswork. Log structured fields, including the trace ID, on every line.

Consequence. Without correlation, a slow incident spanning three services can take hours, because each team reads its own logs and none can prove which service started the delay.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking app's seat-hold service shows its error rate jumping from 0.1 percent to 6 percent just after a Tuesday afternoon deploy. Step 1: the error-rate metric shows the jump and the minute it started. Step 2: you open one failed request's trace and see that the span calling the inventory service returned an error after 30 ms, while the other spans look normal. Step 3 is blank here and you must fill it in: ___. Which action completes the investigation in the right order?
choices: Raise the alert threshold to 10 percent so the notifications stop while the team looks into it later.
Create a new metric for average CPU use across all services and wait a day for it to show a trend.
Copy that failed request's trace ID and filter the logs by it, so the log lines show the exact inventory error and the inputs sent.
Roll the service back to the previous version without reading any logs, then close the alert.
questions.why: After the trace has pointed to the failing span, the trace ID is what links that one request to its log lines, which then reveal the specific error and inputs.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a span?
choices: A single step of timing inside one request's trace as it moves through services.
A count of how many requests an app handled in one minute.
A unique label that is stamped on a request to match its log lines.
A grouped list of repeated exceptions shown as one entry.
questions.why: A span is one timed step inside a trace, while a metric is a count, a trace ID is a label, and Error Reporting groups exceptions.

questions.prompt: A nightly reconciliation job writes timestamped log lines with the account numbers it processed, but no request or trace identifier on any line. An engineer later sees a slow run across three services. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: Error Reporting refuses to group the job's exceptions into a single entry.
The job's timing is recorded as a metric with a p95 value, which removes the need for any logs.
The metrics for the job are deleted automatically by the platform after one night.
The log lines cannot be tied to the trace spans of the slow requests, so the team has to guess which service caused the delay.
questions.why: Without a shared identifier the log lines cannot be matched to the spans of the same request, so correlating the slow run across services becomes guesswork.

questions.prompt: A background worker hits the same database connection exception 4,000 times in one hour. What does Error Reporting most usefully show the team?
choices: Four thousand separate entries, one per failure, so each can be read individually.
A count of the exceptions as a metric, but with no grouping or stack information attached.
A single grouped entry for that exception, so the one bug is visible rather than counted thousands of times.
Nothing, because Error Reporting only handles exceptions from web requests and not from workers.
questions.why: Error Reporting groups repeated exceptions into one entry so a single underlying bug is not counted once per occurrence.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says, 'Errors went up on the dashboard, so let's read every log line from the last hour.' Explain to them how you would narrow down the cause using observability signals, and name one limit of the approach you would use.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not read everything. The dashboard metric tells us that errors rose and roughly when, so I start the search at that time window and filter to the affected service. Next I look at the error groups to see whether one exception dominates, because a single bug usually produces most of the count. Then I pick a failing request, open its trace, and find the span where the time or the error appears. The trace ID from that span lets me pull only the log lines for that one request, which show the actual message and the inputs. The limit of this approach is that traces are often sampled, and metrics are aggregated, so a rare failure may not appear in any trace I look at. In that case I widen the time window and check the logs directly, and I state that my conclusion rests on sampled evidence.
rubricPoints: Metrics show that something changed and when, but not why.
Traces locate which service or span is slow or failing.
Logs matched by trace ID give the exact error and inputs.
Error Reporting groups repeated exceptions so one bug is not read as many.
Names a limit such as sampling, aggregation, or logs missing trace IDs.

suggested.rationale: That mission has you read logs to find why an API is failing, which is the core habit of narrowing down an issue, though it uses a Linux server rather than Cloud Observability itself.

lessons.plain: When an application crashes or throws an error, the details are usually written to a log, which is a running record of events. Reading thousands of log lines to find out whether the same problem keeps happening is slow. Error reporting is a service that collects those error records, recognises when many of them are really the same underlying bug, and groups them into one entry. For each group it shows how often the error happens, when it first and last appeared, and a stack trace, the list of code steps that led to the failure. It works like a sorted pile of incident slips instead of a heap of receipts.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app logs 5,000 lines saying 'divide by zero' from three different servers over an hour. Before reading any further, what would you want a tool to tell you about those lines, and what would you still need to check yourself?
lessons.teach:
Error reporting is a service that gathers error events from your application, groups the ones that share a cause, and shows each group with counts and history. An error event is one recorded failure, usually an exception or a crash, that carries a message and a stack trace. A stack trace is the chain of function calls active at the moment of failure, listed from the outermost call down to the line that broke. A group is a set of events the service judges to have the same root cause, normally by matching the error type and the top frames of the stack trace.

Why it works: the same bug produces the same stack shape each time, so the service can count repeats instead of making you read every line. Each group shows the number of occurrences, the first and last time seen, and often the service and version involved, so you can tell whether a problem is new, growing, or already gone.

Worked example: a checkout service throws a timeout error 400 times in an hour. Step 1: each failure is recorded as an event with a stack trace ending in a call to the payment client. Step 2: the service sees the same error type and the same top frames in all 400, so it places them in one group. Step 3: the group shows a count of 400, first seen at 09:02, last seen at 10:01, and version 2.4. Step 4: you now know one bug is recurring since the 2.4 release, not 400 separate problems.

Common mistake: treating grouping as proof of one cause. Two different bugs can share a top frame and get merged, and one bug whose messages include changing IDs can split into several groups. Check the stack traces, not only the group title.

Consequence: in a running system, an error group whose count climbs after a deploy is an early warning, and a notification can tell the on-call engineer before customers report the problem. Error reporting shows what failed, where, and how often; it does not fix the code or prove the root cause.

questions.prompt: A ride-share app's pricing service logs 120 failures in one afternoon. Each event has the error type FareRoundingError and a stack trace whose top frames all sit in the same rounding function. Step 1: each failure is recorded as an event with a stack trace. Step 2: the service places events that share the error type and top frames into one group. Step 3 is missing from this write-up. Step 4: the group shows count 120, first seen 13:05, last seen 16:40, version 5.0, so the problem has recurred since release 5.0. Which choice correctly fills the missing Step 3?
choices: Rewrite the rounding function right away, because the grouping itself proves the cause.
Add the 120 events to the counts from other groups to get the total number of distinct bugs.
Open several events in the group and check that their stack traces truly match before treating the group as one bug.
Clear the events from the service so the count resets to zero before the next release.
questions.why: Grouping can merge different bugs that share a top frame, so you check the stack traces themselves before concluding the group is one cause.

questions.prompt: Which of these best describes a stack trace?
choices: A label the service gives to events that it judges to share a cause.
The chain of function calls that were active at the moment of failure, listed from the outermost call down to the line that broke.
A message sent to the on-call engineer whenever a group's count grows.
A count of how many times one error has occurred within an hour.
questions.why: A stack trace is the ordered list of active function calls at the moment of failure, from outermost to the breaking line, as the teaching text defines it.

questions.prompt: A team finds that two different bugs ended up in one error group. Based on how grouping works, what is the most likely reason?
choices: The service groups events by time of day, so unrelated errors at the same hour merge.
The two bugs share an error type and top frames, and grouping matches on those features.
The version number was missing, so the service cannot separate one release from another.
The events were recorded without any stack trace, so the service had nothing to compare.
questions.why: Grouping normally matches on the error type and the top frames of the stack trace, so two bugs sharing both can be merged into one group.

questions.prompt: A group's count rises sharply right after a deploy. What is the best immediate use of that signal?
choices: Delete the group so the dashboard stays clean for the next release.
Treat it as an early warning and alert the on-call engineer.
Wait for the service to resolve the group automatically before acting.
Conclude the code is fixed, because error reporting has already identified the cause.
questions.why: A climbing count after a deploy is the early warning the teaching text describes, and it lets the on-call engineer react before customers report the problem.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what error reporting does with a thousand identical exception lines, and name one limit you would check before trusting its grouping.
lessons.modelAnswer: Error reporting collects the error events from our application logs and groups events that look like the same bug, using the error type and the top of the stack trace. Instead of a thousand lines, we see one group with a count, a first-seen and last-seen time, and the version it appears in. That tells us whether the problem is new, rising, or stopped after a deploy. The limit is that grouping is a heuristic: two different bugs that fail in the same function can be merged into one group, and one bug whose messages include changing IDs can split into several. So before acting, I open a few stack traces in the group and confirm they really share a cause. The tool tells us where and how often something failed; it doesn't tell us why, and it doesn't fix anything.
rubricPoints: Explains that error events are collected from logs and grouped by a shared cause, such as error type and top stack frames.
Says what a group shows: occurrence count, first and last seen times, and version or stack trace.
Names a limit: grouping can merge distinct bugs or split one bug into several groups.
States that the tool shows where and how often a failure happens, not the fix or the proven root cause.

suggested.rationale: That mission has you read log evidence to find why an API is failing, practising the same grouping and tracing habit by hand.

lessons.plain: When one user request passes through several services, each service writes its own logs and timings, and they can look unrelated. Distributed tracing is a way to follow one request across all those services. A shared tag, called a trace ID, is attached when the request starts and is passed along with every call it makes. Later you can search for that tag and see every step the request took, in order, and how long each step lasted. It is like giving a parcel a tracking number that every courier scans, so you can see where it got stuck.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user reports one slow request. Three services each have logs full of lines, and none of the lines share an identifier. How would you find the lines that belong to that one request, and what could go wrong with your method?
lessons.teach:
A trace is the full record of one request as it moves through several services. A span is one timed step inside that trace, such as 'the API handled the request' or 'the API called the route service'. Each span has its own span ID. A child span records the span ID of the span that started it, so a tool can rebuild the tree of calls. The trace ID is one identifier shared by every span that belongs to the same request. It is the thread that ties the pieces together.

It works through propagation, meaning the ID is passed along. The first service to receive the request creates the trace ID. Every outgoing call, whether an HTTP request, a message put on a queue, or a call to another API, carries that ID in a header or message attribute. The receiving service reads the ID and records its spans under the same trace. No central database is needed; the ID travels with the request.

Worked example: a driver app calls a positions API, which calls a route service. The edge creates trace ID abc123 and a root span of 300 ms for the whole request. The positions API receives abc123, records a child span 'load cache' of 2 ms, then calls the route service with abc123 attached. The route service records its own child span 'compute route' of 265 ms under abc123. Reading the trace, you see that most of the 300 ms was spent in the route service, not in the positions API.

Common mistake: a service starts a fresh trace ID instead of reading the incoming one, or a background worker drops the header when it pulls a job from a queue. The result is a set of unrelated fragments, each looking healthy, and the slow hop disappears from view.

In a running system, a dropped ID means the on-call engineer must match timestamps across logs by hand, which is slow and error prone. Writing the trace ID into every log line lets you filter all logs to one request.

Keeping one trace ID across every hop is what turns separate service logs into one picture of one request.

questions.prompt: A shop app calls a payments service, which publishes an order message to a queue for a fulfilment worker. The app creates trace ID k7-410 with a root span of 480 ms. The payments service receives k7-410, records a child span 'charge card' of 120 ms, and publishes the order message with k7-410 attached as a message attribute. The fulfilment worker pulls the message from the queue. Missing step: what the worker does with the trace ID before it does any work. After that step, it records its child span 'reserve stock' of 35 ms under the same trace.
choices: It reads the trace ID from the message attribute and records its span under k7-410.
It sends its span ID back to the payments service, which stores the trace ID.
It creates a new trace ID for its work, so the stock span starts a separate trace.
It logs the order ID and later matches the stock span to the trace by timestamp.
questions.why: Propagation means the receiving service reads the incoming trace ID, here from the message attribute, so its spans join the same trace; the other choices either start a new trace or fall back to manual timestamp matching.

questions.prompt: Two spans recorded for one request have different span IDs. Which single identifier tells a tool that both spans belong to the same request?
choices: Their durations added together
The timestamp of the first log line
The trace ID carried by both
The span ID of the child span
questions.why: The trace ID is the one identifier shared by every span of the same request, while each span has its own span ID.

questions.prompt: A checkout request takes 900 ms end to end. Its trace shows a gateway root span of 900 ms, a cart span of 40 ms started by the gateway, and a pricing span of 810 ms started by the cart service. Which service should an engineer examine first?
choices: Gateway, since its root span covers the whole request time
None, because spans with different IDs cannot be compared
Cart, since it sits between the two others
Pricing, the largest single step
questions.why: Reading the span tree, the pricing span accounts for most of the time, so that hop is where the delay sits, and spans can be compared by their recorded durations within one trace.

questions.prompt: A background worker reads jobs from a queue, but its client library drops the trace header. Its errors show up in logs with no link to the web request that enqueued the job. What is the direct consequence for the trace?
choices: The queue deletes the worker's logs after processing them
The queue reorders the jobs and delays them
Its spans form a separate, unlinked trace
The web request waits until the worker finishes its job
questions.why: When the header is dropped, the worker starts or records under a different trace ID, so its spans become an unrelated fragment and the slow hop vanishes from the request's trace.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a trace ID helps you find the slow step across three services. Name one limit of this approach, such as what happens when a hop drops the ID or when sampling skips a request.
lessons.modelAnswer: A trace ID is generated when the request first enters the system and is attached to every outgoing call, so each service records its spans under the same ID. When a user reports slowness, I search all services for that ID and see the spans as a tree with timings, which shows which hop took the time. The limit is that the ID only works if every hop passes it along. If a service starts a new trace, or a queue consumer drops the header, the trace splits into fragments and the slow step vanishes. Also, many tracing systems sample only some requests to save cost, so the request you care about may not have been recorded at all. Checking that each service propagates the header, and logging the ID, prevents most of these gaps.
rubricPoints: A trace ID is shared by every span of one request, and spans form a parent-child tree.
The ID must be passed along with every outgoing call, including queue messages and background jobs.
Including the trace ID in log lines lets you filter all logs for one request.
A dropped ID or sampling can leave gaps, so the slow step may not appear.

suggested.rationale: Explaining how the ID travels and where it breaks is the core skill here, and no listed mission teaches distributed tracing directly.

lessons.plain: When a service misbehaves, you need to understand what it is doing from the records it leaves behind. AI-assisted observability means using an AI helper on top of those records. It can read a large pile of logs, summarize what went wrong, suggest a search to run, or propose a likely cause. Think of a colleague who reads very fast but sometimes guesses confidently. It saves time on the reading, but it does not replace checking the evidence yourself. The skill is knowing what to ask, what to verify, and when to distrust the answer.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your service's error rate doubled right after a deploy. Before using any tool, what would you check first, and why might a fast AI summary of the logs not be enough on its own?
lessons.teach: Observability is the ability to work out what a running system is doing from the evidence it produces. That evidence comes in three main forms. Logs are timestamped records of individual events. Metrics are numbers tracked over time, such as error counts or response latency. Traces follow one request through several services; each step along the way is a span, and a trace ID ties the spans of one request together. AI-assisted observability adds an AI helper that reads this evidence with you. You ask a question in plain language, and the helper may write a log query, summarize matching records, or propose a likely cause. It helps because it can scan far more lines than a person can in minutes and notice patterns. It does not know the truth about your system. It works only from the data it is given, and it can be confidently wrong. Worked example: error rates for a positions service jump at 09:02, two minutes after a deploy at 09:00. You ask the helper why requests are failing, and it replies that most failures are timeouts calling the database. Check it step by step. First, confirm the time window: does the spike begin right after the deploy? It does. Second, run the log query yourself for 08:55 to 09:15 and count the timeout messages; the count should match the summary. Third, open one failed trace ID and read its spans: the database span takes about thirty seconds while the others are short, which supports the suggestion. Fourth, compare the deploy's configuration with the database connection settings to test the proposed cause. Only when the evidence agrees do you act. Common mistake: treating the first fluent answer as the diagnosis, or pasting secrets or personal data into a prompt. Consequence: rolling back the wrong component extends the outage, and a pasted credential becomes a security incident. The assistant is a fast reader, but you remain responsible for the conclusion.

questions.prompt: A checkout API's 95th-percentile response time doubles at 14:07, five minutes after a configuration change at 14:02. An AI helper suggests the payment provider is slow. You check it step by step. Step 1: the slowdown begins after the change, so the time window fits. Step 2: you run your own log query for 13:55 to 14:15 and count the slow-request warnings, and the count matches the helper's summary. Step 3: you open one slow trace ID and read its spans: the fraud-scoring span takes about four seconds while the others are short. Step 4: ______. What completes the check before anyone acts?
choices: Accept the payment-provider diagnosis, because the helper's summary, the timing and the counts all agree with each other and three steps have already been checked
Paste the trace's API key into the helper so it can read the fraud-scoring settings and suggest a fix
Roll back the whole checkout service at once, since the helper and the spike point the same way and waiting only extends the slowdown
Compare the configuration change with the fraud-scoring client's timeout and retry settings to test whether the change explains that slow span
questions.why: The correct step tests the proposed cause against the deploy configuration, which is the evidence-based check the teaching text describes before acting, while the other choices either skip verification or expose a secret.

questions.prompt: In a trace for one order request, you see a list of timed records: inventory check, price lookup and receipt email, each with a start time and duration. What are these timed steps called, and what identifier ties them to the same request?
choices: Spans, linked by the trace ID
Metrics, tracked by the request count
Spans, linked by the deployment version
Logs, linked by the server timestamp
questions.why: Each timed step along one request is a span, and the trace ID is what groups the spans of that single request together.

questions.prompt: An AI helper tells a team that 412 requests failed in the last hour. Their own log query returns 37 timeout messages for the same window. What is the right next action?
choices: Accept the 412 figure, since the helper read more lines than a person could
Ask the helper to rewrite its summary in fewer words so the number is easier to trust
Roll back the service now, because the helper's higher count shows the outage is larger
Rerun the log query yourself, compare the counts, and treat the helper's summary as unverified until they agree
questions.why: The helper works only from the data it is given and can be confidently wrong, so the learner should verify its count against their own query before acting on it.

questions.prompt: You want an AI helper to explain why a customer's login is slow. Which piece of evidence is the safest to paste into the prompt?
choices: A customer's full name, email address and card number from the failed order
A redacted log line showing the timestamp and status code
The database password copied from the environment file, to give the helper context
The full service account key file, so the helper can check whether its permissions look wrong
questions.why: A redacted log line gives the useful timing and status evidence without exposing secrets or personal data, whereas pasting credentials or personal data into a prompt can create a security incident.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should let the AI assistant decide the root cause of tonight's error spike because it is faster. Explain to them how you would use an AI helper in observability, what it is good for, and one limit or risk you would guard against.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use the helper to speed up the reading: to turn a question into a log query, to summarize a few thousand error lines, or to suggest which trace to open. It is good at spotting patterns across large volumes of records. But it works only from the data it was given, so it can miss lines outside the time window or make a confident claim the evidence does not support. Before acting, I would rerun the query myself, check the time window against the deploy, and read a failing trace to see which step is slow. I would also keep secrets and personal data out of the prompt. The helper gives me a hypothesis, and I am still the one who confirms it and decides what to change.
rubricPoints: AI helper speeds up reading and querying logs, metrics, or traces
Its output is a hypothesis that must be checked against the raw evidence
Watch for limits such as incomplete data, wrong time windows, or confident errors
Do not share secrets or personal data in prompts; the engineer owns the conclusion

suggested.rationale: An exam-style incident where the learner must weigh an AI suggestion against logs and traces adds the most to this objective, and no listed mission already covers AI-assisted investigation.

scenarios.title: Ticket Release Burst at Harbor Lantern
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Lantern is a fictional company that sells tickets for local music festivals. Its engineering team is building a new order service that customers reach over HTTP, the standard request-and-response web protocol. The service is stateless, meaning it keeps no memory of a customer between requests, so any running copy of it can handle any request. Traffic stays quiet most of the year but jumps to about fifty times normal for a few minutes whenever a festival releases new tickets. The team has three decisions to make. 1. Choose the compute platform for the order API from Compute Engine (virtual machines you configure and maintain yourself), GKE (Google Kubernetes Engine, a managed Kubernetes cluster where you still manage nodes and cluster settings), and Cloud Run (a managed service that runs a packaged container image, scales the number of copies up and down with traffic, and can drop to zero copies when idle). Name your choice and explain why a near-miss option fits worse. 2. After an order is accepted, a payment confirmation step and an email step must run. The order API must answer the customer quickly, and no order may be lost if the email service is temporarily down. Choose between Pub/Sub (a managed message queue where a publisher posts a message to a topic and separate subscriptions each receive their own copy until acknowledged) and Cloud Tasks (a managed queue that dispatches individual task requests to one target endpoint with retry and rate controls), and justify the choice. 3. The database password must not be written into the container image or the source code. Choose the Google Cloud service that stores and versions the secret, name the identity (a service account, which is an identity used by software rather than a person) the service should run as, and explain how that identity is limited to only what it needs.
modelAnswer: Cloud Run. It runs the packaged container, scales copies out quickly during the burst and back toward zero afterwards, and removes the need to patch machines or manage cluster nodes. Compute Engine is a weaker fit because the team would have to build and maintain their own autoscaling group and machine images, which reacts more slowly and adds operational work. GKE could run the service, but it adds cluster-level management (node pools, upgrades, cluster networking) that a single stateless API does not need, so it is a near miss rather than the best answer.

Pub/Sub. The order API publishes a message to a topic and returns to the customer immediately. A payment subscription and an email subscription each receive their own copy, so the two consumers stay independent. Messages are retained until a subscriber acknowledges them, so if the email consumer is down the message waits instead of being lost. Cloud Tasks is the near miss: it is built to send each task to one target endpoint with retry and rate controls, not to fan one event out to two independent consumers. A consequence to note: if a handler fails to acknowledge, the message is delivered again, so both handlers must be idempotent, meaning running them twice with the same order produces no duplicate charge or duplicate email.

Secret Manager stores the database password as a versioned secret, so it can be rotated later without changing code. The Cloud Run service runs as a dedicated service account, and that account is granted a read-only access role on that one secret only. This follows least privilege, meaning the identity receives only the permissions its job requires. Near misses to reject: granting a broad project-wide editor role, or running the service under a personal user account. Cloud KMS is also related but is for managing encryption keys, not for storing the password itself.

scenarios.title: Order Intake Service Pre-Release Checks at Harbor Lane Goods
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Lane Goods is a fictional online retailer that sells kitchen equipment. Its engineering team is preparing a small Python service called order-intake. The service receives new orders, saves each one to a Firestore database (a managed NoSQL document database), and publishes a message to a Pub/Sub topic (a managed message queue that other services read from). A new developer, Priya, joined two weeks ago and has been asked to help get the service ready for its next release. She works in an editor (an IDE, or integrated development environment, where code is written) that has the Google Cloud SDK, which is the gcloud command-line tool, and an AI coding assistant, which is a tool that suggests code from a written request and is meant to be reviewed by a human before it is used. Her team lead, Marcus, sets three tasks. Priya must complete each one and explain her choices. 1. Marcus wants unit tests for the order-intake code that can run on a laptop with no connection to the real Google Cloud project. Name the gcloud approach that lets the code talk to a local stand-in for Firestore and Pub/Sub, explain what a unit test is, and describe how she would point the code at the stand-in during the test run. 2. Priya wants to use the AI coding assistant to draft the unit tests. Explain where the assistant fits in this work, what she must check before accepting its output, and why it should not be the final judge of whether the tests are correct. 3. Marcus wants every merge to run the full integration test suite (tests that check the service working with the real cloud services in a test project) in Cloud Build (Google Cloud's managed build and automation service), and the built container image should be stored in Artifact Registry (a private storage place for container images). Describe the build configuration Priya should set up so that a failing integration test stops the build and the image is only pushed when all tests pass.
subParts: Local emulator approach and unit test setup
Proper use of the AI coding assistant
Cloud Build integration tests and Artifact Registry storage
modelAnswer: A unit test is a small automated check that exercises one piece of code in isolation, so that a failure points to that piece and not to some outside system. To keep the tests on a laptop with no internet connection to the real project, Priya should use the Google Cloud emulators that the gcloud CLI can start locally. An emulator is a program that imitates the behaviour of a cloud service on the developer's own machine. For this service she would start the Pub/Sub emulator and the Firestore emulator with gcloud beta emulators commands, which launch each one on a local port. She then runs the env-init or equivalent step that prints the environment variables for that emulator, such as the Pub/Sub emulator host setting, and exports them in her shell or test runner. The Google client libraries read these variables and send their requests to localhost instead of the live service. The common mistake is forgetting to set the variables, so the tests quietly reach for the real project or fail with a confusing connection error. Consequence: if the tests run against a live project by accident, they can write fake orders into real data and slow the team down, which is why the test setup should fail loudly when the emulator variable is missing.

The AI coding assistant is meant to help draft code, such as test functions, fixtures (reusable test setup code), and suggestions for edge cases, from a plain-language request in the editor. Priya should treat its output as a first draft. Before accepting it she must read every line, confirm the test imports and calls match the real library version the project uses, make sure no real project ID or credentials were typed into the code, and run the tests to see that they actually pass for the right reason. She should also check that each test has a clear expected result and would fail if the behaviour broke. The assistant should not be the final judge because it can produce tests that look plausible but assert the wrong thing, or that pass even when the code is broken. A human reviewer and the running test results are the real check. Consequence: a test that always passes gives the team false confidence, and the bug reaches customers after release.

Priya should write a cloudbuild.yaml file in the repository that defines ordered steps. The first step runs the unit tests against the emulators. A later step starts the integration tests against a dedicated test project, using a service account (a non-human identity with limited permissions) that has only the roles those tests need. A build step fails when its command exits with an error, and Cloud Build stops the remaining steps when one fails, so the image step that comes after the tests will not run if a test fails. Only after the tests pass should a step build the container image from the source, and a final step push it to an Artifact Registry repository, where it can be stored under a tag and later checked by other tools. Common mistake: placing the push step before the tests, or running the integration tests with `|| true` so errors are ignored. Consequence: a broken image would be stored and could be deployed, and the build would show green even though the checks failed, so the team would ship a regression they believed had been tested.

scenarios.title: Tidewater Parcel Co. order-tracking launch
scenarios.scenario: Tidewater Parcel Co. is a fictional courier firm. Its new order-tracking team is moving two services into production. The first is a small Python service that records parcel scans. Cloud Run is Google Cloud's managed service for running containers without managing servers, and it can scale down to zero instances when nothing is calling it. The team wants to deploy this service straight from its source folder, without writing a container image definition by hand. The second is a checkout component that will run on GKE (Google Kubernetes Engine), which is Google's managed Kubernetes service. Kubernetes runs containers in small groups called Pods, and it can restart or replace them automatically. The team has seen Pods that hang without crashing, and it expects traffic spikes at lunchtime. Your task is to answer three questions from the team lead, in your own words. 1. Describe how the scan service is deployed to Cloud Run from source, what Google Cloud does with the source to make it runnable, and one thing the code must do to receive traffic correctly. 2. The team wants each new message published to a Pub/Sub topic (a managed message queue where publishers write messages and subscribers read them) to invoke the scan service automatically. Explain how Eventarc (a Google Cloud service that routes events from sources such as Pub/Sub to a target service) is configured to deliver these events, and what permission the trigger's identity needs. 3. For the GKE checkout Deployment, explain which health check restarts a hung container and which health check removes an unready Pod from receiving traffic, and name the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (a Kubernetes component that changes the number of Pod replicas based on metrics) settings that set the minimum and maximum replica counts and that control how quickly it scales up or down.
subParts: Deploy from source to Cloud Run and listening correctly
Eventarc trigger from Pub/Sub to Cloud Run and invoker permission
GKE liveness versus readiness probes and Horizontal Pod Autoscaler settings
modelAnswer: Deploying from source means pointing the Cloud Run deploy command at the source folder instead of a prebuilt image. Google Cloud uses buildpacks, which are automated build tools that inspect the language of the source, install dependencies, and package the result into a container image stored in Artifact Registry. Cloud Run then runs that image as a service. The code must listen for HTTP requests on the address 0.0.0.0 and on the port given by the PORT environment variable, which Cloud Run sets (commonly 8080). If the app hard-codes another port, requests never reach it and the revision fails to start.

Eventarc is the event routing layer. You create a trigger that names the event source, here the Pub/Sub topic, and the destination, here the scan Cloud Run service. Eventarc then delivers each event to the service as an HTTP request, so the service does not need to poll the topic. The trigger runs under a service account (a non-human Google identity that software uses). That identity must be granted permission to invoke the Cloud Run service, typically the Cloud Run Invoker role. Without it, deliveries are rejected with an authorization error even though the trigger itself exists. A common mistake is creating the trigger but forgetting this invoker grant, so events are silently refused and the team sees no scans processed.

A liveness probe is a check Kubernetes runs against a container; if it keeps failing, the kubelet (the node agent that manages Pods) restarts that container. This is the right check for a hung process that never exits. A readiness probe decides whether a Pod should receive traffic; if it fails, the Pod is removed from the Service's endpoints but is not restarted. This is the right check for a Pod that is alive but not yet able to serve, such as while it warms a cache. Confusing them is a common mistake: a readiness check that is too strict can keep healthy Pods out of service, while a liveness check that is too aggressive can restart a slow but working container in a loop. For scaling, the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler reads minReplicas and maxReplicas to set the floor and ceiling on Pod count, a metrics target (such as average CPU utilization) to decide how many replicas are needed, and a behavior section that controls how quickly it scales up or down, including stabilization windows that prevent rapid oscillation during short spikes.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Parcels: Making Google Cloud Calls Efficient and Reliable
scenarios.scenario: Brightwater Parcels is a fictional delivery company with a small internal web app that its support staff use. The app runs on Cloud Run, which is Google's managed service for running containers without managing servers. Shipment records live in Firestore, a managed document database, and shipment label files live in Cloud Storage, a managed object store for files. The team's developer, Priya, is new to cloud work and has four problems to solve. First, the support dashboard asks Cloud Storage to list every label file in one request, and for a busy month that is over 40,000 objects, so the page times out. Pagination means splitting a long result into pages and asking for one page at a time, using a token that marks where the last page ended. Restricting returned data means asking only for the fields you actually display. Second, a nightly job must mark 5,000 shipments as 'scanned' in Firestore, and it currently sends 5,000 separate write calls. Those calls hit a per-minute quota, which is a cap on how many requests a project may make in a time window, and some calls fail with the error code 429, meaning too many requests. Batching means grouping many operations into one request. Exponential backoff means waiting progressively longer between retries of a failed call, usually doubling the wait each time and adding some random jitter, and it should be used only for errors that may succeed later. Third, the app looks up each parcel's delivery zone from a reference table that changes about once a day, yet it queries that table on every page view. Caching means keeping a copy of a result for a set time, called a time to live (TTL), so repeated lookups do not call the service again. Fourth, the Cloud Run service must read label files from Cloud Storage. Someone suggests putting a developer's personal Google account key into the container. A service account is a non-human identity that an application uses to call Google Cloud APIs, and it should be granted only the roles it needs. Priya must answer these questions: 1. Which two techniques should she apply to the dashboard listing, and why? 2. How should she change the nightly job, and how should retries work? 3. What should she cache, and what TTL is sensible? 4. Which identity should the Cloud Run service use to read label files, and what is the risk of the personal-key idea?
subParts: Dashboard listing: pagination and restricted fields
Nightly job: batching writes and exponential backoff on retryable errors
Zone lookup: caching with a TTL
Cloud Run access: service account with least privilege instead of a personal key
modelAnswer: Use pagination so the app requests one page of results at a time (for example, a fixed page size with a next-page token) instead of one huge list that times out. Also restrict returned data by requesting only the fields the dashboard shows, such as file name and date, so each response is smaller and faster. Both reduce the work per call; neither changes which files exist.

Batch the 5,000 updates into groups of operations sent in single requests, so the job makes far fewer calls and stays under the per-minute quota. For failures with error 429 or temporary server errors (5xx), retry with exponential backoff: wait a short time, then double the wait on each retry, add a little random jitter, and stop after a maximum number of attempts. Do not retry errors that will never succeed, such as a permission error, because retrying them only wastes quota and time.

Cache the zone reference table in the app's memory or a shared cache, keyed by parcel zone code, with a TTL of about a few hours or until the next daily refresh. Repeated page views then read the cached copy instead of calling the service. The trade-off is that a change may take up to one TTL period to appear, which is acceptable for a table that changes once a day.

Give the Cloud Run service its own service account and grant it only a role that allows reading objects in the label bucket, such as a Storage object viewer role on that bucket. Google Cloud then attaches the identity automatically at runtime, so no key file is needed. Putting a personal account key in the container is risky because the key is a long-lived secret that can leak with the image, it is tied to a human who may leave, and it grants that person's broader access rather than the minimum the app needs.
